en: Moggallāna-vuttivivaraṇapañcikā.
Together with the Vutti.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Having paid homage to the Tathāgata, who possesses the virtues of true Dhamma and freedom from sloth, and to the true Dhamma and Saṅgha, I shall speak of the characteristics of the Magadha language.
The forty-three syllables, beginning with *a* and ending with the nasalized (*niggahīta*) consonants, are called "phonemes" (*vaṇṇā*): *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *ka*.
kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ;
by this, what is the purpose of the statement “ñonama vaṇṇe”? The expression “thirty-four” (tittālīsa) indicates the elision of a phoneme in certain instances;
by this, forms such as *paṭisaṅkhāyoni so* are established.
Regarding vowels (*sarā*):
Among those, the first ten letters are called vowels (*sara*). What is the purpose of that [definition]? [It is for rules] such as "there is elision of a vowel before a vowel" (*saro lopo sare*).
Two by two, they are of the same class (*savaṇṇā*).
Among those [vowels], each pair is called "homogeneous" (*savaṇṇa*); what is the purpose of the phrase "also homogeneous when followed by a consonant"?
"The preceding is short.

Among those two pairs, whichever is the preceding one is designated as "short" (*rassa*). Among them, *e* and *o* are seen only before a conjunct consonant; what is the purpose of the phrase "the short indeed," etc.?

"Whatever follows those two [vowels] is designated as long (dīgha); what is the use of that? [It is used] for the elision of *y* and for [the application of] the rule 'a long vowel' (*kvayolopanisu dīgho*)," and so forth.
"The consonants beginning with *ka* are *byañjana*."

The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with the *niggahīta* (the nasal stop) are designated as *byañjana* (consonant); what is the purpose of this? [It is for rules] such as: "In the case of a consonant, long and short [vowels are treated as single syllables].
There are five groups (*vaggā*), each consisting of five [consonants].
The five sets beginning with *ka* are called the five groups; what is the purpose of this? [It is for rules] such as: "In a group, the final [consonant of that group... and so forth.
The *bindu* is the *niggahīta*.

That which, among the phonemes (*vaṇṇa*), consists merely of a dot (*bindu-matta*) is designated by the technical term *niggahīta*. What is the purpose of this? [It is for the rule] beginning with "the *niggahīta*," etc.; the creation of this designation of heaviness (*garu-saññā*) is for the sake of a designation that corresponds to its actual meaning (*anvattha-saññattha*).
The vowels *i* and *u*, along with *jjhalā*, are [heavy] when they stand at the end of a noun (*nāmanta*).

In a nominal stem (*nāma*), the vowels *i* and *u* occurring at the end are designated as *jhal*, according to their respective order; what is the use of that? [It is for the rule] "after *jhal*, *ve*" (Cādi).

In the feminine (*itthiyaṃ*)—the vowels *i* and *u* occurring at the end of a nominal stem occurring in the feminine are designated as *pas*; what is the use of that? [It is for the rule] "after *ya*, *pa* replaces the vowel" (Ye passivaṇṇassa), etc.
Ghā—The vowel *ā* occurring at the end of a noun (*nāma*) that is currently in the feminine gender becomes the substitute *gha*; what is the purpose of this? [It is for] "ghabrahmādite" and so forth.
Cādi. Gosyālapane—

In the context of address (*ālapana*), *ga* is designated as a technical term (*saññā*); what is the purpose of that [designation] in [the rule] "ge ve" (Pāṇini 6.1.69) and so forth? This concludes the section on technical designations (*saññā-adhikāra*). [Now follows: "A grammatical operation (*vidhi*) applies to that which ends in a specific qualifier (*visesananta*)."

The grammatical operation (*vidhi*) should be understood as applying to that which ends with the specified [element]: *“ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe”* (from *nara*, the forms *nara* and *nare*). Regarding the locative case (*sattamī*):

in the description of the locative, the operation should be understood as belonging only to the preceding [element]: *“saro lopo sare”* (a vowel is elided before a vowel). Why is it not the case here that *tam* (that) destroys *veḷaggaṃ*? Because in that context, the vowel is called the proximate substratum (*upasilesikādhāra*), and it is taught that the operation belongs only to the preceding [element], not to the subsequent one.
Regarding "of another" (*parassa*) in the fifth [case]:

in the exposition of the fifth case, it should be understood that the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) applies to another. For example: *ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe* (Pāṇini 7.1.2). Thus, *narā nare*; here it does not apply in the case of *jantuyo anantā*. Why does it not apply here? Because the operation applies to what is immediately following (*anantare*), and there is no operation for what is separated by an intervening element (*vyavahitassa*), as the purpose has already been fulfilled in the immediate proximity. Regarding "of the first" (*ādissa*).
The grammatical operation (*kāriya*) to be understood for a following vowel (*vaṇṇa*) that is being taught should be known as "counted by *r*.

For example, in *rājinā*. "Of that which is indicated by the genitive": the grammatical operation taught [in a rule] with the genitive case should be understood as applying to the final vowel (*anta-vaṇṇa*) [of the word]. For example, in *rājassi nāmhi*. *Rājinā*.
*Ṅ-anubandho*:

That which has the letter *ṅ* as its *anubandha* (suffix) becomes final. [Example: “*gossāvaṅi*”. *Gavāssaṃ*. *T-anubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassa*: [A suffix] consisting of more than one syllable that has *t* as its *anubandha* replaces the whole [of the preceding word].
That which has the letter *ṭ* as its *anubandha* is a multi-syllabic substitute for the whole [word]. [In the rule] “*imassānitthiyaṃ ṭe*,” [the word] *esu* [is used];
[in the rule] “*nāmhanimi*. By this [rule].

Those beginning and ending with a letter having *ñ* or *ā* as their *anubandha* [are substitutes] for that which is indicated by the genitive case. [In the rule] “*bruto tissīña*,” [the word] *bravīti* [is used]; [in the rule] “*bhussa vuka*,” [the word] *babhuva*.
The letter *m* is the suffix (*anubandha*) for those [roots] ending in vowels, followed by a vowel.

That which has *m* as its suffix is followed by a vowel; thus, for the roots *rudh* and others, it is stated: "and *mañ*. [Example: *rundhati*. [The particle] *va* is used in the sense of negation (*vippaṭisedhe*).
In the case of two or three persons acting together: "the other goes, you go, you both go"; "he goes, you go, and I go, we go.

A convention (*saṅketa*) that is indivisible (*anavayava*) is to be known as a suffix (*anubandha*); this applies to *la*, *tu*, *pi*, etc., when followed by *asi*. [The term] *kattā* [is used here]; the inclusion of the word "convention" (*saṅketaggahaṇaṃ*) [is for the purpose of excluding cases where the suffixes are not conventional].
What [is the purpose]? It is so that the entire complex beginning with *pakati* does not become a *anubandha*. For a complex is without parts precisely because it is a complex;

why, then, would there be a mention of "without parts"? [The answer is: "By this [rule], *janena*. Since the elision (*lopa*) is already understood by this very [rule], the statement was not undertaken for the sake of the elision of an *anubandha*. Also, by the rule "a similar vowel (*savaṇṇo*) following a phoneme (*vaṇṇa-")... [the elision follows].

Because the word *vaṇṇa* follows, even a similar vowel (*savaṇṇa*) is included, as in *saṃva rūpaṃ*; [this is because] "another [vowel] replaces the semi-vowels (*yuvaṇṇa*). In *vāteritaṃ*, [the suffix] *sam* is elided.
Regarding *ntu*, *vantu*, *manatvā*, *vantu*, *tavantu*, and *sambandhi*:

only that which is related to *vantu* and so forth is understood as *ntu*, according to the rule: "The *nto* of *ntu* and *tantu* is [retained] when *yo* follows in the nominative. Thus, *guṇavanto*. Why say "related to *vantu* and so forth"? [Consider] *jantu* and *tantu*.
Paribhāsās: "Saro lopo sare" (A vowel is elided before a vowel).
Before a vowel, a vowel is to be elided. Here are examples: *saddhindriyaṃ*, *no hetaṃ*, *bhikkhunovādo*, *sametāyasmā*, *abhibhāyatanaṃ*, *puttā matthi*, *asantettha*.

In some instances, elision (*lopanīya*) occurs; that too, as before, only when the preceding and following vowels are identical. What does "in some instances" mean? This heading [of the rule] applies up to the end of the section on *pariccheda*; therefore, there is no over-extension of the rule. "Or both":
in some instances, both the preceding and following vowels are not elided; for example, *latā iva* becomes *lateva*, which further becomes *latāva*.

When a vowel is elided, the following *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels optionally become *ñ* [nasalized], respectively: *tassedaṃ*, *vāteritaṃ*, *nopeti*, *vāmoru*, *ateva’ññe*, *vodakaṃ*. How is it that *paccorasmaṃ* occurs?
[It is so] because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*); [thus] *tassidaṃ* [is established] as "only when there is *vā*" (*vātveva*).
What is elided? [The vowels *i* and *u*,] as in "like a creeper" (*latā iva*).

When a vowel follows, the vowels *i* and *u* become *y* and *v* respectively: *vyākato*, *iccassa*, *ajjhiṇamutto*, *svāgataṃ*, *bhavāpanalānīlaṃ*; *vāttheva-itissa*; and in some cases, even when *i* follows, as in *itthiyānīdha* and *sūpaṭṭhitaṃ*.

Ñoṇaṃ—Ñoṇaṃ occurs before *yava*, *honti*, or vowels, according to the sequence: *tyajja*, *te’jja*, *svāhaṃ*, *so’haṃ*, *kvacitveva*—the *putta* suffix exists here even when [the preceding vowel] is absent.
Gossāvaṅi.
In the case of *sare* (vowels), it becomes *avaṅ*; as in *gavāssaṃ*. *Yathariva* and *tathariva* are merely particles (*nipātā*); in *bhusāmiva*, the word *iva* has the sense of *eva* (just/only).
Regarding the rule "long and short [vowels] before a consonant":
in certain instances, long and short vowels become long and short respectively before a consonant; examples of this are: *munīvare*, *sammadeva*, and *mālahārī*.
After a vowel, there are sometimes two forms of another consonant: [the first is] *paggaha*. Regarding "after a vowel"—why [is this said]? [Example: *taṃkhaṇaṃ*.
This [occurrence] applies only to the fourth and second [consonants], not to the third and first.

In the case of the fourth and second [vowels], when followed by other fourth and second vowels within the same group, they become the third and first [vowels] respectively due to proximity (*paccāsatti*): *mahaddhano*, *yasa thero*, *apphuṭaṃ*, *abbhuggato*. In the examples *eso* and *iti*, what is the word? *Thero*. In the examples *esaṃ* and *iti*, what is the word? *Pattho*. Regarding the rule *vitisseve vā*:
when the word *eva* follows, the substitution of *vo* for *itissa* occurs optionally: *ittheva* or *icceva*. In the example *eva*, what is the word? *Iccāha*.

In the case of *vaṇṇe*, *ñonaṃ* sometimes becomes *a*; as in: "having seen a beggar arrive," "akarambhasate," "esa attho," "esa dhammo," "maggo aggamakkhāyati," "svāyatanaṃ," "hiyyattanaṃ," and "karassu";
[it is said] "vātveva" when a beggar has arrived—this is the meaning.
The word *dhammo*; what does it praise? It praises *so*.
Regarding the *niggahīta*:
the *niggahīta* sometimes becomes a substitute (*āgama*); for example, *cakkhuṃ udapādi* becomes *cakkhu udapādi*, and *purimañjāti* becomes *purimajāti*.

Much wholesome [deed] is to be done. In cases such as *avaṃ siro*, because the rule is permanently established as an alternative (*vibhāsā*) within its governing scope (*adhikāra*), it follows by implication (*sāmatthiyena*);
and that [substitution] occurs only for a short vowel (*rassa*), because it is accompanied by a short vowel. [The following is] elision (*lopa*).

The elision of *niggahīta* occurs optionally in some instances; for example, *kyāhaṃ*, *kīmahaṃ*, *sā ratto*, *saṃratto*. However, in cases such as *sallekho*, *gattukāmo*, and *gantumano*, it occurs invariably.
Regarding *para-sara*:
the elision of the following *sara* (vowel) after a *niggahīta* occurs optionally in some instances; for example, *tvaṃsi* or *tvamasi*.

Regarding a nasal (niggahīta) before a group of consonants (vagga): when a nasal occurs before a group of consonants, it becomes either the final letter of that same group [according to the teacher]; for example:
*taṅkaroti* becomes *taṃ karoti*, *tañcarati* becomes *taṃ carati*, *taṇṭhānaṃ* becomes *taṃ ṭhānaṃ*, *tandhanaṃ* becomes *taṃ dhanaṃ*, *tampāti* becomes *taṃ pāti*; this is constant.
In the middle of a word, after having gone [to that position], it remains even elsewhere.
Regarding *ye* and *va*:
in the presence of the sounds *ye* and *va*, the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) optionally becomes *ñ*. Examples: *yayaññadeva*, *taññeva*, *tañbhi*; *vātveva-yaṃyadeva*.
In the case of *saṃ* and *saṃsadda*, the *niggahīta* becomes *ña* before the letter *ya*; thus, *saññamo* and *saṃyamo*.
[The suffix] *maya* occurs before a vowel.
The *mayada* [substitutes] for *niggahīta* occur optionally before a vowel in certain instances: *tam ahaṃ*, *tayidaṃ*, *tad alaṃ*;
and *vā tu eva taṃ ahaṃ*.
There are also *āgamas* [augmentations] such as *vanataragā*. These *mayadas* and *āgamas* occur optionally before a vowel in certain instances: *tivaṅgīkaṃ*, *ito nāyati*, *cinitvā*, *tasmātiha*.
"Devoid of essence," they say, "this is indeed distinct from one's own welfare; let there be rather one's own welfare.
In the phrase "it is indeed too early," it is the word *paga* itself that is the first member [of the compound]. *Chā ḷo-* [is the grammatical rule].
The letter *ḷ* is optionally an augment (*āgama*) for the vowel following the word *cha*. Examples: *chaḷahaṃ*, *chaḷāyatanaṃ*; however, it is not so in *cha abhiññā*.
Regarding *tadaminādīni*: are words such as *tadamina* correct? *Tadaminā* means "by that [person]"; *sakadāgāmī* means "one who comes once more"; *ekaṃ idha*... [and so forth].

I am one here alone (*ekam-idāham*); arranging and carrying away is *saṃvid-āvahāro*; carrying water is *vāriṇo vāhako*, hence *valāhako* (cloud); bound up with life is *jīvanassa mūto*, hence *jīmūto* (cloud);

a bed for the skin is *chavassa sayanaṃ*, hence *susānaṃ* (cemetery); above the sky is *uddhaṃ khamassa*, hence *udukkhalaṃ* (mortar); he crushes (*pisi*) and devours (*tāso*), hence *pisāco* (goblin);
he cries in the earth (*mahiyam*), hence *mayūro* (peacock). In this way, other applications should also be understood; furthermore, forms such as *pisodara* and others are to be seen among others.

For the *tavagga* (t, th, d, dh, n) and *varaṇa* (p, ph, b, bh, m) consonants, the *cavagga* (c, ch, j, jh, ñ) and *bayañña* (y, r, l, v, m) consonants are substituted respectively when followed by the letter *ya*;

as in *apūccaṇḍakāyaṃ*, *tacchaṃ*, *yajjevaṃ*, *ajjhattaṃ*, *thañaññaṃ*, *dibbaṃ*, *payyesanā*, *pokkharañño*; and in some cases, even after *itthi* and *eva*. These [substitutions] occur following a *vagga* or a *lasa* (liquid) consonant.

In some cases, the gutturals and palatals (*vaggalasa*) of another [word] become gutturals and palatals [before a following consonant]; as in *sakkate*, *paccate*, *aṭṭate*, *kuppate*, *phallate*, *assate*. However, in some instances, it is simply *kyāhaṃ*.
There is a substitution of *ha* for *ya*:
there is a substitution of *ha* for the letter *ya*; as in *guyhaṃ*.
There is the perversion of *ha* into *va*; thus, *bahv-ābādho* becomes *bahv-ābādho*.
Likewise, for *ta*, *tha*, *na*, and *ra*, there are *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, and *la*.

For *tatha* and *nara*, there may be *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, or *la*; [the following apply]: *dukkaṭaṃ*, *aṭṭhakathā*, *gahaṇaṃ*, *paligho*, *palāyati*, and *vātveva*—in these cases there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);

in some instances, however, it is well-spoken (*sugata*). Regarding the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*): in certain cases, there is an elision of that constituent which is the initial part of a conjunct consonant; for example: *pupphaṃsā* and *jāyate’gini*.
Regarding the two types of distributive repetition (*vīcchābhikkhañña*):

in the case of distributive repetition (*vīcchāyamābhikkhaññe*), there are two forms for that which occurs. *Vīcchā* is the incorrect [repetition] applied when the meaning is pervaded by an action, a quality, or a substance;
as in: "he waters tree after tree" (*rukkhaṃrukkhaṃ siñcati*) or "every village is delightful" (*gāmogāmo ramaṇīyo*).
In every village there is water; in every house there is a master; he eats flavor upon flavor;
he is worthy of action after action. Even in a sequence (*ānupubbi*), there is desire: it is coarse at the root and fine at the tip.
For if there were no distinction between root and tip here, there would be no sequence either. (Insert each elder one after another) penny by penny.
"Give two [coins] to you both from this kahāpaṇa"—from this, a distributive sense (*vīcchā*) is understood as "one māsaka each.

However, by means of another word, there is a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) expressed as "from this kahāpaṇa. In the cases "they flower one by one" (*pubbaṃ pubbaṃ pupphanti*) and "they ripen one by one" (*paṭhamaṃ paṭhamaṃ paccanti*), it is a distributive sense.
Regarding the statement "these two halves—of these two, which is the half of which?"—it refers to all of them.
These are "repeatedly" (*aḍḍha*); what is the repetition among these? Here too it is just like desire (*icchā*):
repeatedly, again and again, merit, he cooks, he cooks, he broils, he broils; having cut, having cut, he cuts; having eaten, having eaten, he goes;
he makes a clattering sound, it makes a clattering sound.
The elision of *sy-*, etc., occurs before a single preceding [vowel].

When there is a doubling of a single vowel, the elision of *sy-* and so forth occurs before the preceding [vowel]; for example, in *ekeka-ssa*. How is it in the case of *matthakam-atthakena*? It is because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating "the elision of *sy-* and so forth occurs before the preceding [vowel]"; and by means of this division of the rule, there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), as the desired result is established. [This applies] to words beginning with *sabba-* when used in the sense of exchange (*vītihāra*).

In the case of *sabbādi* and other such words, when used in the sense of "exchange" (*vītihāra*), two forms occur: there is the elision of the preceding [particle], as in *syādi-lopa*; they are mutual reciprocators (*aññamaññassa bhojakā*), meaning they are reciprocators with one another (*itarītarassa bhojakā*).
Up to the point of awakening (*yāva bodhaṃ*) is "confusion" (*sambhama*).
Confusion is the indication of a word that is a cause for haste; when that exists, the meaning is expressed by as many sounds as are present here.
So many sounds as are employed are indeed cognized: "snake, snake, snake," "awake, awake, awake," "the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split.
[This applies] frequently.
This governing rule (adhikāra) extends until the end of the section on *āsatta* (proximate connection); therefore, there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), and the desired result is established.
Thus ends the first section (*kaṇḍa*) in the Moggallāna-vyākaraṇa.

[The suffixes] *si*, *yo*, *aṃ*, *yo*, *nā*, *abhisanaṃ*, *smā*, *hisanaṃ*, *smiṃ*, and *su* occur after a noun (*nāma*) when two [words] are in apposition, or when one or many [words] are in apposition.
From these nouns, there are two forms each when occurring in the singular and plural senses:
*muni*, *munayo*; *muniṃ*, *munayo*; *muninā*, *munīhi*; *munissa*, *munīnaṃ*; *munismā*, *munīhi*; *munissa*, *munīnaṃ*; *munismiṃ*, *munīsu*.
Likewise, *kumārī*, *kumāriyo*; *kaññā*, *kaññāyo*. These seven pairs constitute the seven case endings (*vibhattiyo*); this is the analysis (*vibhāgo*).
Regarding the term *vibhatti* (case ending): here, by the rule *kimaṃsisū*, the forms *si* and *am* include the vowel *i*. These are for the purpose of technical convention (*saṅketa*).

The second case (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object (*karman*). That which is performed—that is, that which is connected with the action of the agent—is the object; in that [object], the second case ending occurs; e.g., *kaṭam* (the mat).
In expressions such as “he cooks rice,” “rice is being cooked,” “he sees the sun,” and “rice is cooking,” the status of the object (*kamma*) is not understood from the word "rice" (*odana*);

rather, it is understood from the verb (*ākhyāta*). In the expression “he makes a large, beautiful mat” (*kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ dassanīyaṃ*), the status of the object indeed exists for that which is connected with a quality (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, the dative case is established even in the sense of what is desired, as in the status of the object: “he milks the cow for milk” (*gāvuṃ payo dohati*), “he buys a cow for a herd of cows” (*gomantaṃ gāvaṃ yāvati*), and “he restrains the cow” (*gavamavarundhati*).
He asks the boy for a path; he begs for a cow from one who has cattle; he gathers fruits from a tree; he speaks the Dhamma to his pupil;
he instructs his pupil in the Dhamma. Thus it is also in the case of what is not desired:
he leaps over a snake; he eats poison. That which is neither desired nor undesired: [he eats] the sacrificial offering (yañña).

In this case as well, the second [case] is established: one going to the village approaches the foot of a tree, he will lie down upon the earth, he stands over the village, he sits upon the tree—thus, in the usage of the verbs *adhiśī* (lie upon), *adhisthā* (stand upon), and *adhyās* (sit upon), there is a desire for the object to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

For grammatical relations arise from the speaker's intention; as for example: "The lightning flashes from the cloud," "The lightning flashes on the cloud," "The cloud flashes," "The lightning flashes in the cloud," or "The lightning flashes by means of the cloud."

Likewise for one who has entered upon [a state], such as "he enters upon the Dhamma" (*dhammam abhinivisate*) or "he enters upon the Dhamma" (*dhamme abhinivisate*); similarly for one who dwells near, as in "he dwells near a meal" (*abhojana-nivuttim āvasantassa*). Examples include:

"he dwells near a village" (*gāmam upavasati*), "he dwells in a village" (*gāmaṃ anuvasati*), "he dwells on a mountain" (*pabbataṃ adhivasati*), and "he dwells in a house" (*gharaṃ āvasati*). Regarding the phrase "of one whose speech concerns the cessation of eating" (*abhojana-nivutti-vacanassa*):

what does it mean? "He dwells near the village" (*gāme upavasati*) means he effects the cessation of eating. Even in the case of "conducting oneself by that" (*tappānācāre*), it is because it is a verbal action (*kamma*).
The second case (accusative) is established [in the sense of] "she crosses the river," "she wanders through the village"; likewise in cases such as "if she does not speak to me.
In the case of a prefix (*paṭi*), the second case is indeed prescribed: *paṭibhantu taṃ cunda bojjhaṅgā* means "let the factors of enlightenment respond to him" (*taṃ paṭi bojjhaṅgā bhāsantu*).
However, when *pati* is joined with a verbal root (*dhātu*), because it is not connected with that [noun], the sixth case (genitive) is used for the relationship, and *tassa nappaṭi* [is the result].

Regarding "it shines" (*bhāti*): there is a desire for the expression of the object, the instrument, and the locus, as in "one plays with dice," "one plays by means of dice," or "one plays upon the dice.
Regarding time and distance:
when there is a connection of time and distance with an action, a quality, or a substance in its entirety, that is "absolute connection" (*accantasaṃyoga*); when that is understood—
The second case ending occurs after words denoting time (*kāla*) and distance (*addhā*); for example: *māsam adhīte*, *māsaṃ kalyāṇi*.
*Māsaṃ guḷadhānā*, *kosaṃ adhīte*, *kosaṃ kuṭilā nadī*, *kosaṃ pabbato*. Why is it said "in the sense of absolute connection" (*accantasamyoge*)?
[Because in the following cases it does not apply: *māsassa dvīham adhīte*; *kosasseka dese pabbato*; *pubbanhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā*; *ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā*; *imaṃ rattiṃ*.

In such cases as "the four great kings" (*cattāro mahārājā*), the accusative case is established because of absolute connection with words denoting time. Alternatively, it is established through the transposition of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*), since [such usage] is frequently prescribed.

In the attainment of the fruit, there is the completion of the action; when that is understood, the third case is intended for the duration of time (*kāla*) and distance (*addhāna*) in absolute connection with an action.
That too is established simply as the instrument (*karaṇa*): "The recitation was completed in a month" (*māsena anuvāko adhīto*), "The recitation was completed in a *kosa*" (*kosena anuvāko adhīto*).

Because it does not bring about liberation and lacks the status of being the most effective instrument (*asādhakatama*), the instrumental case (*karaṇa*) is absent; thus, only the accusative occurs: "He has studied the *anuvāka* for a month," and it is not by means of this [month] that he has grasped it.

Among the factors of action (*kāraka*), those which express time and distance are intended to take the locative and ablative cases: "Having eaten today, Devadatta will eat in two days" (*dvīhe*) or "in two days" (*dvīhā*).
In this context, the arrow hits the target in the treasury (*kosā*); here, the locative case is used.
The statement "he pierces the target" (*lakkhaṃ vijjhati*) is thus established solely by the speaker's own intention regarding the words expressing the respective actions.

[This applies] when employing verbs such as those meaning motion (*gati*), cognition (*bodha*), eating (*āhāra*), sound (*sadda*), intransitives (*akammaka*), and those beginning with *bhajja* (to fry).
[That is to say, it applies] when employing verbs whose meanings are motion, cognition, eating, or sound, as well as intransitive verbs and those beginning with *bhajja*.
The accusative case occurs after a verb of cutting (*kattari*);
and it is understood that through its capacity and by means of the activity of the instigator (*payojaka*), the objecthood (*kammatā*) of this [object] arises.
Examples: *gamaṃ gameti māṇavakaṃ*, *gāmaṃ yāpeti māṇavakaṃ*, *dhammaṃ bodheti māṇavakaṃ*, *dhammaṃ vedeti māṇavakaṃ*, *odanaṃ bhojeti māṇavakaṃ*, *odanaṃ āseti māṇavakaṃ*, *ajjhāpeti*.
He causes the boy to recite the Veda (*vedaṃ pāṭhayati māṇavakaṃ vedam*); he causes Devadatta to sit (*āsayati devadattam*); he causes Devadatta to lie down (*sāyayati devadattam*);

he causes another to fry (*aññaṃ bhajjāpeti*); he causes another to pound (*aññaṃ koṭṭāpeti*); he causes another to spread out (*aññaṃ santharāpeti*). Regarding "of these very [roots]": what is the example?

Devadatta causes Yaññadatta to cook rice (*pācayati odanaṃ devadattena yaññadatto*). Regarding "when *pay-pp-*": what is the example? Devadatta goes (*gacchati devadatto*); when, for instance, he causes him to go (*gamayati*).

When another causes Devadatta to sacrifice by means of Yajñadatta, then one should say "he causes Devadatta to sacrifice by means of Yajñadatta," because the root *gam* has the sense of "causing to go" (*agamana*).
Or, it is like the case of *harati* and other such roots.

The second case ending optionally occurs for the agent when used with roots such as *harati* (to take away), *ajjhoharati* (to swallow), *kāreti* (to cause to do), *dassayati* (to show), and *abhivādayati* (to salute).

For example: *hāreti hāraṃ devadattaṃ devadattena vā*, *ajjhoharati sattuṃ devadattaṃ devadattena vā*, *kāreti devadattaṃ devadattena vā*, *dassayate janaṃ rājā janena vā*, or *abhivādayate guruṃ devadattaṃ devadattena vā*.

Not [after the causative suffix] *ṇi* when the agent is the prompter (*payojaka*) of the actions of eating (*khāda*), etc.—the second case ending does not occur after the causative suffix *ṇi* when the agent is the prompter of the actions of eating and so forth: *khādayati devadattena*, *ādayati devadattena*, *avhāpayati devadattena*, *saddāyati devadattena*, *kandayati devadattena*, *nāyayati devadattena*. Not [after the causative suffix] *ṇi* when the action is that of carrying (*vaha*) and the agent is not the driver (*aniyantuka*).

He causes Devadatta to carry the burden (*vāhayati bhāraṃ devadattena*). Why say "not when meaning to restrain" (*aniyantuketi*)? He causes the oxen to pull the cart (*vāhayati gāraṃ balivaddā*). Regarding "for eating" (*bhakkhissāyaṃ*):
he causes Devadatta to eat the sweetmeats (*bhakkhayati modake devadattena*). Why say "for non-harming" (*ahiṃsāyaṃ*)? He causes the oxen to eat the grain (*bhakkhayati balivaddā sassaṃ*).
[The rule] beginning with *dhi*:

When joined with *dhi* and so forth, does the second case ending occur? [Examples include: *dhiratthu maṃ pūtikāyaṃ* (Fie on me, this putrid body!), *antarā ca Rājagahaṃ* (Between Rājagaha and...), *antarā ca Nāḷandaṃ* (Between Nāḷanda and...), *samādhānam antarena* (Without concentration), and *mucalindaṃ abhito saraṃ* (Near the Mucalinda lake)—these are instances where there is an exception to the sixth case.
[The rule] beginning with *lakkhaṇa*, *itthambhūta*, *vīpsā*, and *sabbhi*.

The second case ending occurs after a word joined with *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic) and so forth, as well as with *ahi* (snake) and *vattha* (clothing). Examples: *rukkhaṃ abhivijjotate vijjū* (the lightning flashes across the tree), *sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ abhi* (it is good that Devadatta is toward his mother), *rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ abhitiṭṭhati* (he stands facing each tree).

The second case ending occurs after words joined with *pati* and *pari*, as well as with *bhāga* (portion) and *vattha* (clothing), when used in the sense of *lakkhaṇa* and so forth. Example: *rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate* (it flashes against the tree).
"Lightning, it would be well if Devadatta were to go toward his mother; he stands tree to tree, thinking, 'Whatever might be here toward me, may lightning strike that tree.
Lightning, it would be well if Devadatta were to go around his mother; he stands tree after tree, thinking, 'Whatever might be here around me, may lightning strike that tree.'"

The second case ending occurs after a word joined with *anunā* when it has the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth. Examples: *rukkhaṃ anuvijjotate vijju* (lightning flashes following the tree), *saccakiriyaṃ anupavassi* (it rained following the act of truth).

Furthermore, *hetu* (cause) and *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic) [are included]; examples: *sādhu devadatto mātaramanu* (Devadatta is good following his mother), *rukkhaṃ rukkhamanu tiṭṭhati* (he stands following tree after tree).
Regarding "anusiya" here:
after a word ending in "anu," when joined with "sahatthe" (in the sense of accompaniment), the second case ending occurs; as in *pabbatamanutiṭṭhati* (he stands along the mountain).
In the sense of inferiority, when joined with a word denoting inferiority, the second case ending occurs: "those possessing wisdom followed Anusārīputta.
[The word] "paññavanto" is in the nominative plural.
*Upena-*:

When joined with *upa* in the sense of inferiority (*hinattha*), the second case ending occurs; e.g., *upasāriputta paññāvanto* ("inferior to Sāriputta in wisdom"). *Adhikye*: [The seventh case ending occurs] in the sense of excess (*adhikya*).
The seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *upa* in the sense of superiority: *upakhārayaṃ doṇo* (“a *doṇa* measure [is superior] to a *khāraya*”).
With *adhi* in the sense of ownership:

the seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *adhi* in the sense of the state of being the owner: *adhibrahmadatte pañcālā* (“the Pañcālas [belong to] Brahmadatta”), *adhipañcālesu brahmadatto* (“Brahmadatta [rules] over the Pañcālas”).
The third case ending occurs in the sense of the agent and the instrument.
The third case is used for the agent: *purisena kataṃ* (done by a man); for the instrument: *asinā chindati* (he cuts with a sword); for the natural state:

*pakatiyā abhirūpo* (handsome by nature); for lineage: *gottena Gotamo* (a Gotama by clan); for name: *Assumedho nāma* (named Assumedha); for birth: *jātiyā sattavassiko* (seven years old by birth). [The third case is also used] for the source of origin, as in *bhūdhātussa sambhavā* (arising from the element of earth).
Thus the third [case]; likewise: "he runs on level ground," "he runs on uneven ground," "he buys grain for two *doṇas*," "he buys livestock for five.

In a construction with *sahatthena* (together with), the third case may occur: *puttena sahāgato*, *puttena saddhiṃ āgato* ("he has come together with his son"). The third case, like the sixth, occurs only when [the companion] is subordinate (*appadhāne*).

Regarding the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*): the third case ending may be used when expressing a characteristic. For example: *tidaṇḍakena paribbājakaṃ addakkhi* (he saw the wandering ascetic by means of his triple staff); *akkhinā kāṇo* (blind in one eye). For by that limb, the modification of the possessor of the limb (*aṅgin*) is characterized.
Regarding the cause (*hetu*).
The third case may be used for that which is fit for a counter-action: *annena vasati* (he lives by means of food), *vijjāya yaso* (fame by means of knowledge).
Regarding the fifth case: *iṇe vā*.
The fifth case optionally occurs when there is a debt or a cause: *jaḷattā baddho* (bound because of stupidity), or *satena vā* (or bound for a hundred [pieces of money]).

When a cause functions as a subordinate factor (*parāṅgabhūta*) to a quality (*guṇa*), the fifth case ending optionally occurs: *jaḷattā baddho* (bound because of dullness) or *jaḷattena*; *paññāya mutto* (liberated by means of wisdom). Because of non-existence after having been [present], they are impermanent; from the cessation of formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
The sixth case ending is used with words expressing a cause.

When joined with words expressing the sense of cause (*hetu*), the sixth case may optionally occur after the word denoting the cause: *udarassa hetu* (the cause of the belly), *udarassa kāraṇā* (for the sake of the belly).
Regarding "from *sabba* etc., all [cases]":

when joined with words expressing the sense of cause beginning with *sabba*, all case endings occur after *sabba* and its synonyms: *ko hetu* (what is the cause?), *kaṃ hetuṃ* (whom as cause?), *kena hetunā* (by what cause?).
[The suffix -tā is used] after words expressing the sense of cause (*hetu*), such as: *tassa hetussa*, *kasmā hetusmā*, *kassa hetussa*, *kasmiṃ hetusmiṃ*;

*kiṃ kāraṇaṃ*, *kena kāraṇena*; *kiṃ nimittaṃ*, *kena nimittena*; *kiṃ payojanaṃ*, *kena payojanena*—and so forth. [This is indicated by the rule] "after words having the sense of cause" (*hetvatthehi*). [The fourth case ending (*catutthī*) is used] in the sense of recipient (*sampadāna*).

When something is rightly given to someone, the fourth case (dative) may be used: *saṅghassa dadāti* ("he gives to the Saṅgha"). In the sense of a receptacle (*ādhāra*), the seventh case (locative) may also be used: *saṅghe dehi* ("give to the Saṅgha"). Regarding the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādatthya*):

when the state of being for the sake of something is to be expressed, the fourth case may be used after a noun: *sītassa paṭighātāya* ("for the warding off of cold"), *atthāya hitāya devamanussānaṃ* ("for the welfare and benefit of gods and men"), *nālaṃ dārabharaṇāya* ("not capable of supporting a wife"), *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"), *pākāya vajaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to the forest for cooking," etc.).
"To whom does what is sweet not please? May the Venerable Ones not find pleasure in a schism in the Saṅgha. "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha;
it does not suit him to eat"—in these cases, the genitive is used for the purpose of expressing a relationship. Nor would there be a contradiction here, because of the similarity of form;

and since a relationship of this kind is accepted by grammarians (*saddika*) in such instances, [the genitive] is used in the sense of the mere object, as in: "Whose Dhamma do you approve?"—here the nominative is used.
In this way, other [examples] should also be understood from other sources according to tradition.

In the case of "he bears the hundred [of the king]" (*rañño sataṃ dhāreti*) or "he bears the royal parasol [for the king]" (*rañño chattaṃ dhāreti*), the genitive is used for the relationship [of the object]. Likewise:

"he praises the king" (*rañño silāghate*), "he strikes the king" (*rañño hanute*), "he stands near the king" (*rañño upatiṭṭhate*), "he reviles the king" (*rañño sapate*); and "even the gods envy that Tathāgata" (*tassa... pihayanti*). In these cases, the genitive is used for the object.
Be angry, O Great Hero, with him at whom I might be provoked; the rain-cloud rains upon all directions alike.
He who harms those who have done him no wrong—what offense have I committed against you, noble ladies?
The heretics envy the ascetics; what cause for jealousy can there be in those who conduct themselves according to the Dhamma? It is the king’s fortune that the king loves. The king’s...

He seeks fortune; whether asked or unasked, he grants him cattle, he consents to the cattle, they respond to the Blessed One, "So be it," he accepts, he agrees, "I shall cause you to mount, I shall announce it to you; I will teach you the Dhamma.
"As our Teacher would explain it: enough for you with dwelling here; what use have you, O dull-witted one, for matted locks?"

"A wrestler is worthy of a wrestler"—in this phrase, the dative case is used in the sense of "regarding" (tādatthya), meaning "he does not value even his life as a blade of grass"; that is, he does not value it even for the sake of what might be gained by a blade of grass.
As it is said: "He who regards neither cold nor heat as more than a blade of grass."

"Thinking life to be like grass"—here the case endings refer only to the object (*savisayāva*). In "he goes for the sake of heaven" (*saggāya gacchati*), the dative is used in the sense of purpose (*tādatthye*);
for when one goes to heaven, that going is for the sake of that [heaven]. However, when there is an intention to express the direct object (*kammavavanicchāyaṃ*), the accusative alone is used:

"he goes to heaven" (*saggaṃ gacchati*). "May there be long life for you! May there be a long, auspicious, and beneficial life! (*āyuṃ bhoto hotu, ciraṃ jīvitaṃ bhaddaṃ kalyāṇaṃ atthaṃ*)—[here the dative is used in the sense of purpose].
May it be purposeful, wholesome, free from affliction, beneficial, suitable, pleasant, and agreeable for you. It would be well if you were to reveal the secret matter to this son;
Sakka appeared before me, and he sent a message to him; he dispatched a messenger to the monks;
the *āyoga* (suspension) is permitted for ascetics; it suffices for one, two, or three; here is a simile for you.
"I shall do it," "I grasp your joined palms," "his well-being," "the welfare of the world," "homage to you,
O noble steed among men," "safety for him," "a wrestler is a match for a wrestler," "a champion is a match for a champion," "his benefit, his happiness," "welcome to you,
O Great King"— in all these cases, the genitive case is used to express a relationship.
Other instances of this kind should also be understood in accordance with the tradition.
The fifth case ending denotes the limit (avadhi).

The fifth case ending occurs when there is a limit to the meaning of the word; for example: *gāmasmā āgacchati* ("he comes from the village"), likewise *corasmā bhāyati*, *corasmā uttasati*, *corasmā tāyati*, *corasmā rakkhati* ("he fears the thief," "he trembles before the thief," "he protects himself from the thief," "he guards himself from the thief").

"Save yourselves from suffering, seeing danger in negligence, for they tremble before punishment"—here, even the sixth and seventh case endings occur when there is a desire to express a relationship or a substratum (*sambandha-ādhāra-vacana*), such as "he defeats by means of study" (*ajjhenā parājeti*) or "he defeats the opponent" (*paṭipakkhe parājeti*);

thus all the case endings (*vibhattiyo*) are indeed used. If one says, "I shall defeat the fisherman" (*kevaṭṭassa parajjissāmi*), the sixth case ending also occurs when there is a desire to express a relationship.
"He keeps the cows away from the barley"—here the fifth case (*pañcamī*) has its proper domain.

"One should restrain the mind from evil"—here it is seen as having the sense of the accusative (*dutiyā*) in the sense of the object. "He disappears from the preceptor" and "He studies from the preceptor"—here the fifth case has its proper domain.
"Sorrow is born from desire"—here too the fifth case has its proper domain; likewise, "from that very place there are even enemies."

The Gaṅgā originates from Himavantā; "Quickly desist from taking life"—here the ablative case (*pañcamī*) has the same referent as *añño* (different from) and *devadattā* (than Devadatta), namely, "Devadatta is split";

likewise, "He is far from the destruction of the taints," "the other than Devadatta," "above the soles of the feet," "below the hair of the head," "prior to the village," and "prior to full enlightenment."
In the phrase "tato param," "tato aparena samayena," and "tatuttariṃ," the genitive case is used when there is a desire for a connection [of time]; as in:
"in front of the village" (*purato gāmassa*), "to the south of the village" (*dakkhiṇato gāmassa*), "above the mountain" (*upari pabbatassa*), and "below the palace" (*heṭṭhā pāsādassa*).

In the sense of a limit (*avadhi-vacanīcchāyaṃ*), it is used as follows: "having ascended the palace, he looks out" (*pāsādam āruyha pekkhati*) or "from the palace he looks out" (*pāsādā pekkhati*); "having sat down on the seat, he looks out" (*āsane upavisitvā pekkhati*) or "from the seat he looks out" (*āsanā pekkhati*).
The fifth case [is used] in the sense of asking and explaining: "From where are you coming? "From Pāṭaliputta. Likewise, it is used for place and time:
"Rājagaha is seven *yojanas* from Pāṭaliputta," or "in seven *yojanas*"; likewise, "after the passing of three months from here.
The fifth case is used in the sense of a quality obtained with difficulty: "I have mastered it with great effort" (*kacchena*), where the fifth case is used in the sense of cause or instrument.

Or else, it is the third [case]; thus, in "released by a little" (*thokena mutto*) and "released by a little" (*thokena mutto*), the second case is used for the object as an adverbial modifier of the action, meaning "it turns slightly.
Even when joined with words having the sense of "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the fifth and sixth cases would indeed occur within their own scope:

*dūrā gāmā* (from a distant village), *antikā gāmā* (from a near village), *dūrassa gāmassa* (of a distant village), and *antikassa gāmassa* (of a near village). However, when the sense of "far" and "near" is intended, all [cases] would indeed occur within their own scope.
[The accusative is used] due to the absence of a sublater (bādhaka); for example, "a distant village" (*dūro gāmo*), "a near village" (*antiko gāmo*), and so forth.

However, some say that because of the causes [expressing] non-existence (*asattā*), the second, third, fifth, and seventh cases have the meaning of the first case, whereas all [cases] have their own respective domains when expressing existence (*sattā*).

But those [views] are refuted by others; for example, "a distant path" (*dūraṃ maggo*) and "a near path" (*antikaṃ maggo*) are adverbs (*kriyāvisesana*) because they qualify the verbal root *gam* (to go).
Pure from things that provoke greed, liberated from suffering, and secluded indeed from sensual pleasures—[a lake] one *yojana* in depth and breadth, and one *yojana* in length, starting from there;
from when I remember myself, the grammatical case-endings have been exclusively within the domain of *attanantī*. [The prefixes] *apa-* and *pari-* are used in the sense of exclusion (*vajjana*).

The fifth case ending occurs after a word denoting exclusion (*vajjana*) when used with words expressing separation (*apaparī*). For example: *apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā* (the merchants come from outside the hall), *parisālāya āyanti vāṇijā* (the merchants come from around the hall);
the meaning is "having excluded the hall. Why say "denoting exclusion"? [Consider: *rukkhaṃ parivijjotate vijju* (the lightning flashes around the tree).

In the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*), the fifth case is used as in *āpāṭaliputtasmā vassi devo* (it rained as far as Pāṭaliputta); however, this is without [excluding] Pāṭaliputta.
The suffix *saha* is used with the sense of "together with" (*veti-viśeṣo*); thus [the examples] continue up to "it rained at Pāṭaliputta.
With the suffix *patinā* in the senses of "representative" (*paṭinidhi*) and "exchange" (*paṭidāna*):
when used in conjunction with *patinā* in the senses of representing or exchanging, the fifth case ending occurs after a noun; for example, *buddhasmā*.
Regarding *pati*: "Sāriputta gives a jar of oil to him. Regarding "in the sense of a substitute or a counter-gift": what [example is there]? "He leaps toward the tree.
Regarding *rite* with the second case:
With the word *rite*, when used in conjunction with a noun, the second case and the fifth case occur; for example, *rite saddhammaṃ* (without the true Dhamma) and *rite saddhammā*.

*Vinā* and *aññatra*: when used in conjunction with the words *vinā* and *aññatra*, the third case ending occurs after a noun, as do the second and fifth case endings. For example: *vinā vātena* (without wind), *vinā vātaṃ*, *vinā vātasmā*; *aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakena* (except for one person carrying alms-food), *aññatra dhammaṃ*, *aññatra dhammā*.
[The same applies] to *puthu* and *nānā*.
With these [words expressing] conjunction (*yoga*), the third and fifth case endings occur: *puthageva janena*, *puthageva janasmā*, *janena nānā*, *janasmā nānā*.

**The seventh case ending occurs for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*):** When there is a support for the action—that is, when there is a support for the agent or the object which serves as the basis for the action—the seventh case ending occurs after the noun denoting that grammatical factor (*kāraka*). Examples: *kaṭe nisīdati* (he sits on a mat), *thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati* (he cooks rice in a pot), *ākāse sakuṇā* (birds in the sky), *tilesu telaṃ* (oil in sesame seeds), *gaṅgāyaṃ vajaḥ* (the Vajra [is] in the Ganges).

In the sense of a cause (nimitta), the locative case occurs; for example: "The leopard is killed on account of its skin" (*ajinamhi haññate dīpī*), or "there is an offense of expiation for speaking falsehood" (*musāvāde pācittiyaṃ*).
The state of something [serving as] a characteristic of another state is called "characteristic of a state" (*bhāvalakkhaṇa*).
When the state (*bhāva*) of one thing becomes the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of another state, the seventh case (*sattamī*) occurs:
"He went while the cows were being milked; he returned when they had been milked. What is meant by "state"? "He eats with matted hair. What is meant by "characteristic of a state"?
"He who eats—that is Devadatta. "It rains for him at the wrong time; it does not rain for him at the right time"—this is the locative of domain (*visaya-sattamī*).
And the sixth [case] is used in disregard.
When one state is the characteristic of another state, the sixth case is employed, and the seventh case is also used when disregard is to be understood.
"He led him away while striking him, even as the King of Sivi looked on."
Death goes away taking [them] while the great multitude looks on.
In "the owner of the cows," the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) expresses the relationship of ownership; in "the owner among the cows," the seventh case (*visayasattamī*) expresses the locus.

Thus: the lord of the cows, the master of the cows; the overlord of the cows, the ruler of the cows; the heir of the cows, the inheritor of the cows; the witness of the cows, the observer of the cows.
He is a guarantor for cattle, a guarantor for cows; he is born of cattle, born of cows; he is skilled in dance and song, skilled in dance and song;
he is appointed to the making of mats, appointed to the making of mats. Thus, when there is a desire for words to be maintained, the locative case is reached.
They pay homage to the monks by kissing their heads, by taking hold of their arms, and by clasping their hands as they walk along.

"They go on paths," "they protect elephants among the plantains"—these are examples of the locative case (sattamī) used for the object of perception (*ñāṇasmiṃ pasanno*). "One who is confident in knowledge" (*ñāṇena pasanno*)—this is the instrumental case (tatiyā) used in the sense of an instrument.
Likewise, "one who is zealous in knowledge" (*ñāṇasmiṃ ussukko*) and "one who is zealous by means of knowledge" (*ñāṇena ussukko*).
From this [it follows] the rule of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

Selection (*niddhāraṇa*) is the setting apart of a portion of a whole by way of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*); because it is performed from that [whole], the sixth and seventh cases occur.
For example: *sāliyo sūkadhaññānaṃ pathyatamā* (of the grains of rice, the rice is the most wholesome), *sāliyo sūkadhaññesu pathyatamā* (the rice is the most wholesome among the grains of rice);

*kaṇhā gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā* (the black cow is the one with the most excellent milk), *kaṇhā gāvīsu sampannakhīratamā* (the black cow is the one with the most excellent milk among the cows); [and] *gacchatam*...
"Among those who run, he runs the fastest"—in this instance, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used for the limit (*avadhi*).

At the end of the first meaning—namely, when there is merely a name as the designatum—the first case ending (*paṭhamāvibhatti*) occurs; this includes gender (*liṅga*) as well, such as "tree," "female," "male," and "neuter."

The meanings of words such as *doṇa*, *khārī*, and *āḷhaka* are indeed the meanings of words (*saddattha*), as are measures of quantity. Numbers such as one, two, and many are also the meanings of words.
Regarding the vocative:

when there is an addressing (*āmantana*) by means of a word to bring someone face-to-face, the first case ending occurs in that context; for example, *bho purisa*, *bho itthi*, *bho napuṃsaka*. The sixth case ending occurs in relation to connection (*sambandha*).

A relationship (*sambandha*) born from the notions of action and agent, caused by the state of being a possessor (*assedaṃbhāva*), is called "relationship" (*sambandha*); in that case, the sixth case-ending (*chaṭṭhīvibhatti*) occurs:

*rañño puriso* (the king’s man), *sarati rajjassa* (he remembers the kingdom). In this relationship, the sixth case is used; the meaning is "he performs remembrance directed toward what is related to the kingdom.
However, when there is a desire for the expression of the object (*kamma*), the second case alone is used: *sarati rajjaṃ*. Likewise, *rajakassa vatthaṃ dadāti* (he gives a cloth to the washerman).
The fool fills his back with [the weight of] watchfulness and fulfills himself with evil, thinking:
“O father, know these ministers who are wise and skilled in affairs.
This applies to those who, three times a day, or once every fortnight, fill a jar to the brim with gold and bullion, and so forth.
In the *Kitaka* rules regarding the agent and the object, the genitive case is frequently used when there is a desire for a word expressing a relationship: "He is highly esteemed by the multitude";
"The Dhamma-element of the Buddhas is well-penetrated"; "The wise one is a guardian of the Dhamma";
"The Deathless has been enjoyed by them"; "They will speak of him as such"; "He is not a deceiver of the world"; "Relying upon the shameless."

"Derived from the four great elements, [it is] sensitivity," and so forth. However, in the case of words expressing the agent or the object, the third and second cases are used respectively—as in "I was entrusted by my father," or "Do you remember such words being spoken? or "For the purpose of seeing the Blessed One," and so on.
Or, the third case is used in the sense of equality (*tulyārtha*).

When used with words having the sense of "equal" (*tulya*), the sixth case ending occurs, or optionally the third case ending; for example: *tulyo pitu* (equal to the father), *tulyo pitarā* (equal to the father); *sadiso pitu*, *sadiso pitarā* (similar to the father).

They possess the sense of being equal and being comparable.

After *gha*, *pa*, *ta*, *sa*, *ma*, *pa*, *ri*, *sā*, *ya*, or *ra*, the suffix *smin* becomes *yaṃ* or *yāṃ*: *kaññāyaṃ*, *daññāya*, *rattiyaṃ*, *rattiyā*, *vadhuyaṃ*, *vadhuyā*, *sabbāyaṃ*, *sabbāya*, *amuyaṃ*, *amuyā*.
After *tiṃ*, *sabhāparisāya*:
after *tiṃ*, *sabhāparisā* becomes *sabhātiṃ* or *sahāya*; after *tiṃ*, *parisā* becomes *parisatiṃ* or *parisāya*.
After *pada* and other [words], *si* becomes *smin* or *si*: *padasi*, *padasmiṃ*; *bilasi*, *bilasmiṃ*.
Not after *assa* or *sā*.
The suffix *sā* is optionally used after words beginning with *pada*, such as *padasā* or *padena*,
*bilasā* or *bilena*.
It is also optionally used after words beginning with *krodha*, such as *kodhasā* or *krodhena*, *arthasā* or *arthena*.
*Atena*:

For the word *nāvavana* following a vowel ending in *a*, there is the substitution of *en*. Example: *buddhena*. Why "ending in *a*" (*ato*)? Example: *agginā*. *Sissa-*: [The following rule applies to the suffix *si*].
After a noun ending in *a*, the suffix *si* becomes *o*; for example, *buddho*. However, after that [same stem], it becomes *e*—as in *aggī*.

Or else, in some cases, after a noun ending in *a*, the suffix *si* optionally becomes *e*; as in: *yathā vanappagumbe phussitagge* (just as in a forest thicket with its tops in bloom), even in a domain where an exception would otherwise apply.

The suffix *aṃ* is generally substituted for *sa* after a neuter noun ending in *a*. Examples: *vidhānaṃ*, *sukhaṃ*, *dukkhaṃ*. Why [say] "generally"? [To exclude: *vāti kiṃ* ("What does it blow?"). Why [say] "in some cases"?

[To ensure it does not apply] everywhere, as in *pakve* ("in ripe [fruit]"). *Aṃ napuṃsake*: after a noun ending in *a*, *aṃ* becomes the form for the nominative-accusative singular in the neuter gender.
*Yonaṃ ni-*:

After a neuter noun ending in *a*, *yonaṃ* becomes *ni*; [the forms] *sabbāni*, *rūpāni*—[these are examples of] the first case (*paṭhamā*) in the rule for the constant suffixes (*nicca-vidhāna*), such as *phalaṃ*, *ekaccaṃ*, etc., ending in *a*. *Jhalā vā*: [The suffix *ni* is optionally used after a neuter noun ending in a consonant (*jhal*).]
After a *jhal* [consonant], the suffix *-yaunam* becomes either *-vā* or is neuter: *aṭṭhinī*, *aṭṭhī*; *āyūni*, *āyū*. *Lopa-*: After a *jhal*, there is elision (*lopa*) of *-yaunam*:
*aṭṭhī*, *āyū*, *aggī*, *bhikkhū*. Why is it not the case that [elision occurs] even after *jhal* in *aggayo*? Because the substitution of *ākāra* (the long vowel) is an internal rule (*antaraṅga*).

Or, by means of the *jantu* and *hetu* bases ending in *ī*: there is optionally the elision of the following *yona* (the suffixes *-ya* and *-no*) when the terms *gha* and *pasaññī* follow; [thus] *jantu*, *jantuyo*;
*hetu*, *hetuyo*; *daddhī*, *daddhīyo*; *kaññā*, *kaññāyo*; *rattī*, *rattiyo*; *itthī*, *itthiyo*; *deṇū*, *deṇuyā*; *vadhū*, *vadhuyo*.

The elision of the *iva*-vowel (*i* or *ī*) occurs optionally before the letter *y*, provided it is preceded by a vowel (*e* or *o*). Examples: *ratyo*, *ratyā*, *ratyaṃ*; *pokkharañño*, *pokkharaññā*, *pokkharaññaṃ*.
However, this does not apply in the case of *rattiyo*. Why "preceded by a vowel"? Witness *daddhiyo*. Why "of the *iva*-vowel"? Witness *dhenuyo* and *vadhuyā*.
How so? "I am permitted," [is the thought]. These are the divisions of the *yoga* (rules).
After the word *gasī*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *gasī* suffix when a vowel (*vijjha*) follows; "O man, this is a staff."

With all [words] that are *asaṅkhya*—that is, with those for which no number exists—the elision (*lopa*) of all subsequent case-endings (*vibhatti*) occurs, as in *va*, *vā*, *eva*, *evaṃ*. From this very indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is inferred that the arising of the suffix *syā* [is applicable] after *asaṅkhya* words. This is because they share the same referent (*ekatthatā*).
In the case of becoming a single word (*ekatthībhāva*), there is generally (*bahulaṃ*) elision of all case endings (*vibhatti*):
*puttīyati*, *rājapuriso*, *vāsiṭṭho*. In some instances it does not occur because of the general rule (*bahulaṃ vidhānā*):
*parantapo*, *bhagandaro*, *parassapadaṃ*, *attanopadaṃ*, *gavampati*, *devānampiyatisso*, *antevāsī*, *janesuto*, *mamattaṃ*, *māmako*.

*Pubbasamāsadato*: When a compound has a prior member that is a single-word compound (*ekatttha*), there is elision of all case endings (*vibhatti*) following it. [Exception: *adhitthī* does not occur here because the rule is stated as "mostly" (*bahulaṃ*). Examples: *yathāpatti*, *yayathāparisā*. Why say "from a prior member"? [Counter-example: *gāmaṃ gato*. [Exception: Not after the fifth case ending (*pañcami*).

When a compound ending in *am* (the accusative case) has a single meaning with a preceding word, there is no elision of any of the case endings (*vibhatti*) following it—except for the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Examples: *upakumbham*. Why say "except for the fifth case"? Example: *upakumbhā ānaya* ("Bring from near the jar").

Alternatively, the third and seventh cases may optionally take the suffix *am*: When a compound ending in *am* (the accusative case) has a single meaning with a preceding word, the third and seventh case endings following it may optionally become *am*. Examples: *upakumbhena kṛtam* or *upakumbhaṃ kṛtam* ("made by means of the jar"); *upakumbe nidhehi* or *upakumbhaṃ nidhehi* ("place in the jar").
*Rājassi* means "I am a queen.
It occurs either as *rājassi* or *rājasi*; [it is used] by King Sabbadatta. *Vātve* means "in the forest.
*Sunaṃhisū* means "in the sun."
*Rāja* becomes *rājassa* optionally before the suffixes *su*, *naṃ*, and *hi*; [it remains] *rājūsu*, *rājesu*, *rājūnaṃ*, *raññaṃ*, *rājūbhi*, *rājebhi*.
*Imassa anitthiyaṃ ṭe*:

for the word *ima*, when not feminine, *ṭe* is optionally substituted before the suffixes *su*, *naṃ*, and *hi*; [thus: *esu*, *imesu*, *esaṃ*, *imesaṃ*, *ehi*, *imehi*. Why "not feminine"? [Because in the feminine it is: *imāsu*, *imāyaṃ*, *imāhi*.

*Nāmbhanimi-*: For the word *ima*, when not feminine, the substitutes *nā* and *anaimi* occur [respectively in the nominative singular and the instrumental singular]; thus: *anena* (by this), *iminā* (by this); but specifically when not feminine: *anitthiyaṃ tveva*—*imāya* (by this).
This [is the rule] for the neuter *sīmbha*.
For the neuter form of the word *ima*, *ayaṃ* occurs in the nominative singular (*simhi*); for example: *ayaṃ puriso* (this man), *ayaṃ itthī* (this woman).

Why say "for the non-neuter"? [Because otherwise it would apply to the neuter: *imaṃ*. Regarding *tya*, *ta*, and *eta*: for these non-neuter forms, *so* replaces *tassa* in the nominative singular; for example: *syō puriso* (that man), *syā itthī* (that woman). Likewise: *so*, *sā*, *eso*, *esā*. For the neuter, however, they are respectively: *tyaṃ*, *taṃ*, *etaṃ*.
*Massāmussa-*:
In the nominative singular (*simhi*), the *m* of a neuter word other than *asu* becomes *s*; for example, *asu puriso*, *asu itthi*. Or, *ke vā-*... [the rest of the rule follows].
Regarding the word *amussa*: what is its form? It is *asuko*, *amuko*, *asukā*, *amukā*, *asukaṃ*, *amukaṃ*, *asukāni*, *amukāni*.
Regarding that word, *tassa* occurs as *no* in all case endings (*sabbāsu vibhattīsu*): *ne*, *te*, *nāyo*, *tāyo*, *naṃ*, *taṃ*, *nāni*, *tāni*, and so forth.
In place of *ta*, *sma*, *smiṃ*, *ssā*, *yassaṃ*, *ssāsaṃ*, *mbhā*, *mhi*, *savimassa*, *ca*, *sādisvimassa*, *tata*, and *ssa*, there is optionally *ṭa*:

*assai* (for *asmai*), *assā* (*asmā*), *imas-mā* (*imasmā*), *assim* (*asmiṃ*), *imasmiṃ*, *assāya* (*imissāya*), *assaṃ* (*imassaṃ*), *assā* (*imissā*), *āsaṃ* (*imāsaṃ*), *amhā* (*imamhā*), *amhi* (*imamhi*); *assa*.

From it, from that; in it, in that; of her, of that; on her, on that; of her, of that; of them, of those; from me, from that; in me, in that. The inclusion of "ssā" and so forth is intended so that [the substitution] does not occur when there is a different replacement for the "m".
[The suffixes are: Ṭā, si, smi, smā.

After the word *isi* (sage), the suffixes *te* or *vā* are optionally used for the first case (*issā*) and the sixth case (*yona*). For example: *atthadhammavidū ise* (to the sage who knows the meaning and the Dhamma); or likewise, *isī*.

For the second case (*yossa*), after the word *isi*, the suffixes *duyā* or *yossa* are optionally used for the sixth case. For example: *samaṇe brāhmaṇe vande sampannacaraṇe ise* (I revere the ascetics and brahmins, the sages perfected in conduct); or likewise, *isayo passa* (behold the sages). Why "for the second case"? [As in: *isayo tiṭṭhanti* (the sages stand).
*Ekaccādigato*:

After *ekacca* and other words ending in *a*, the suffix *ṭā* is substituted for *ya*. Examples: *ekacce tiṭṭhanti*, *ekacce passa*. Why [is it] "after *at*"? Example: *ekaccāyo*. Thus ends the first section of the *esa* [chapter]. *Na nissa ṭā*: [The suffix] *ṭā* is not [substituted] for *nissa*.
The suffix *ṭā* does not occur after *nissa* following *ekacca-* and others; thus, *ekaccāni*.
The suffix *ṭā* does not occur after *nissa* following *sabba-* and others; thus, *sabbāni*.
[The rule] *yeyānameṭa-* [applies].
The suffix *yaṃ* occurs after the pronouns beginning with *saba-* when they end in the vowel *a*: *sabbe tiṭṭhanti*, *sabbe passa*;
[but] *ato tveva sabbāyo*.

Furthermore, this does not apply to those that are subordinate to a noun. Whatever has been stated regarding the pronouns beginning with *saba-* when they function as nouns or are subordinate, and whatever other grammatical operation (*sabbādi-kāriya*) applies to them, it does not take place: *te sabbā*, *te piyasabbā*, *te atisabbā*.
In the case of the third meaning:

when there is a connection with the sense of the third [case], whatever has been stated regarding the *sabba*-group and whatever other grammatical operation (*kāriya*) belonging to the *sabba*-group does not take place; for example, *māsena pubbānaṃ* becomes *māsapubbānaṃ*. In a compound expressing the fourth meaning (*catthasamāse*).

In the domain of catu-samāsa (four-term compounds), that which has been stated for the *sabba*-group and other grammatical operations applicable to the *sabba*-group do not occur; [this rule applies] except for *dakkhiṇa*, *uttara*, and *pubba* in a compound. Why [is this said]? [Consider: *amuñca tesañca dehi*. Veṭa:
In the domain of catu-samāsa, the substitution of *ya* for the *sabba*-group is optionally applied when it has been so prescribed; thus, one forms either *pubbuttare* or *pubbuttarā*.

[The suffix] *eta* optionally occurs after these six [words], beginning with *pubba*, when they refer to their own respective domains (*savisaye*). *Pubbe* becomes *pubbā*; *pare* becomes *parā*; *apare* becomes *aparā*; *dakkhiṇe* becomes *dakkhiṇā*; *uttare* becomes *uttarā*; *adhare* becomes *adharā*. Why say "after the six"? [Observe: *ye*.
[The suffixes] *smiṃ*, *saṃ*, *nā*, *sma*, *naṃ*, *sisa*, *so*, *sā*, *sā* occur after [the words] beginning with *mana*.
From *manā* and so forth, the nominative and vocative cases of *samīma* and so forth are formed respectively: *manasi*, *manasmiṃ*; *manaso*, *manassa*;
*mano*, *manaṃ*; *manasā*, *manena*; *manasā*, *manasmā*. How so? [As in:

"A son was born to Avetasa," "The wise one departs, having left behind," "Clad in pure white garments," and "Clad in garments of golden silk"—in these instances, the suffix *-a* occurs in the sense of the reflexive pronoun (*sakatthe*).
Mind, darkness, heat, brilliance, head, heart, speech, vitality, sovereignty, fame, feet, arrows,
rain, wind, residence, consciousness, reservoirs, destruction, iron, and cloth— these are the objects of the senses.
One who is mindful among the virtuous...
The word *santa* becomes *sabba* before the letter *bha*; [thus,] *sabbhi*.
Alternatively, for the word *bhavanta*, there is the substitution of *bhonta* when the feminine suffix *gī* is elided; [thus,] *bhonta*, *bhavaṃ*, *bhonto*, *bhavanto*, *bhotā*.
*bhavatā*, *bhoto*, *bhavato*—the particle *bho* is used for addressing. [The form] "Come, you three men, sir!

(*āgacchatha bho tayo janā*) is established by means of the words *bhante* and *bhadda*; [the form] *bhaddanta* is established through the doubling of the syllable *da*. [The suffix] *-ni* follows after a word ending in *s*.
In the case of *aggimā*, the suffix *s* becomes *ni* optionally; thus:
*aggini*, *aggi*.
In the locative singular (*ntasse*), the suffix *nta* becomes *am* optionally; thus: *gaccham*, *gacchanto*.
From the *bhū* root, *aṃ* replaces *nta* in the nominative singular (*sīmhi*) invariably due to subsequent re-statement; thus, *bhavaṃ*.
For the words *mahant* and *rājā*, *ṭā* optionally [replaces *nta*].
In the locative case (*simhi*), the suffix *ṭā* optionally replaces the ending of a word ending in *nta*; thus: *mahā*, *mahaṃ*, *arahā*, *arahaṃ*.
Regarding words ending in *ntu*: in the locative case, *ṭā* replaces the ending of a word ending in *ntu*; thus: *guṇavā*.

The *aṃ* and *ṅa* [substitutes] occur for the *ntu* [suffixes] in the neuter in the locative case (*simhi*); for example, *guṇavaṃ kulaṃ* (the virtuous family) and *guṇañca ntaṃ kulaṃ* (and the virtuous family ending in *nta*). Why "in the neuter"? [Consider: *sīlavā bhikkhu* (the virtuous monk).
Or, [the suffixes *o* and *aṃ* occur] after *himavato*.
In the case of *himavant*, there is optionally the substitution of *o* for *a*; thus, *himavanto* or *himavā*.
Regarding the rule beginning with *rājādi* and *yuvādi*:
after words beginning with *rājā* and those beginning with *yuvan*, *ā* is substituted for *s*. Thus: *rājā*, *yuvā*—[the groups are] *rāja*, *brahma*, *sakha*, *atta*, *ātuma*.
*Dhammo* is used in the sense of another [thing] (*aññattha*).
*Daḷhadhammā*; (*daḷhadhammo*) *asmā*. This [suffix] occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
*Animā*, *laghimā*—now hear that well, O Maghavan, regarding the masculine forms.
In the case of words such as *rājan* and those beginning with *yuvan*, the suffix *anaṅ* becomes *vām* before the ending *am*; thus: *rājānam*, *rājam*; *yuvānam*, *yuvam*.
The term *yuvan* takes the suffix *-māna-* when preceded by *rājan* and so forth, as well as by *yuva* and so forth. Thus: *rājāno*, *yuvāno*; or alternatively: *rājā*, *rāje*; *yuvā*, *yuve*.
Also, [the suffix *-māna-* occurs] after *āya* and *sakhā*.
From *sakha*, there are *yona*, *māyona*, *vā*, *āna*, and *ca*; [namely] *sakhāyo*, *sakhino*, *sakhāno*. But rather, [the forms] *sakhā* and *sakhe* [occur].
[The rule] *ṭe smino-*:
from *sakha*, *ṭe* becomes *smin*. This undertaking is for the sake of establishing the constant state (*niccattha*) [of the suffix].

In the case of *sakha*, when followed by endings beginning with *n* or *ṇ*, the substitution of *i* occurs: *sakhassa*, *sakhino*, *sakhinā*, *sakhissa*. Or, before endings beginning with *sm* or *ṅ*, [the substitution of *a* occurs].
In the case of *sakha*, [the suffix] *ā* optionally occurs before *araṅ*, *yo*, *svaṃ*, *hi*, *su*, and *sma*, *naṃ*, and *su*.
Thus: *sakhāro*, *sakhāyo*; *sakhāresu*, *sakhesu*; *sakhāraṃ*, *sakhaṃ*; *sakhārāhi*, *sakhehi*; *sakhārā*, *sakhārasmā*, *sakhārānaṃ*, *sakhānaṃ*.

In the case of words ending in the suffix *latu* and of words such as *pitṛ*, when the suffix *araṅ* follows, the form *bho* occurs, except in the following instances: *kattāro*, *pitaro*; *kattāraṃ*, *pitaraṃ*; *kattārā*, *pitarā*; *kattari*, *pitari*. Why say "except" (*aññatra*)? [To exclude] *kattuno*, *pituno*. In the case of the suffix *nam*, it is optional.
In the case of *nam*, there is optionally the substitution of *ā* for *latu-pitā*-type stems: *kattārānaṃ*, *kattunaṃ*, *pitarānaṃ*, *pitunnaṃ*.
In the case of *ām*, there is optionally the substitution of *ā* for *latu-pitā*-type stems: *kattānaṃ*, *kattūnaṃ*, *pitānaṃ*, *pitunnaṃ*.
*Salopo*:

The elision (*lopa*) of *sa* optionally occurs after *latu*, *pitā*, and so forth; as in *kattu*, *kattuno*; *sakamandhātu*, *sakamandhātuno*; *pitu*, *pituno*. *Suhisvāraṅi*: [The elision of *su* occurs] before *hi*, *sva*, and *aṅ*.

In the case of *latu*, *pitā*, and so forth, the suffix *ā* optionally occurs before the locative plural ending *-su*: *kattāresu* or *kattūsu*, *pitaresu* or *pitusu*; and before the instrumental plural endings *-ehi* and *-hi*: *kattārehi* or *kattuhi*, *pitarehi* or *pituhi*.
Regarding the word *nadi* (river), the suffix *ā* optionally occurs before the nominative plural ending *-yo*: *najjāyo* or *nadiyo*.
*Ṭi*: From what [number] does *ṭi* arise? *Ṭi* arises from the word *kati*; for example: *kati tiṭṭhanti*, *kati passa*.
*Ṭa* arises from the fourteen [numbers] beginning with five.

The suffix *ṭo* is substituted for the genitive case ending after the numbers beginning with five (*pañca*) up to fourteen (*cuddasa*). [Examples: *pañca pañca*, and so on up to *aṭṭhārasa*. Why "beginning with five"? [Counter-example:

*dve tayo cattāro*. Why "fourteen"? [Counter-example: *dvāvīsatiyo*. After the word *ubhago*, the suffix *ṭo* is substituted for the genitive case ending. [Examples: *ubho ubho*, *gāvo gāvo*. How so? In the phrase *imāya ekarattiṃ ubhayo vasāma*, when *ṭo* follows, there is the augment *y*.
Āraṅismā:

After the substitution of *āraṅ*, the suffix *ṭo* is substituted for subsequent personal endings (*yonaṃ*); e.g., *sakhāro*, *kattāro*, *pataro*. Ṭoṭe vā: [The following rule applies] when *ṭo* or *ṭe* follows.
After a substitute ending in *āra*, the suffixes *ṭo* and *ṭā* occur respectively: *sakhāro*, *sakhāre*, *sakhāro*. The inclusion of *ṭo* is for the sake of brevity.

*Ṭā* occurs after [stems] ending in *nā* and *smā*: *kattārā*, *kattārā*; in some cases it does not occur due to the rule governing the plural (*bahakula*). Such forms arise from the suffix *sakhāra*.
*Ṭi* replaces *smin*:
after the substitution of *āraṅ*, *ṭi* occurs in place of *smin*; as in *kattari* (agent) and *pitari* (father). [This applies] to roots beginning with *div*.
After nouns ending in *div* and similar stems, *smin* becomes *ṭi*; in *divi* and *bhuvi*, the letter *v* is always inserted.
Before the suffix *smi*, the long vowel *ā* becomes short: as in *kattari* and *nattari*.

In the case of *pitā* and so forth, when they are not [in the forms] beginning with *nattā*, the vowel of *pitā* and so forth becomes short in all case endings (*vibhatti*). Examples: *pitaro*, *pitaraṃ*. Why "not [in the forms] beginning with *nattā*"? [Answer: *nattāro*.
In the case of *yuvan* and so forth, [the vowel becomes short] before *su*, *hi*, and *svānaṅ*.
In the case of *yuvan* and other such words, *ānaṅ* is substituted for the final syllable before the nominative plural ending *su*; [thus] *yayuvānesu*, *yuvānehi*.
Before the endings *nonānesvā-*, *ā* is substituted for the final syllable of *yuvan* and others; [thus] *yuvāno*, *yuvānā*, *yuvāne*.
*Smā*, *asmin*, and *naṃ* are substituted for [the endings] *bhyām*, *bhis*, and *bhyas* respectively, when followed by *yuva-* and so on: *yuvānā*, *yuvāne*.
*Yonaṃ* or *none* [is substituted for *bhyas*].

After [stems ending in] *yuvan* and so forth, *yo* and *no* optionally occur in the masculine according to their respective order: *yuvāno*, *yuvano*; *yuvāno*, *yuvāne*. Why is *yuvan* mentioned? To see [the form] *yuve*. The mention of *n* is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). **Itto ’ññatthe pume**:

After a noun ending in *ikāra* (i) used in the sense of another word (*aññattha*), *yo* and *no* optionally occur in the masculine according to their respective order. For example: *tomaraṅkusapāṇino*, *tomaraṅkusapāṇine*. Even when *vā* (optionality) applies: *tomaraṅkusapāṇayo*. Why "in the sense of another word"? Witness: *pāṇayo* (where it refers to the same referent).
*Ne smino kvaci*:

In some instances, when expressing a meaning other than that of the word itself (aññapadattha), the suffix *smin* becomes *ne* optionally after a noun ending in *i*. Namely: 1. In the case of "a grateful person who is virtuous and noble in conduct" (*kataññumhi ca posamhi sīlavante ariyavuttine*), it is used as *vā tveva* (or indeed) for the state of being noble in conduct (*ariyavuttimhi*). 2. In the masculine gender (*pumetva*), it is used as *eva* for the one who is noble in conduct (*ariyavuttiyā*). The term *pumā* refers to the masculine.
Regarding the word *pumā*: that which is prescribed after the sound *pu* may optionally occur; [thus] *pumā* or *pume*. Regarding the suffix *nām*:
that which is prescribed for *pumā* before the suffix *nām* may optionally occur; [thus] *pumānā* or *pumena*.
*Sumhā ca*:

After a masculine [stem ending in] *sum*, that which was stated [as *yaṃ*] becomes *ā*, *ca*, or *vā*; [thus: *pumānesu*, *pumesu*, *pumāsu*. *Gassaṃ*: [The following rule applies] to the genitive plural (*gassaṃ*).
After the word *puma*, *aṃ* optionally replaces *g*. Thus: *bho pumaṃ*, *bho puma*, *bho itthipumaṃ*, *bho itthipuma*.
In the case of the word *sā*, *ānaṅ* is substituted [for *sā*] before the locative ending (*aṃse*) and the vocative (*ge*). Thus: *sānaṃ*, *sānassa*, *bho sāna*.
*Vattahā* [is used] for *sanannaṃ* and *nonānaṃ*;
they become *vattahā* and *vattahānānaṃ* respectively; or *brahmassu*.
Brahmāsu vā hoti sanamhi; brahmunā, brahmuno, brahmussa, brahmūnaṃ, brahmānaṃ.
Nāmhi—brahmassu hoti nāmhi; brahmunā.
In the case of *puma*, [the forms] are:

*pumassu* (locative plural) and *sasmāsu* (locative plural); in the past (*pudīnam*), it is *ho* (nominative singular) and *vā* (vocative singular); [in the genitive singular] *nāmhi*; [the forms are] *pumuno*, *pumassa*;
*pumunā*, *pumānā*, *pumunā*, *pumānā*; *kammuno*, *kammassa*; *kammunā*, *kammasmā*; *kammunā*, *kammanā*; *ṭhāmuno*, *ṭhāmassa*; *ṭhāmunā*.
From *ṭhāna*: *ṭhānasmā*; *ṭhānā*, *ṭhānena*; *addhuno*, *addhassa*; *addhunā*, *addhasmā*; *addhunā*, *addhanā*.
The word *yuvan* takes the suffix *sassan*: *yuvan* becomes *yuvassan*; *yuvino*, *yuvassa*.
Nottātumā-. [The suffix] -ka is applied after *attā* and *ātumā*. Thus: *attānaṃ*, *attānā*; *ātumānaṃ*, *ātumānā*. Or: *attano*, *attassa*; *ātumano*, *ātumassa*.
[The suffix] -ka is applied after *suhī*.

The word *atta* (self) does not take the suffix *-naka* when followed by *suhi* (in those who are well). [The forms are: *attanesu*, *attesū*, *ātumanesu*, *ātumesu*; *attanēhi*, *attehi*; *ātumanehi*, *ātumēhi*. How so? Because of the separation of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating "not after *verinesu*" (*naka*).
Regarding *smāssa* and *brahmā*:
the suffixes *smā*, *assa*, and *nā* do not occur after *brahma* or after *atta* and *ātuma*. [The forms are: *brahunā*, *attanā*, *ātumanā*.

In the case of the substitution of *ena* for these [words], there is the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). For the words *ima* and *eta*, when used in the context of a statement followed by a retort, the substitution of *ena* occurs in the second case:
*imaṃ bhikkhuṃ vinayamajjhāpaya, atho enaṃ dhammamajjhāpaya*; *ime bhikkhū vinayamajjhāpaya, atho ene dhammamajjhāpaya*. In this same way, it should be applied to *ta* as well.
The declension of *kiṃ* in all cases: *kissa*, *ko*, *sabbāsu*.
In all case endings, *kiṃ* becomes *kassa*; [the forms are] *ko*, *ke*, *kā*, *kāyo*, *kaṃ*, *kāni*, *kena*, and so forth.
In the feminine, it is *kā* in the locative singular (*sasmin*) and *su* (locative plural).
In the neuter, after *anitthiyaṃ*, what [form] occurs for *kissa*, *kiṃ*, *sasmiṃsu*, *kissa*, *kassa*, *kismiṃ*, *kasmiṃ*? For *anitthiyaṃ*, it is *kiṃ*;
for *ko*, it is *kaṃ*.
For this (*imassa*), there is *idaṃ* or *vā*. After *aṃsisu*, together with those, there is *idaṃ* or *vā* in the neuter: *idaṃ*, *imaṃ*; *idaṃ*, *imaṃ*.
**Amussāduṃ**:
In the nominative plural (*aṃsi*), together with those [plural endings], *aduṃ* or *amuṃ* occurs for this [demonstrative pronoun] in the neuter gender: *aduṃ*, *amuṃ*; *aduṃ*, *amuṃ*.
[The rule applies to] *sumbhāmbhassāsmā-*...
*Asmā* occurs after *ahaṃ* or *sumhi*; *bhattīrasmāsu sā tava*; and *vātveva-amhesu*.

In the case of *namhi*, for the words *ti* and *catu*, *tissa* and *catassā* occur respectively when [the referent] is feminine: *tissannaṃ* and *vatassannaṃ*. Why "when feminine"? [Answer: *tiṇṇaṃ*, *catunnaṃ*.
*Tissocattasso yomhi savibhattīnaṃ*: In the locative case (*yo*), for the three and four [numbers] accompanied by their case-endings, *tisso* and *catasso* occur respectively in the feminine;
as in *tisso*, *catasso*. *Tīṇicattāri napuṃsake*:
In the locative case (*yo*) for the three and four [numbers] accompanied by their case-endings, *tīṇi* and *cattāri* occur respectively in the neuter; as in *tīṇi*, *cattāri*.
*Pume tayocattāro*:
In the masculine gender, for the forms *ti* and *cattāri* when accompanied by case endings (*savibhattīnam*), *tayo* and *cattāro* occur respectively;
or [the form] *caturo* occurs for *cattāri*.

Whatever [form] belongs to the word *cattāro* (four) together with its case endings is either *caturo* in the masculine gender; as in *caturo janā saṃvidhāya* ("four people having made an arrangement"). How so? Because of a transposition of genders (*liṅgavipallāsa*), as in *caturo nimittena addasāsiṃ* ("I saw four by means of a sign").

For the forms *mayaṃ*, *amhaṃ*, *assa*, *yeyaṃ*, *svaṃ*, and *amhaṃ* together with their case endings, the forms *asmākaṃ*, *amhākaṃ*, *mamaṃ*, and *mama* occur respectively; that is, *asmākaṃ*, *amhākaṃ*; *mamaṃ*, *mama*.
*Simhi ahaṃ*:
after *sim*, when followed by a case ending, *ahaṃ* becomes *amhaṃ*; thus, *amhaṃ*.
*Tumhassa tuvaṃ tvam amhi ca*: after *tumha*, [the forms] *tuvaṃ*, *tvaṃ*, and *amhi* [occur].
In the case of *amha* and *simha*, when followed by a suffix containing the vibhatti (case ending) *tuvaṃ*, they become *tuvaṃ* and *tvaṃ* respectively: *tuvaṃ*, *tvaṃ*.
For *taya* and *tayīnaṃ*, there is optionally *tvaṃ*;
for *tassa* and for *taya* and *tayīnaṃ*, the letter *ta* becomes *ta*: *tvayā*, *tayā*; *tvayi*, *tayi*.
*Smāmhi tvamhā-*:

After *smāmhi*, *tvamhā* optionally occurs for the form *tumha* when it possesses a case ending (*savibhatti*). *Pattā nissaṃsayaṃ*: [This rule] certainly applies to the forms ending in *tvamhā*. *Vātveva tvayā*: Or rather, [the substitution] becomes *tvayā*.
*Ntantunaṃ nto yo mhi paṭhame-*: In the first [chapter], *nto* is substituted for *nta* and *tu-naṃ*.
In the first [case], for words ending in *-nt* along with their case endings, the substitution of *nto* optionally occurs: *gacchanto*, *gacchantā*;

*guṇavanto*, *guṇavantā*. In the [sixth] case ending *-nam*, for words ending in *-nt* along with their case endings, the substitution of *tam* optionally occurs: *gacchataṃ*, *gacchantānaṃ*; *guṇavataṃ*, *guṇavantānaṃ*.
