In place of the suffixes *sādi*, *sū*, *tanta*, and *naṃ* when accompanied by case endings, *to*, *tā*, *ti*, and *ta* optionally occur respectively: *gacchato*, *gacchantassa*;
*guṇavato*, *guṇavantassa*; *gacchatā*, *gacchantamhā*; *guṇavatā*, *guṇavantamhā*; *gacchati*.
*gacchante*; *guṇavati*, *guṇavante*; *gacchatā*, *gacchantena*; *guṇavatā*, *guṇavantena*.
Regarding the rule *ṭaṭāaṃ ge*:

when *ge* follows, the substitutes *ṭa*, *ṭā*, and *aṃ* occur for the forms ending in *nta* and *tuna* along with their case endings; thus: *bho gaccha*, *bho gacchā*, *bhoka gacchaṃ*; *bho guṇava*, *bho guṇavā*, *bho guṇavaṃ*.
In the case of *yomhi*, for the word *dvi* when accompanied by a case ending, *duve* and *dve* both occur individually: *duve*, *dve*.
In the case of *namhi*, [the forms] are optionally [the same].
Before the suffix *nam*, for the word *dvi* together with its case ending, there is optionally *duvinaṃ*; [alternatively] *duvinaṃ* or *dvinaṃ*.
For the word *rāja*: *raññaṃ*.
Before the suffix *nam*, for the word *rāja* together with its case ending, there is optionally *raññaṃ*; [alternatively] *raññaṃ* or *rajānaṃ*.
*Raññā* does not [occur] among us.
*Raññā* is not known among us with its distinctively analyzed vowel; [examples are] *raññā kataṃ* (done by the king) and *raññā nissaṭaṃ* (escaped from the king).
*Rañño*, *raññassa*, and *rājino* are [the forms].
For the word *rājan* when followed by a case-ending (*savibhatti*), the forms *rañño*, *raññassa*, and *rājino* occur;
[and] *raññe*, *rājini*.
In the locative singular (*smimhi*), for *rājan* when followed by a case-ending, the forms *raññe* and *rājini* occur.
Or in a compound:

In the domain of compounds, these substitutions for *rāja* optionally occur: *kāsiraññā*, *kāsirājena*; *kāsiraññā*, *kāsirājasmā*; *kāsirañño*, *kāsirājassa*; *kāsiraññe*, *kāsirāje*. In [the locative suffix] *smiṃ*, [the forms] *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* [are substituted].
*Tayi* [is substituted for *tvaṃ*].
In the case of the words *tumha* and *amha* with their case endings, *tayi* and *mayi* occur respectively: *tayi*, *mayi*.
In the case of the words *tumha* and *amha* with their case endings, *taṃ*, *maṃ*, *tavaṃ*, and *mamaṃ* occur respectively: *taṃ*, *maṃ*, *tavaṃ*, *mamaṃ*.

*Nāsmāsutayāmayā-*: In our place (*asmāsu*), the forms *tayā* and *mayā* replace the words *tumha* and *amha*, respectively, along with their case endings (*savibhattīnaṃ*). For example: *tayā kataṃ* (done by you), *mayā kataṃ* (done by me); *tayā nissaṭaṃ* (escaped by you), *mayā nissaṭaṃ* (escaped by me).
[The forms] *tava*, *mama*, *tuyhaṃ*, and *mayhaṃ* [are used for the genitive].
The forms *tava*, *tumhaṃ*, *tuyhaṃ*, *mama*, and *mayhaṃ* arise respectively from the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* when they are accompanied by case endings: *tava*, *tumhaṃ*; *mama*, *mayhaṃ*.

In the locative singular (*namhi*), the forms *ṅaṃ*, *ṅā*, and *kaṃ* arise individually from the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* when they are accompanied by case endings: *tumhaṃ*, *tumhākaṃ*; *amhaṃ*, *amhākaṃ*. Here, the correspondence [of specific forms to specific cases] is not intended to be strictly observed.

In the second person, in the dative case (*yomhi*), the forms *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ*—along with their respective case endings—optionally become *ṅaṃ*, *ṅā*, and *kaṃ*. Thus: *tumhaṃ/tumhākaṃ/tumhe*; *amhaṃ/amhākaṃ/amhe*.
[This applies] from the ablative onwards (*apādādo*) within a single sentence (*padatekavākye*).

This much should be understood as the subject matter: that by which a meaning is conveyed is a *pada* (word), whether it ends in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) or a personal ending (*tyādyānta*); a collection of words is a *vākya* (sentence). Regarding the rule *yonaṃ hisva pañcamyā vo no*:

when the forms *yuṣm-* and *asm-* occur after a word ending in a case other than the ablative (*apañcamiyā*), and stand within a single sentence (*ekavākye ṭhitānaṃ*) following a word beginning with *p-*, they are replaced respectively by *vo* and *no*. (Note: This refers to the grammatical substitution rules for the second and first person pronouns in Pali.)
The forms with case endings for you (plural) and us (plural) are as follows, in their respective order: *tiṭṭhatha vo*, *tiṭṭhatha tumhe*;
*tiṭṭhāma no*, *tiṭṭhāma mayaṃ*; *passati vo*, *passati tumhe*; *passati no*, *passati amhe*;
*dīyate vo*, *dīyate tumhaṃ*; *dīyate no*.

*Diyyate amhaṃ*; *dhanaṃ vo*, *dhanaṃ tumhaṃ*; *dhanaṃ no*, *dhanaṃ amhaṃ*; *kataṃ vo*, *kataṃ tumhehi*; *kataṃ no*, *kataṃ amhehi*—excluding the ablative case (*apañcamyāti*). For example: *nissaṭaṃ tumhehi*, *nissaṭaṃ amhehi*; and specifically regarding the ablative:
*“Balañca bhikkhūnamanuppadinnaṃ, tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakan”* (And strength was bestowed upon the monks;
by you, abundant merit has been produced).

*Padato tveva tumhe tiṭṭhatha*: "You stand"—this occurs when there is a single sentence, such as: *Devadatto tiṭṭhati gāme, tumhe tiṭṭhatha nagare* ("Devadatta stands in the village; you stand in the city"). *Savibhattīnaṃ tveva*: "Even with case endings"—as in: *Arahāti dhammo tumhādīnaṃ; arahāti dhammo amhādisānaṃ* ("The Dhamma is worthy for those like you; the Dhamma is worthy for those like us"). *Teme nāse*:
Regarding *te* and *me*, when they follow a word ending in the ablative (*apādāda*) within a single sentence, [the following rules apply] to the words *tumha* and *amha* standing [in that position].
In the case of forms with case endings (*savibhattīnaṃ*), *te* and *me* are used respectively, as follows: *kataṃ te*, *kataṃ tayā*; *kataṃ me*, *kataṃ mayā*;
*dīyate te*, *dīyate tava*; *dīyate me*, *dīyate mama*; *dhanaṃ te*, *dhanaṃ me*, *dhanaṃ mama*. [This applies] in subsequent reference (*anvādese*).

In the context of repeating what has been stated, the substitutes for the words *tumha* and *amha* always occur as alternative forms (*punabbidhāna*). For example: "The village is your possession," and "the country is your possession.

Alternatively, when preceded by another word ending in the nominative case (*paṭhamantā*), the substitutes for *tumha* and *amha* may optionally occur even in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādese*), provided that a preceding word exists.
"In the village a cloth is yours, and in the city a blanket is yours; and in the city a blanket is yours. What is the purpose of *sapubbā*?
"A cloth is yours, and a blanket is yours. What is the purpose of *paṭhamantā*? "In the city a cloth is yours, and in the village a blanket is yours.
[This rule does not apply] in the case of the *vavāha* and *heva* suffixes.
When used in conjunction with *ca* and other particles, the substitutes for the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* do not occur:
"The village is your possession and my possession"; "The village is either your possession or my possession";
"The village is your possession indeed, or my possession indeed"; "The village is your possession alone, or my possession alone."
Thus it should be illustrated in all cases. What is the meaning of *yoge* (in connection with)? "The village is your possession (*pariggaha*), and the city is my possession.
In the sense of seeing (*dassana*), excluding the act of looking (*ālocana*).

When words denoting the sense of seeing—excluding those referring to the act of looking—are employed, there is no substitution of *tumha*, *amha*, or *sadda*. Examples: "The village has come for your sake," "The village has come for our sake. Why "excluding the act of looking"? Example: "The village looks at you," "The village looks at us."

The vocative preceding [the possessive pronoun] is as if non-existent—meaning it is as if not present—when the words *tumha* and *amha* undergo their respective substitutions; for example: *devadatta tava pariggaho*.
Why "vocative"? [Counter-example: *kambalo te pariggaho*. Why "preceding"? [Counter-example: *mayā etaṃ sabbaṃ akkhātaṃ*.
O best of the twice-born, if something does not exist for another, would there not be a prohibition against it being called an ablative (*apādāna*)? What is the purpose of the particle *iva*?
It is so that "hearing" (*savana*) may occur.
A general term is not used when the sense is already singular.
In a construction of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), when a general term follows [another word], it does not exist as if it were non-existent, and thus it serves as an address.

In the example “*māṇavaka jaṭilaka tepariggaho*” (O young man with matted hair, this is your possession), even though another person is present, the substitution occurs by taking the preceding form. What is meant by “a general term”? For example:

“*Devadatta māṇavaka tava pariggaho*” (O young man Devadatta, this is your possession). Why is it specified that they must have the same referent (*ekattha*)? For example: “*Devadatta yaññadatta tumhaṃ pariggaho*” (O Devadatta and Yaññadatta, this is your possession).
Regarding *bahūsu vā*:

when a plural vocative is present, the general term (*sāmaññavacana*) does not appear as if it were non-existent within the compound; for example: *brāhmaṇā guṇavanto tumhākaṃ pariggaho* (virtuous Brahmins are your retinue) or *brāhmaṇā guṇavanto vo pariggaho*.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the suffixes beginning with *si*, in the *Vutti* commentary on the *Moggallāna-vyākaraṇa*.

"Syādi with syādi becomes a single word"—it should be understood that this is the governing rule (*adhikāra*): that which ends in a *syādi* suffix becomes a single word when combined with another [word] ending in a *syādi* suffix. Furthermore, this state of becoming a single word from things that have different meanings is called a compound (*samāsa*).
[The following words are used] in the sense of "innumerable," "case-ending completion," "proximity," "totality," "absence," "according to," "after," and "simultaneously."

An indeclinable (*asaṃkhya*) ending in *syādi* (the suffixes of the nominative case, etc.), when occurring in the sense of a case ending (*vibhatti*), forms a compound (*ekattha*) with another word ending in *syādi*.

In that regard, first concerning the sense of a case ending: "discourse proceeded among women" (*itthisu kathā pavattā*) becomes *adhitthi*; "abundance" (*sampatti*) is twofold: personal abundance (*attasampatti*) and prosperity (*samiddhi*).
Thus, "abundant in Brahmins" (*brahmaṃ sampunnaṃ*) is *sabrahmaṃ*, as in "among the Licchavis" (*licchavīnaṃ*); "abundance of alms" (*bhikkhānaṃ samiddhi*) is *subhikkhaṃ*.
*Upakumbham* (near the jar) means in the vicinity of the jar. *Satiṇamajjho harati* (he carries [it] with the grass in the middle) indicates completeness.

*Sāggyadhīte* (the student has finished his studies) indicates the absence of an action. The absence of a related entity is of many kinds: therein, in the case of the absence of power, *viggatā iddhi* (power departed) becomes *iddhivigata*;

in the case of the absence of meaning, *abhāvo makkhikānam* (absence of flies) becomes *nimmakkhikaṃ*; in the case of the absence of exceeding, *atigatāni tiṇāni* (grass exceeded) becomes *nittiṇaṃ*; in the case of the absence of arrival, *atigataṃ*.
*Lahupāpuraṇaṃ* means "very quickly filling"; the meaning is that this is not the time for the enjoyment of a light cloak (*lahupāpuraṇa*).
*Yathā* has many meanings: therein, in the sense of fitness—*surūpo vahati* (he carries it beautifully); in the sense of sequence—*anvaddhamāsaṃ* (every half-month);

in the sense of not overstepping a purpose—*yathāsatti* (according to one's ability); in the sense of similarity—*sadiso kikhiyā sakikhi* (similar to a partridge, "partridge-like"); in the sense of order—*anujeṭṭhaṃ* (by seniority); in the sense of posteriority—*pacchā*.
[The particle] *yathā* is used in the sense of "consequently" (*anurathaṃ*), "simultaneously" (*yugapat*), "in the same object" (*ekattha*), "with a wheel" (*sacakkam*), and "treasure" (*nidhi*).
When *yathā* occurs in the sense of "equality" (*tulyattha*), it does not form a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*); for example: *yathā devadatto tathā yaññadatto*.

*Yāva* in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). When the word *yāva* is used in the sense of restriction, it forms a compound with a form ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*); restriction means limitation to a specific measure. Examples:

*yāvāmattaṃ brāhmaṇe āmantaya* (invite as many Brahmins as there are), *yāvajīvaṃ* (for as long as life lasts). What is the purpose of "in the sense of restriction"? [To exclude cases like: *yāva dinnaṃ tāva* (as much as was given).
I do not remember how much was eaten: "How much was eaten by me?
The suffixes *pari*, *ā*, *pa*, *upa*, *paccā*, and *vā* optionally form a single compound with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*).
For example: *paripabbataṃ vassi devo* (the rain fell all around the mountain) or *paripabbatā*.
The rain fell away from the mountain, from away from the mountain; the rain fell up to Pāṭaliputta, up to Pāṭaliputta; outside the village, from outside the village;

across the mountain, from across the mountain; before the meal, from before the meal; after the meal, from after the meal—this is the section on "near" (*samīpa*) and "away" (*āya*) in the governing rule for *vīti*.

The word *anu*, when used in the senses of proximity (*sāmīpya*) or extension (*āyāma*), optionally forms a compound with a noun ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*). Examples: *anuvanamaṃ asani gatā* ("the thunderbolt went along the forest") and *anugaṅgaṃ Bārāṇasī* ("Vārāṇasī [lies] along the Gaṅgā"). Why say "in the senses of proximity and extension"? Consider: *rukkhaṃ anu vijjotate vijju* ("the lightning flashes near the tree"). Regarding *tiṭṭhagvādini*:

words such as *tiṭṭhagu* and others are treated as indeclinables (*nipāta*) in the sense of forming a compound. *Tiṭṭhagu* means "the time at which cows stand. (Note: *tiṭṭhanti gāvo yasmiṃ kāle ti tiṭṭhagu*).
*Kālo* (time); *vahaggu*, *kālo*; *āyatigavaṃ*, *khaleyavaṃ*, *lūnayavaṃ*, *lūyamānayavaṃ*, etc.—here too there is the suffix *-vanta*.

*Kesākesi* (hair-to-hair), *daṇḍādaṇḍi* (staff-to-staff)—likewise, it also has the sense of "limit" (*velā*) and "manifestation" (*pabhāva*). *Pāto nahānaṃ* (morning bathing) = *pātanahānaṃ*; *sāyaṃ nahānaṃ* (evening bathing) = *sāyanahānaṃ*;
*pātakālaṃ* (morning time), *sāyakālaṃ* (evening time); *pātamaghaṃ* (morning cloud), *sāyamaghaṃ* (evening cloud); *pātamaggaṃ* (morning path), *sāyamaggaṃ* (evening path).

*Ore*, *paṭi*, *pāre*, *majjhe*, *heṭṭhā*, *uddha*, and *adho* optionally form a compound with a word ending in the sixth case (genitive). Due to conventional usage (*nipātana*), they take the form of a single vowel:

*ore gaṅgaṃ* (on this side of the Ganges), *upari sikharaṃ* (above the peak), *paṭi sotaṃ* (against the current), *pāre yamunaṃ* (beyond the Yamunā), *majjhe gaṅgaṃ* (in the middle of the Ganges), *heṭṭhā pāsādaṃ* (below the palace), *uddha gaṅgaṃ* (above the Ganges).
*Adhogaṅgaṃ*; *antopāsādaṃ*—furthermore, there are also forms such as *vāvidhānā gaṅgā* or *oramiccā*. That which is neuter:

whatever single-meaning word has not been [previously] analyzed should be understood as being of the neuter gender; likewise, it has been illustrated [above]. Or, in some cases, by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), as in *yathāparisaṃ*, *yathāparisāya*; the meaning is "according to each respective assembly" (*sakāya sakāya parisāyā*).
Amādi-:
A word ending in *amā* and so forth frequently forms a single compound with a word ending in a *syādi* (nominative) case-suffix; e.g., *gāmaṃ gato* becomes *gāmagato*;
*muhuttaṃ sukhaṃ* becomes *muhuttasukhaṃ*. In the case of a *upapada* compound, it may optionally occur; e.g., *kumbhakāro*, *sapāko*, *tantavāyo*, *carā*.
*harantam*, *anaktavantam*, and *vākyam* are [examples of] the accusative case ending in *-am*; likewise, *dhammaṃ suṇanto*, *dhammaṃ suṇamāno*, and *odanaṃ bhuttavā*.

*Raññā hato* is "killed by the king" (*rājahato*); *asinā chinno* is "cut by a sword" (*asicchinno*). *Pitusadiso* is "like a father"; *pitusamo* is "equal to a father. *Sukhasahagataṃ* is "accompanied by pleasure.

*Dadhinā upasittaṃ bhojanaṃ* is "food sprinkled with curds" (*dadhibhojanaṃ*); *guḷena misso odano* is "rice mixed with sugar" (*guḷodano*). Since the action of being sprinkled and so forth is expressed by the word itself (the noun), there is no possessive relation (*ayuttattha*) [between the noun and the implied action].

In some cases there is only the compound (vutti); in others, only the sentence (vākya). For example: *urago pādapo* (a snake-tree), where there is only the sentence; *pharasunā chinnavā* (cut by an axe). [Examples of compounds:

*dassanena pahātabbā* (to be abandoned by seeing); *buddhasadeyyaṃ* (given to the Buddha) means *buddhadeyyaṃ*; *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post) becomes *yūpadāru*; *rajanāya doṇi* (a vat for dyeing) becomes *rajanadoṇi*. Here it does not occur: *saṅghassa dātabbaṃ* (to be given to the Saṅgha)—how so? Because the meaning is "this is for that purpose," it occurs when another word’s meaning is involved (*aññapadatthe*).

Examples: *savarahiṃ bhayaṃ* (fear from the Savaras) becomes *savarabhayaṃ*; *gāmaniggato* (gone out from the village); *methunāpeto* (driven away from sexual intercourse). In some cases there is only the compound: *kammajaṃ* (born of karma), *cittajaṃ* (born of mind)—here it does not occur: *rukkhā patito* (fallen from a tree).
In the sense of completion through the extraction of the highest degree from a multitude, there is no [suffix] after "rājapurisa" (king’s man)—as in *rañño puriso* = *rājapuriso*.
Examples include: *mamānukubbaṃ* (imitating me); *mamānu kurumāno* (acting like me); *gunnaṃ kaṇhā sampannakhīratamā* (among cows, the black one is the most excellent in milk);

*sissānaṃ pañcamo* (the fifth among pupils); *paṭassa sukkatā* (the whiteness of the cloth). In some cases, it does indeed occur: *vattamānasāmīpyaṃ*—as in *kathaṃ brāhmaṇassa sukkā* (how is the Brahmin’s [cloth] being whitened?).
Because of the presence of expectation (*sāpekkhatā*), it does not occur—yet here there is indeed the scent of sandalwood, the sound of a river, the form of a maiden, and the touch of the body.
"The taste of fruit" means: the sourness of fruits, the bitterness of fruits, the sweetness of fruits. "The Brahmin’s purity" means:

they take [it] from the house. Because of the presence of expectation, it does not occur—[in the phrase] "the wealth of King Pāṭaliputtaka," the genitive case is used because of the relationship with the wealth.

In the case of *pāṭaliputtaka*, there will be no connection because of the absence of relation; in the phrase "the king’s cow, horse, and man," due to the distinctness of the referents, there is only a syntactical construction (*vākya*).

However, in the state of unity of meaning (*ekatthibhāva*), the compound form occurs: "the king’s cow-horse-man" (*rājagavāssapurisa*). Examples of this are: *dānesoṇḍo* (greedy for giving), *dānasoṇḍo*; *dhammarato* (delighting in the Dhamma);

*dānabhirato* (delighting in giving)—in some cases, these occur only as compounds. Other examples: *kucchisayo* (lying in the womb), *thalaṭṭho* (standing on dry land), *paṅkajaṃ* (born from the mud).
In this context, there is no lotus regarding moderation in food; [there is] guarding the doors of the sense faculties; and when seated on a seat, one should sit on the seat.

Regarding "qualification by way of co-referentiality" (*visesanamekatthena*): a qualifying word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) forms a compound (*ekattha*) with a qualified word (*visessa*) ending in a case-suffix that is coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*); for example, *nīlañca*...
"Taṃ uppalañce" means a blue lotus; "chinnañca taṃ parūḷhañce" means cut and grown back; "satthiva satthī" means like a sword, [thus] "satthī ca sāsāmā ce" means a sword-bearer;
"sīhova sīho" means like a lion, [thus] "muni ca so sīho vā" means a sage-lion; "sīlameva dhanaṃ" means virtue-treasure—these are merely examples of compounds.
Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and Citta the householder are [proper names]. In some cases, it is simply a grammatical function (vutti).
"Black snake"; "red rice. [Question: What is the purpose of the qualification "viśeṣanaṃ"? [Answer: "Woodcutter-snake" (a snake that is a woodcutter). [Question:

What is the purpose of the qualification "ekatthe" (in a single meaning)? [Answer: "Different from black"—how so? "One who lives by leaves," "one who has attained livelihood," "born in the month"—these will occur in the sense of a different word (*aññapadatthe*). [The rule applies] to the negative particle (*nañ*).
When *nañ* ending in a case-suffix is combined with another word ending in a case-suffix, it forms a single compound (*ekattha*). For example: *abrāhmaṇo* ("one who is not a brahmin").

Due to the governing rule of "generally" (*bahulādhikārato*), this occurs even with certain words that lack semantic compatibility: *apunageyyā gāthā* ("a verse not to be sung again"), *amūlamūlaṃ gantvā* ("having gone from root to root"), and *īsakaḷāro īsapiṅgalo* ("slightly grey, slightly tawny")—in such cases, the compound is formed with *nañ* ending in a case-suffix.
However, this does not apply to a full sentence, because there is no possibility of over-extension (*atippasaṅgābhāvā*).

In the rule concerning *niccam-asy-ādi* (always [forming a compound] with words beginning with *asya*), the word *ku-* and words beginning with *pā-* form a single meaning with a word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) always, except in the scope of other rules such as *syadi-vidhi*; for example:
*kucchito brāhmaṇo* (a contemptible Brahmin) becomes *kubrāhmaṇo*; *īsaṃ uṇhaṃ* (slightly warm) becomes *kaduṇhaṃ*. Also: *panāyako*, *abhiseko*, *pakarittvā*, *pakataṃ*.

A bad man (*duppurisa*), a bad deed (*dukkata*); a good man (*supurisa*), a good deed (*sukata*); praised (*abhitthuta*), excessively praised (*atitthuta*); one who is eager (*ākaḷāra*), one who is bound (*ābaddha*).
The suffixes beginning with *pā-* occur after a word in the nominative case when it has the sense of "gone" and so forth: *pācariyo* ("one who has gone beyond the teacher," i.e., a student).

The suffixes beginning with *anta-* occur after a word in the accusative case when it has the sense of "gone beyond" and so forth: *atimañco* ("one who has gone beyond the bed"), *atimālo*. The suffixes beginning with *ava-* occur after a word in the instrumental case when it has the sense of "thrown down" and so forth: *avakuṭṭhaṃ*.

*Vana* becomes *ava* before *kokila*, as in *avakokila*; *maya* becomes *ava* before *pūraya*, as in *avapūraya*. *Pari* and *adhi* become *pa* and *a* respectively when followed by a word in the fourth case (*catutthī*) in the sense of "sickness" and so forth, as in *parigilāna* ("sick") and *adhyetavya* ("to be studied").

*Pa* and *a* become *pa* and *a* respectively when followed by a word in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of "separation," as in *pariggaha* ("seizing") and *adhyayana* ("study"). *Ni* becomes *ni* or *nī* before a word in the seventh case (*sattamī*), as in *nikkhanta kosambiyā* ("departed from Kosambī"), becoming *nikkosambi*. Regarding the rule for *assa* and other such forms, [it is asked]:
"What tree does it shine upon? (*kiṃ rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate*).
Cī with words denoting action.
A word ending in the suffix *cī* forms a compound with words ending in *syat*, provided they denote an action; e.g., *malinīkariya*.
[The suffix *alaṃ* is used] in the senses of ornament, respect, and disrespect.

Words such as *bhusa* (excessively), *alaṃ* (enough), *sakkaccaṃ* (respectfully), and *asakkaccaṃ* (irrespectfully) become compound words (*ekattā*) with forms ending in the *syādi* (case endings) that denote an action (*kriyāttha*). Examples: *alaṃkariya*, *sakkacca*, *asakkacca*. Why "in the sense of *bhusa* and so forth"? Consider:
*alaṃ bhutvā gato* (having eaten enough, he went); *sakkatvā gato* (having honored, he went); *asakkatvā gato* (having not honored, he went).
The meaning is: "sufficient," "beautiful," or "not beautiful."

And others—other words also frequently become compound expressions (ekattha) with words ending in case-suffixes (syādyanta) that denote action (kriyāttha); for example: *purobhuya*, *tirobhuya*, *tirokariya*, *urasikariya*, *manasikariya*, *majjhekariya*, *tuṇhibhuya*. [The rule applies] optionally when there is not a single meaning (*vānekaññatthe*).
A plurality [ending] may become singular in the sense of another word: "one who has many riches" is *abahu-dhana*;
"one whose ears are long" is *lamba-kaṇṇa*; "one who has a thunderbolt in his hand" is *vajira-pāṇi*;
"a forest where there are many rutting elephants" is *matta-bahu-mātaṅgaṃ vanaṃ*; "this monkey has climbed the tree" is *ārūḷha-vānaro*. [Examples of] conquered...
One whose faculties are not conquered is "one with unconquered faculties" (*ajitindriyo*). One for whom food has not been given is "one who eats what is not given" (*adinnabhojano*).

That from which the black [parts] have departed, as in the case of a cloth, is "one from whom the black has departed" (*apagatakāḷako*). Those to whom the *daśā* (fringes/stages) have approached are "those with approaching *daśā*" (*upadasā*);

that is, those with *daśā* close at hand, or those with *daśā* not far off. They are those for whom the *daśā* are excessive, or those whose measure is three *daśā*, thus "the Thirty-three" (*tidasā*). How so? Because the word *daśa* is used here in the sense of "manifestation" (*khyāne*).

Due to the proximity of the word *parimāṇa* (measure/number), as in: "five is the measure of these" (*pañcaparimāṇaṃ imesaṃ*) = *pañcakā* (groups of five); "two or three is the measure of these" (*dve vā tayo vā parimāṇaṃ imesaṃ*) = *dvattayo*;
or in the sense of the word *vā* (or), as in: "two or three" (*ve vā tayo vā*) = *dvattayo*;

"that which is the intermediate space between the southern and eastern directions" (*dakkhiṇassā ca pubbassā ca disāya yad antarālaṃ*) = *dakkhiṇapubbā* (southeast); or "the south and the east" (*dakkhiṇā ca sā pubbā ca*); or "together with... (*saha*).
"Puttenāgato" means "accompanied by a son," with the sense of "possessing hair" (salomako) being that "hair exists" (vijjamānalomako); likewise for "sapakkhako.

In the phrase "atthikhīrā, brāhmaṇi," the word *atthi* is a particle used in the sense of existence (*vijjamānatthe*). In some instances, when its meaning is already conveyed, other words are not employed.
"Kaṇṭhekāḷo" means one whose throat-region is black. "Oṭṭhamukho" means one whose mouth is like a lip. "Kesasaṅghāto" means a mass of hair.
‘He has a crest of hair’ is *kesacūḷo*; ‘he has an ornament made of gold’ is *suvaṇṇālaṅkāro*; ‘his leaves have fallen’ is *papatitapaṇṇo*, [which is] *papaṇṇo*;
‘he has no sons existing’ is *avijjamānaputto*; ‘there are no sons for him’ is *aputto*—in some places the negative particle *na* does not occur [before the possessive suffix].

“He possesses five meals” (*pañcabhuttavanto*) or “he has his brother’s son” (*bhātuno putto assa atthi*) [are examples], according to the predominance of the rule [for the possessive suffix *vanta*].

In that context, having taken up [something] with that which is similar in form (*sarūpa*), whether it be in the locative or instrumental case, and having struck with it in battle—when there are multiple items of the same form, having taken them up with that [other] in battle, they become a single compound referring to another object. For example:
*kesākesi* (“grasping hair by hair”), as in “having grasped each other by the hair, a battle ensued”; likewise, *daṇḍādaṇḍi*.
"Having struck with sticks and being struck with sticks, a battle took place"—this is *daṇḍādaṇḍi*. "With fists against fists, they struck one another"—this is *muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi*.

Regarding the term *ci*: *ci* is a contraction of *ca* and *isi*. As for the form *nti*: therein, what is the meaning of *tena*? A battle took place having seized body against body (*kāyena kāyena*). Having seized and having struck—what is meant?
A battle took place having stood chariot against chariot (*rathe rathe*). What is meant by "battle"?
Having grasped hand to hand, friendship was established. [Question: What about being of similar form? [Answer:
Having struck with clubs and maces, battle proceeded. [This is] the meaning of *cattha*.

That which has multiple case-endings may become a single meaning; the meanings of the word *ca* (and) are: conjunction (*samuccaya*), aggregation (*aṇvācaya*), mutual connection (*itarītarayoga*), and collective totality (*samāhāra*).
Among these, the state of having multiple meanings is possible in the cases of conjunction and aggregation.

For therein, conjunction is the accumulation of things that are mutually independent and primarily focused on themselves toward some specific action—just as in the example: "He [gives] fuel... (*dave*).

And [the rule] "he cuts from the *khadira* and the *palāsa*" is an *anvācaya* (consecutive addition), wherein one [element] is prescribed as the primary factor (*padhāna*) and the other as secondary (*guṇa*), as in:

"Go for alms and drive the cows. However, when another type is possible—namely, where there is a mutual dependence between the parts of a whole following a distinction [of status], that is *itarītarayoga* (mutual conjunction)—as in "Sāriputta and Moggallāna," because the parts themselves are primary.

It is always plural; for it is a collective (samāhāra) compound—wherein the distinction between the parts is concealed and the whole is predominant—in which the members are mutually dependent, such as *chattupāhana* (umbrella and sandals).
However, because this [latter type] has the whole as its predominant meaning, it takes the singular number.

Furthermore, these two types—the collective (*samāhāra*) and the reciprocal conjunction (*itaretarayoga*)—are prescribed extensively and have restricted domains; herein is the classification of their domains as found in the *Nirutti-piṭaka*.
For hands, musical instruments, equipment, and body parts; for constant enemies; for notions of number and measurement;
for small creatures; for cooking pots and hearths; for those sharing a common practice; for the teachings of different schools; for distinctions of gender; for various opposing things;
and for directions and rivers—there is always a compound in the sense of a collective whole (*samāhāra-ekattha*).
Or, there is the mutual conjunction of grass, trees, cattle, birds, wealth, grain, condiments, and countries. Of the limbs of a living being—the eye and ear;
the mouth and nose; the jaw and neck; the skin, flesh, and blood; name-and-form; aging and death.
Of the components of musical instruments—the lute, drum, and tambourine; the muraja drum and the gomukha horn; the conch and the cymbal.

The soft and the drum-like; singing and instrumental music; the clapping of hands—these are for those who are fit; the plow and the hoe; the yoke and the ploughshare—these are for the components of an army:
the sword, the spear, the javelin, and the club; the sword and shield; the cat and the mouse; the crow and the owl;
the Naga and the Supaṇṇa—these are for designations of number and measure: one and two, two and three; three and four, four and five; ten and eleven—for small creatures: the insect and the moth.
The Kutthaki and Pillika; the Daṃsa and Makasa; the Makkhika and Kipillika—[these being] the Pavana and Vaddhāla;
the Orabbhika and Sukarika; the Sākuntika and Māgavika;
the Sapāka and Vaddhāla; the Vena and Rathakāra; the Pukkusa and Chaṇḍāla—[these being] the Caraṇasādhāraṇa; the Atisabha and Bhāradvāja; the Kaṭha and Kālāpa.
Virtue and wisdom; serenity and insight; knowledge and conduct—the *Ekajjhāyana* and the *Pāvacana*;

the *Dīgha* and *Majjhima*; the *Ekuttara* and the *Saṃyuttaka*; the *Khandhaka* and the *Vibhaṅga*; the *Liṅgavisesāna*, namely the *Itthivimāna* and *Purisavimāna*; the *Dāsivimāna* and *Dāsavimāna*; robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
grass, wood, branches, and foliage; and also: "He is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
It is seen as various opposites: wholesome and unwholesome; blameworthy and blameless; inferior and superior;
dark and bright; clever and wicked; lower and higher; east and west among the directions;
south and north; southeast; northeast; southwest; northwest; and the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, the Mahī and Sarabhū among rivers.
Of specific types of grasses: *kāsakusaṃ*, *kāsakusā*; *usīrabīraṇaṃ*, *usīrabīraṇā*; *muñjababbajaṃ*, *muñjababbajā*. Of the remains of trees:
*khadirapalāsaṃ*, *khadirapalāsā*; *dhavāssakaṇṇaṃ*, *dhavāssakaṇṇā*; *pilakkhanigrodhaṃ*, *pilakkhanigrodhā*;
*assatthakapitthanaṃ*, *assatthakapitthānā*; *sākasālaṃ*, *sākasālā*. Of specific types of animals: *gaja*...
A cow and a goat, a cow and a goat; a cow and a buffalo, a cow and a buffalo; an antelope and a cow-buffalo, an antelope and a cow-buffalo; an antelope and a boar, an antelope and a boar;

a goat and a sheep, a goat and a sheep; a dog and a pig, a dog and a pig; an elephant, a cow, a horse, and a mare—an elephant, a cow, a horse, and a mare—[and among specific birds] a swan and a quail, a swan and a quail;
a kāraṇḍava duck and a crane, a kāraṇḍava duck and a crane; a heron and a balāka crane, a heron and a balāka crane—[and among riches] gold and bullion.
Gold and silver; gems, conch shells, pearls, and coral; gems, conch shells, pearls, and beryl; gold and silver; gold and silver—of grains:
rice and barley; rice and barley; sesame, mung beans, and black gram; sesame, mung beans, and black gram—of pulses:
peas and lentils; peas and lentils—of condiments: potherbs and onions; potherbs and onions; cow’s milk and buffalo’s milk.
Gabya and Mahisa; Eneyya and Varaha, Eneyyas and Varahas; Migamayu and Mayura, Migamayus and Mayuras—[these are] the names of countries:
Kasi and Kosala, Kasikas and Kosalas; Vajji and Malla, Vajjis and Mallas; Ceti and Vamsa, Cetis and Vamsas; Maccha and Surasena, Macchas and Surasenans;
Kuru and Pancala, Kurus and Pancalas.
Mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is as follows: the moon and the sun, ascetics and brahmins, mother and father, and so forth.

In this section on the state of being a single referent (*ekatthibhāva*), that which was stated previously is placed first; because there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence, it remains as it was.

However, in some cases, even an inversion occurs due to the rule of "frequently" (*bahula*). For example: "the king of teeth" is *rājadanta* (the front tooth). In some instances, disregard for the sequence is shown by placing the prior time [element] last.
This is an irregular formation (*paranipāta*). [Examples include: *littavāsita*, *naggamusita*, *sittasammaṭṭha*, *bhaṭṭhaluñcita*.

Regarding the rule that when there is a single meaning in a compound, some authorities restrict the first member to various forms, it should be understood here that this is not stated because of the observation of exceptions.
In a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the neuter gender is used.

In a compound expressing a single meaning (*ekattha*) through a collective sense (*samāhāra*), that [compound] takes the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*); this has been illustrated as follows: "in some cases it does not occur," as indicated by the examples *sabhāparisā* ("an assembly of the council") and *ādhipaccaparivāro* ("a retinue of subordinate authority"). Also: *chandapārisuddhi* ("intention and purity") and *paṭisandhippavattiyaṃ* ("in the occurrence of rebirth-linking").

Regarding numbers and so forth: in a collective compound expressing a single meaning, a number and so forth take the neuter gender; for example, *pañcagavaṃ* ("five cows") and *catuppathaṃ* ("a crossroads"). Because the collective sense is a unity, there is only the singular number. Only in the case of a collective [sense] do we have *pañcakapālo pūvo* ("a five-bread cake") and *tiputto* ("having three sons").

In some instances, there is neuter gender and singular number in the sense of the sixth case (genitive). For example: ‘the shadow of locusts’ becomes *salahacchāyaṃ*; likewise, ‘the shadow of birds’ becomes *sakuntacchāyaṃ*. [Examples of the sixth case in other forms:
*pāsādacchāyāyaṃ*, *pāsādacchāyāya*; *gharacchāyāyaṃ*, *gharacchāyā*. When referring to non-human beings (*amanussa*), the word *sabhā* takes the neuter gender and singular number.

The assembly of Brahmas (*brahmasabhā*); the assembly of gods (*devasabhā*); the assembly of Indra (*indasabhā*); the assembly of *yakkhas* (*yakkhasabhā*); the assembly of *sarakas* (*sarabhasabhā*)—the assembly of humans (*manussasabhā*), the assembly of kṣatriyas (*khattiyasabhā*), the assembly of kings (*rājasabhā*), and so forth.
Why [is it specified] "in some cases"? [Answer: *rājapuriso* (king’s man). In the case of *syādi* and similar suffixes, there is shortening.
In the neuter gender, when occurring before suffixes such as *si*, the final vowel becomes short. *Salabhacchāyaṃ*—why say "before suffixes such as *si*"? [Answer: *Salabhacchāye*.
Regarding the rule "of a *gha*-ending [word] that is not predominant":

for a *gha*-ending word that is not predominant and forms part of a compound, the final vowel becomes short before suffixes such as *si*; e.g., *bahumālo*, *poso*, *nikkosambi*, *ativāmoru*. Why say "that forms part of a compound" (*antassa*)? [Answer: *Kaññāpiyo*. Why say "not predominant" (*appadhānassa*)? [Answer: *Rājakumārī*; *brahmabandhū*.

In the case of *go* (cow), when it is not the predominant factor (*appadhāna*) and ends in *u*, the vowel *u* becomes *ū* before suffixes such as *syādi*; for example, *cittagū* (one who has gone to the mind). However, when it is the predominant factor, it remains *go*; and when it ends in *a* and is the predominant factor, it is *gokulaṃ*.
This applies to feminine nouns ending in *ā*.
The suffix *āp* occurs after a feminine noun ending in the letter *a*; for example, *dhammadinnā*.
After nouns beginning with *nada*, the suffix *ṇḍī* occurs in the feminine sense; for example, *nadī*, *mahī*, *kumārī*, *taruṇī*, *vāruṇī*, *gotamī*.
*Goto vā*. *Gāvī*, *go*;

this is a class-name (*ākati-gaṇa*). The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of specification, according to the rule: “In place of *ṅi*, there is optionally *to* for words ending in *n* or *t*. Also, [the suffixes] *yakkha*, etc., occur after the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*).
After *yakkha* and so forth, the suffix *inī* occurs in the feminine, and the suffix *ṅī* also occurs: *yakkhinī*, *yakkhi*; *nāginī*, *nāgī*; *sīhinī*, *sīhī*.
After *ārāmika* and so forth—the suffix *inī* occurs in the feminine after *ārāmika* and so forth: *ārāmikinī*; *anantarāsikinī*; *rājinī*.
In *saññā*, [the word] *mānusī* [is formed from] *mānusa*.
[The suffix] *-ī* occurs except after *mānusa*. For [the vowels] *u* and *vaṇṇa*, [the suffix] *nī* [is applied].

The suffix *nī* is frequently applied after words ending in the feminine suffixes *vaṇṇu* and *vaṇṇa*; for example: *sadāpayaṇtī*, *pāṇinī*, *daṇḍinī*, *khattabandhunī*, *paracittavidunī*. Why is it not applied after the word *mātṛ* (mother) from the beginning? Because the state of being female (*itthatta*) is understood even without a feminine suffix. After a word ending in *kt*, the suffix *nī* is frequently applied in the feminine sense only when another meaning [than the primary one] is intended; for example:

*sāhaṃ ahiṃsāratinī* ("I am one who delights in non-violence"), *tassā muṭṭhassatiniyā* ("of her, whose mindfulness is lost"), *sā vacchagiddhinī* ("she is one greedy for her calf"). Why "when another meaning is intended"? [Answer: *dhammarati* ("delight in the Dhamma").

*Gharaṇī* and others: words beginning with *gharaṇī* are correctly formed by means of the suffix *nī*. Examples are *gharaṇī*, *pokkharaṇī*; [the form] *īssattaṃ* is due to a specific grammatical substitution (*nipātana*). Alternatively, according to some teachers, there is the elision of *ya*:
*ācariyā* [is derived from] *ācariyā* (with the suffix *nī*) and *ācariyā* (with the elision of *ya*).
The suffix *-ānī* is applied after *mātula* and other words to denote a wife.
When denoting a wife, the suffix *-ānī* follows *mātula* and so forth: *mātulānī*, *varuṇānī*, *gahapatānī*, *ācariyānī*.
When not denoting a wife, it is used for a Kṣatriya woman: *khattiyā* or *khattiyānī*; *khattiyā*—according to the Nadā and Dīpa commentaries, when denoting a wife, it is *khattiyī*.

The words *ūru*, preceded by terms such as *upamāna* (comparison), *saṃhita* (joined), *sahita* (accompanied), *saññata* (restrained), *saha* (with), *sapha* (hoofed), *vāma* (left/beautiful), *lakkhaṇa* (characteristic), and so forth, take the feminine suffix *ū*;

for example: *karahorū* (elephant-trunk-thighed), *saṃhitorū* (well-knit-thighed), *sahitorū* (accompanied-thighed), *saññatorū* (restrained-thighed), *sahorū* (with-thighed), *saphorū* (hoofed-thighed), *vāmorū* (beautiful-thighed), *lakkhaṇorū* (characteristic-thighed). By means of the grammatical rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), the word *ū* [is also included]; for example: *brahmabandhū* (a woman who is a relative of a Brahmin). The word *yuvati* [also takes this suffix].
From the word *yuvan*, [the suffix] *hoti* occurs for the feminine: *yuvati*. For words ending in *-nt* and *-tu*, there is optionally *to* before the suffix *ṅīm*:
for words ending in *-nt* and *-tu*, *to* is optionally substituted before *ṅīm*; thus, *gacchantī* or *gacchatī*; *sīlavatī* or *sīlavantī*.
*Bhavato bhoto-*:
Before the suffix *ṅī*, the substitute *bhota* optionally occurs for *bhavata*; thus, *bhotī* or *bhavantī*. *Gossāvaṅi-*: [The substitute *avaṅ* occurs for *go* before the suffix *aṅ*.]
The suffixes *ṅī*, *m*, and *hāvaṅ* are substituted for the word *go*; [thus] *gāvī*.
For the word *puthu*, when *ṅī* follows, *pathava* and *puthavā* are substituted; [thus] *pathavī* and *puthavī*. In the locative singular (*ṭh*), [the form is] *pathaviyā*.
The suffixes *samāsanta* and *samāsanto*, or rather *a*, are prescribed [after a compound] with respect to the ground [of the following words],
such as *pāpa* and so forth.
When *bhūmi* follows words such as *pāpa*, the final member of that compound takes the suffix *-a*; for example: *pāpabhūmaṃ* (an evil land), *jātibhūmaṃ* (one's native land).
When *bhūmi* follows numerals, the final member of that compound likewise takes the suffix *-a*; for example: *dvibhūmaṃ* (two stories), *tibhūmaṃ* (three stories).
In the case of *nadī* and *godāvarī*, when combined with numerals, *a* is the substitute [for the final vowel]; for example: *pañcanadaṃ* (five rivers), *sattagodāvaraṃ* (seven Godāvarīs).
Furthermore, when combined with non-numerals, it occurs in the sense of "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeyya*) and other similar meanings, as in *aṅguli*.

When a numeral is compounded with a word other than "asaṃkhyā" (innumerable), it forms a compound by means of the suffix *samāsanta* (*ahū*); however, if the meaning is not "asaṃkhyā," the compound is simply formed as it is stated.

Examples: *Niraṅgulaṃ*: "that which has gone out from the fingers. *Accaṅgulaṃ*: "beyond the fingers. *Dvaṅgulaṃ*: "two fingers brought together. Regarding the rule "not when another numeral or *asaṃkhyā* is involved": what is the example? *Pañcaṅgulihattho*: "a hand having five fingers. *Upaṅguli*: how is this?

It is a compound in the sense of a word other than the base [meaning], as in "that whose measure is two fingers" (*dvaṅgulipramāṇam asya*), thus *dvaṅguli*. Note that this compound occurs in the sense of a word other than the base.

When the elision (*lopa*) of *matta* and so forth has been performed, it remains there. Alternatively, the word *aṅgula* is a term expressing measure (*pamāṇavācī*), as in "a full hundred *aṅgulas* measured by the *aṅgula* of a soldier" or "fourteen *aṅgulas*.
[The compound] is formed with long days, years, parts, and nights.

The suffix *a* is added to words such as *dīgha*, *asaṅkheyya*, and numerals (*saṅkhā*) when followed by the word *ratti*. Examples include: *dīgharattaṃ* (for a long time), *ahorattaṃ* (day and night), *vassārattaṃ* (the rainy season), *pubbarattaṃ* (the first part of the night), *apararattaṃ* (the latter part of the night), *aḍḍharattaṃ* (midnight).
*Atiratto* means "having passed the night. *Dvirattaṃ* means "two nights combined. Optionally, due to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikārā*), one may also say *ekarattaṃ* or *ekaratti*.

However, this [formation with *a*] occurs only in the sense of "long" (*dīgha*), "not-other" (*anañña*), "number" (*saṅkhya*), and "meaning" (*attha*). Thus, [only] *dīgharatta* is used in these senses.
*Hemanta*; [the rule] *uparatti-*—in some cases it occurs frequently due to specific injunctions, as in *yathārattaṃ*. Regarding the elision (*alopa*) of the word *go* when it is the first member:

after the word *go*, when it is subject to elision at the end of a compound, the suffix *a* is applied; however, there is no such compound when the referent is a garment (*vattha*), nor when the referent is something other than a substance (*aññapadattha*), or when the meaning is not a numeral (*asaṃkhyattha*).
And: *rājagavo*, *paramagavora*, *pañcagavadhano*; *dasagavaṃ*—what does it mean? It means "purchased with five cows," i.e., *pañcagu*.
Why is it not *acattha* (not purchased)? Because [the rule applies] only when there is no other number (*anañña-saṅkhya-atthesu*), as in *cittagu* and *upagu*.
Also: *rattindiva-dāra-gava-caturassa*.

These words ending in *a* are compounded as follows: ‘ratto ca divā ca’ becomes *rattindivaṃ*; ‘ratti ca divā ca’ becomes *rattindivaṃ*; ‘dārā ca gāvo ca’ becomes *dāragavaṃ*; ‘vatasso assiyo assa’ becomes *caturasso*.
In the sense of length, *anugavaṃ* is so compounded: *anugavaṃ sakaṭaṃ*—meaning it is as long as a cow. Why [is it] “in the sense of length”? [As in: *gunnaṃ pacchā anugu* (behind the cows).
*Akṣi* becomes *a* when followed by another word, provided that the compound has a meaning other than its constituent parts: *visālakkho*.
[The same applies] after *dāru* and *aṅguli*: ...
When *aṅgulantā* (words ending in *aṅgula*) are compounded with another word denoting wood (*dārumhi*), the suffix *a* is applied: *dvaṅgulaṃ dāru* (wood two fingers long);

*pañcaṅgulaṃ*—this refers to a piece of wood used for throwing grain and the like that has parts resembling fingers—it is said that [the form] is already established when denoting measure (*pamāṇe*) as in previous cases;
however, words such as *sakharāja* end in *a*, and even the suffix *i* is not seen—as in *gāṇḍīvadhatvā*, which is established by another grammatical tradition (*pakatantarena*).

Dvivītihāre—when reciprocal action is implied, the suffix *ci* occurs after a word denoting another entity (*aññapadatthe*). Examples: *kesākesi* (hair-to-hair), *daṇḍādaṇḍi* (stick-to-stick). The letter *ca* [in the rule] is for the purpose of including the suffix *ac*; thus, forms such as *sugandhi-duggandhi* will not appear as usage. After a feminine base ending in *ū*, the suffix *ko* occurs.

The suffix *ka* frequently occurs after words ending in *i*, *ī*, *u*, or *ū* when used as the feminine gender and governed by the *latu* condition, provided they denote something other than the base word itself (*aññapadatthe*). Examples: *bahukattuko* (having many agents), *bahukumāriko* (having many daughters), *bahubrahmabandhuko* (having many Brahmin wives). This applies extensively, as in the case of *subbhu*. *Vāññato*:
After other [words], the suffix *ka* frequently occurs in the sense of "other than the base word" (*aññapadatthe*). Examples: *bahu mālako* (many garlands), *bahumālo* (having many garlands).
"Uttarapade":
it should be understood that this [term] is the governing heading for what follows.
"Imassidaṃ": [this refers to...]

When a following word (uttarapada) follows this [pronoun], "idaṃ" becomes "imassa," "idam," "aṭṭhitā," "idappaccayā"; there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), and observe that doubling occurs.
For "puṃ": optionally for "pumassa. Optionally, for the word "pumassa," "puṃ" is substituted when a following word follows; thus: *pulliṅgaṃ*, *puṃliṅgaṃ*.
For words ending in *ta*, *na*, and *nu*:

in some cases, when followed by a subsequent word, *ṭa* optionally replaces these [suffixes]; as in *bhavampatiṭṭhā mayam* (we are established in the Blessed One), *bhāgavamamūlakā no dhammā* (our teachings have their root in the Blessed One). By virtue of the rule of "frequently" (*bahula*), this also applies to [words beginning with] *tara* and so forth; for instance, *pageva mahattarī* (how much more so the greater one) and *rattaññumahattaṃ* (the greatness of one long known).
When these [prefixes] precede a word beginning with *u*, there is no substitution; thus, *guṇavanta-patiṭṭho ‘smi*.
[Page reference] *Man-ādi-āpādīnaṃ mo maye ca-* (The *m* of *man* and others, as well as *āpādi*, becomes *mo* before *maya*).

The vowel *o* occurs for *mano*, *seṭṭha*, *rajo*, *jalla*, *āpo*, and *gata* when followed by a word beginning with *maya* or as a second member of a compound (*uttarapada*). Examples: *manomayā* (made of mind); *rajojallaṃ* (dust and mire); *rajomayaṃ* (consisting of dust); *āpogataṃ* (gone into water); *āpomayaṃ* (consisting of water); *anuyanti disodisaṃ* (they follow from place to place). Regarding numbers:

When a number follows as a second member of a compound, the vowel *o* is substituted for the final vowel of the preceding word. Examples: *parosataṃ* (more than a hundred); *parosahassaṃ* (more than a thousand). Why say "when it is a number"? Observe: *paradattupajīvino* (those who live on what is given by others).
When *puthu* is followed by an *uttarapada*, *u* is substituted for [the final vowel]. Thus, one who is distinct (*puthageva*) from the Noble Ones (*ariya*) is a worldling (*puthujjana*).
In the case of *cha* when followed by the word *āyatana*, *so* optionally replaces *cha*; thus: *sāhaṃ*, *chāhaṃ*; *saḷāyatanaṃ*, *chaḷāyatanaṃ*.

In the case of *latu*, *paccayanta*, and *pitā* etc., there is optionally the substitution of *āraṅ* and *araṅ* respectively when a following word (*uttarapada*) follows: *satthāra-dassanaṃ*; *kattāra-niddeso*. In the case of *māta* and *pita*, there is the substitution of *vātū* and *eva*: *satthu-dassanaṃ*; *mātā-pitaro*.
In this context, the relationship is based on knowledge (*vijjā*) and birth (*yoni*).

The substitute *ā* occurs in place of the fourth case ending (*catthi*) when it follows words denoting a relationship by learning (*vijjā-sambandhin*) or a relationship by birth (*yoni-sambandhin*), provided those words themselves are the latter members of a compound expressing such a relationship with *latu*, *pitā*, and so forth.

Examples: *hotāpotāro* (teacher and pupil), *mātāpitaro* (mother and father). Why only *latu*, *pitā*, and so forth? [Counter-example: *puttabhātaro* (son and brother). Why "in that [compound]" (*tatra*)? [Counter-example:

*pitupitāmahā* (father and grandfather). Why "the fourth case" (*catthi*)? [Counter-example: *mātu bhātā* (brother of the mother). Why "relationships by learning or by birth"? [Counter-example: *dātubhātaro* (brothers by the giver).
*Putte-*:

When *putta* follows as a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) within the scope of a *vatthu*, the substitution *ā* occurs for the final vowel of words such as *pitā* and others that denote a relationship through knowledge or birth; e.g., *pitāputtā* (father and son), *mātāputtā* (mother and son). *Cismiṃ-*: [The same applies] when *ci* follows.
When the suffix *cippacca* follows, the letter *ā* is substituted for the final vowel of the preceding word; e.g., *kesākesi*, *muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi*.

When a feminine word is used in apposition (*ekattha*) with a following masculine word as its co-referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*), that feminine word retains its masculine form if it has already been stated in the masculine; e.g., *kurubhariyo*, *dīgha*.
*Jaṅgho*; *yuvajāyo*—in the sense of “woman”? *Kalyāṇīpadhānaṃ*—“one whose striving is beautiful”; *kalyāṇippadhānā*. In the sense of “masculine form”? *Kaññābhariyo*. In the sense of “woman”?

*Gāmaṇikulaṃ diṭṭhi assa*—“he whose view is that of a village headman”; *gāmaṇidiṭṭhi*. In the sense of “having the same referent”? *Kalyāṇiyā mātā*—“the mother of a beautiful woman”; *kalyāṇīmātā*. [The suffix applies] in certain cases when a secondary suffix (*paccaya*) follows.
In certain instances, when a feminine word is used as a condition for a masculine form, it becomes masculine: *vyattatarā*, *vyyattatamā*.

The words beginning with *sabba* (all) become masculine when they denote only the grammatical function (*vutti*). Feminine-denoting words beginning with *sabba* become masculine when expressing only the function: *tassā mukhaṃ* becomes *tammukhaṃ*; *tassaṃ* becomes *tatra*; *tāya* becomes *tato*; *tassaṃ velāyaṃ* becomes *tadā*.
In the case of *chāyā*, the word *jaya* [is substituted] for *pati*.

When *pati* follows, it becomes *jāyā*; thus *jayampatī* and *jānipatī* are established through the grammatical rule (*pakatantarena*). Likewise, there are *dampatī* and *jampatī*. In the formation of technical terms (*saññā*), [the substitution occurs] for *uda* and *udaka*.
In the case of the word *udaka*, the substitution of *uda* occurs when it is followed by the word *dhī*; thus: *udadhī* (the ocean), *udapānaṃ* (a well).

Optionally, when followed by words such as *kumbha*: the substitution of *uda* for *udaka* optionally occurs when followed by words beginning with *kumbha*; thus: *udakumbho*, *udakakumbho* (a water-jar); *udapatto*, *udakapatto* (a water-bowl); *udabindu*, *udakabindu* (a drop of water)—this is an *ākati*-type class.
*Sotādisūlopo*:

In compounds beginning with *sota* (stream) and others, there is the elision of the *us* of *udaka* (water); e.g., *dakasotaṃ*, *dakarakkhaso*. *Ṭa nañssa*: [The suffix] *ṭa* [is applied] after *nañ* (the negative particle *na*).
The letter *ṭ* is substituted for the word *nañ* when it is followed by a consonant in a compound. Example: *abrāhmaṇo*. Why [is it] the letter *ñ*? So that it may apply to the simple compound:
*pāmanaputto*.
When followed by a vowel (*sare*), the word *nañ* becomes *ana* before a following member of the compound. Example: *anakkhātaṃ*.
2. "Ñakāra" applies everywhere.
Regarding "nakhādayo":

words beginning with *nakha* are derived as nouns (*nipacca*) without undergoing the substitution of *ta*. For example: "that which is not fit for him" is *nakha*; and in the case of technical terms (*saññā-sadda*), the formation should be carried out in whatever way is appropriate, even if it results in something merely conventional.

*Nakula* means "there is no family for him"; *nakula* is another word for "non-family. Examples include *nakhā*, *nakula*, *napuṃsaka*, *nakkhatta*, *nāka*, and so forth. *Naga* is optionally substituted for *vā* when it refers to a non-living being (*appāṇini*).

It is substituted when referring to non-living beings: *nagā* (trees) or *nagā* (mountains); *agā* (trees) or *agā* (mountains). Why "when it refers to a non-living being"? [Because in] *ago vasalo sītena* ("the outcaste is cold"), it is not substituted.
*Sahassa so’ññatthe-*:

In a compound where the meaning of another word (*aññapadattha*) is expressed, when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), *sahassa* optionally becomes *sa*; e.g., *saputto*, *sahaputto*. Why "in the sense of another word"? [Consider] *sahakatvā*, *sahayujjhitvā*. [Also, it occurs] in the sense of a name (*saññā*).
In a compound where *sahassa* is the first member, it becomes *sa-*, provided that the following word is a noun (*saññā*). This applies for the sake of euphony (*sāssatthaṃ*): *sapalāsaṃ*.
When not directly perceived (*apaccakkhe*), when "not directly perceived" is understood, *sahassa* becomes *sa-* before a subsequent member: *sāggi*, *kapoto*, *sapisāvā*, *vātamaṇḍalikā*.

*Sakattha-:* When the word *saha* (together with) has its own meaning as the predominant factor, the substitution of *so* occurs before an initial vowel of a following word (*uttarapada*), provided it does not denote time. Examples: *sampannaṃ brahmaṃ* becomes *sabrahmaṃ*; *sacakkaṃ nidhehi*, *sadhuraṃ*. Why "not denoting time"? As in: *sahapubbanhaṃ*, *sahāparanhaṃ*. *Ganthāntādhikye-*: [The same substitution occurs when the word *saha* follows a word ending in *gantha* (knot/binding), or when there is an excess.]

At the end of a compound, the word *saha* becomes *sa-* when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *sakalaṃ jotim adhīte* (he studies the entire *Joti*); *samuhuttaṃ*—here the beginning [of the time] has the sense of duration; *ādhikye*: *sadoṇā khārī* (a *khārī* with an extra *doṇa*); *samāsako kahāpaṇo* (a *kahāpaṇa* coin with an extra *māsaka*); this beginning [of the rule] has the sense of permanence.

Regarding the word *samāna*, it optionally becomes *sa-* before subsequent members such as *pakka* and others. Before subsequent members like *pakka*, *samāna* optionally becomes *sa-*: *sapakkho* or *samānapakkho*; *sajoti* or *samānajoti*. Why say "before *pakka* and others"? [To exclude cases where it does not apply.]

One of similar virtue; [and] by way of faction, light, country, night, wife, husband, navel, kinsman, celibate, name, clan, form, station, complexion, age, speech, Dhamma, birth, and death. In this regard— *Samānasīlo*: one who shares the same virtue. *Pakkha*: by way of faction (e.g., Kshatriya, Brahmin). *Joti*: by way of light (e.g., sun, moon, fire). *Janapada*: by way of country (e.g., Magadha, Kosala). *Ratti*: by way of night (e.g., the same woman as a lover at night). *Pattinī*: by way of wife. *Pattī*: by way of husband. *Nābhi*: by way of navel (e.g., a brother from the same womb). *Bandhu*: by way of kinsman. *Brahmacārī*: by way of one practicing the holy life.

*Nāma*: by way of name. *Gotta*: by way of clan. *Rūpa*: by way of physical form. *Ṭhāna*: by way of social station. *Vaṇṇa*: by way of complexion. *Vayo*: by way of age. *Vacana*: by way of speech. *Dhamma*: by way of doctrine. *Jātiya*: by way of birth. *Ghacca*: by way of death. In this regard, [one should avoid intimacy with those who are not of equal status].
In the case of *udara*, the *s* of *samāna* becomes *so* before the suffix *iya*; thus: *sodariya*, *samānodariya*. Why "in the case of *iya*"?
[Answer: *samānodarataṃ*.
In the case of *rī*, *rikka*, and *kesa*, the *s* of *samāna* becomes *so*: *sarī*, *sarikkha*, *sarisa*.
The substitution of *ā* for *sabbādi*, *rī*, *rikkha*, and *kesu*: *yādī*, *yādikkho*, *yādiso*. For *nta*, *kim*, and *ima*, the substitutions are *ṭā*, *kī*, and *ṭī* respectively.

In place of the words *anta*, *kiṃ*, and *ima* when followed by the suffixes *-rī*, *-rikka*, and *-ke*, the forms *ṭā*, *kīṭī*, and *imasadda* occur respectively: *bhavādī*, *bhavādikkho*, *bhavādiso*; *kīdī*, *kīdikkho*, *kīdiso*; *īdī*, *īdikkho*, *īdiso*.
Regarding the forms *tumha* and *amha*:
"In place of *tumha* and *amha* when singular, *tā* and *mā* occur respectively. Thus: *tādī*, *tādikkho*, *tādiso*; *mādī*.
*mādikkho*, *mādiso*;—in what sense "in one" (*ekasmin*)? [In the sense of] *tumhādī*, *amhādī*, *tumhādikkho*, *amhādikkho*, *tumhādiso*, *amhādiso*.

*Taṃ-mamaññatra*: when another word follows that begins with *rī*, *rikha*, or *kanta*, the forms *taṃ* and *maṃ* replace *tumha* and *amha* respectively; e.g., *tandīpā*, *mandīpā*; *taṃsaraṇā*, *maṃsaraṇā*; in *tayyogo* and *mayyogo*, the bindu (anusvāra) is dropped.
In the case of *vetassa*, it becomes either *rīrikka* or *kesveta*. [Examples: *edī*, *etādī*; *edikkho*, *etādikkho*; *ediso*, *etādiso*.
In words beginning with *vidha*, the *dvi-* becomes *du-*.
After *dvi*, *du* occurs before words such as *vidha*: *duvidho*, *dupaṭṭaṃ*, and so forth.
Before words such as *guṇa*, *di* occurs after *dvi*: *diguṇaṃ*, *dirattaṃ*, *digu*, and so forth.
*Tisva-*:
In the three [cases], *dvi* becomes *a*; as in *dvattikkhattuṃ* (twice or thrice) and *dvattipattapūrā* (two or three bowlfuls).
[The substitution occurs] up to the number *asata*, except when there is no other meaning (*anaññatthe*).

When a numeral is followed by a subsequent word (uttarapada), the word *dvi* becomes *du* before a hundred (*sata*) or a thousand (*sahassa*), provided it does not have the sense of "other than" (*anaññattha*). Examples: *dvādasa*, *dvāvīsati*, *dvattiṃsa*. Why say "a numeral"? (Counter-example: *dirattaṃ*. Why say "before a hundred or a thousand"? (Counter-example: *dvisataṃ*, *dvisahassaṃ*. Why say "provided it does not have the sense of 'other than'"? (Counter-example: *dvidasā*. Regarding *ti*:

When a numeral is followed by a subsequent word, the word *ti* becomes *te* before a hundred or a thousand, provided it does not have the sense of "other than". Examples: *terasa*, *tevisa*, *tettiṃsa*. Why say "a numeral"? (Counter-example: *tirattaṃ*. Why say "before a hundred or a thousand"? (Counter-example: *tisataṃ*. Why say "provided it does not have the sense of 'other than'"? (Counter-example: *tivatukā*.
The word *cattālīsādo* (forty and so on):

there is *tissevā* for *cattālīsādo*; *tecattālīsa*, *ticattālīsa*; *tepaññāsa*, *tipaññāsa*; *tesaṭṭhi*, *tisaṭṭhi*; *tesattati*, *tīsattatī*; *tñasīti*, *tiyāsīti*; *tenavuti*, *tinavuti*—and likewise for *asatādo* (sixty and so on) up to *tisataṃ* (three hundred).
And for *dvi* (two), there is *du*.

In the sense of "not other" (*anaññatthe*), for the word *dvi*, there is optionally the substitution of *catālīsādo* (the form *catālīsa*) after the word *dve*. This applies up to forty-two, namely: *dvācattālīsaṃ*, *dvicattālīsaṃ*, *dvicattālīsaṃ*; *dvāpaññāsaṃ*, *dvāpaññāsaṃ*, *dvipaññāsaṃ*; and so forth. Regarding *bācattālīsādo*:

in the sense of "not other," for the word *dvi*, there is optionally the substitution of *bā* before the word *catālīsādo*. Examples include: *bārasa*, *dvādasa*; *bāvīsati*, *dvāvīsati*; *battiṃsa*, *dvattiṃsa*. Why is it said "before *catālīsādo*"? [To exclude cases where it does not apply, such as: *dvicattālīsa*.
In the groups of twenty-six and eighteen, the [number] for five is fifty-five.
In the subsequent groups of twenty and eighteen, the [numbers] for five are fifty-five respectively: twenty-five and fifteen.
For four, they are thirty and ten.
The word *catu* becomes *cu* when followed by the word *dasa*: *cuddasa*, *coddasa*, *catuddasa*. The word *cha* becomes *so* when followed by the word *dasa*:
this substitution of *so* for *cha* occurs when *dasa* follows; thus, *soḷasa*.
*Eka-ṭṭhāna-mā-*:
When *eka* is followed by *aṭṭhāna*, it becomes *ekādasa* (eleven) or *aṭṭhārasa* (eighteen), provided that ten (*dasa*) follows.
Or, when *ra* follows, it is reckoned as such.
In the case of another’s *dasa*, there is an option (*vibhāsā*): it becomes *ekārasa* or *ekādasa*; *bārasa* or *dvādasa*; *pannarasa* or *pañcadasa*;

*sattarasa* or *sattadasa*; *aṭṭhārasa* or *aṭṭhādasa*. [The substitution] of *panna* and *bā* occurs invariably [in these cases], but here [in the case of *catur*] it does not occur; thus, it becomes *catuddasa*. After [the words] *cha*, *ti*, and *catur*, there is also *ḷ*.
In the case of *parassa*, there is *ḷo* and *ro*; [thus] *soḷasa* becomes *sorasa*, and *teḷasa* becomes *terasa*.

Regarding the fourth and third [vowels], they become "half-and-a-quarter" and "half-and-a-third" respectively for subsequent vowels: “half of the fourth” is *aḍḍhuḍḍha*, and “half of the third” is *aḍḍhatiya*. How so? *Aḍḍhateyyo*: when the suffix *ṇya* is added in its own sense (*sakatthe*), there is vowel strengthening (*uttarapadavuddhi*) of the following member.
For the second [member], together with *diyaḍḍha* and *divaḍḍha*.
When combined with the word *aḍḍha*, the second member becomes *diyaḍḍha* or *divaḍḍha*; for example, "the second by half" is *diyaḍḍha* or *divaḍḍha*.
[The suffix] *-ka* is applied after a vowel in the sense of "other than."

When the word *ku-* occurs before a vowel-initial suffix in the sense of a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*), it sometimes becomes *ka-*; as in *kadannaṃ* and *kadasanaṃ*. Why "before a vowel"? [Counter-example: *kuputto*. Why "in the sense of a subsequent member"? [Counter-example: *kuaṭṭho*, which means "king.
In the sense of "slight" (*appa*), when the word *ku-* occurs before a suffix in the sense of a subsequent member, it becomes *kā-*; as in "slight salt" (*appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ*) = *kālavaṇaṃ*.

*Purisevā-*: The suffix *ka* is added after the word *puruṣa*. [Thus] *kāpurisa*, *kupurisa*—this is an alternative analysis (*vibhāsā*) for the case where the sense is not attained; in the sense of "not attained," the prefix *tu* is always [used]. [Examples: "a man who is a lord" = *kāpurisa*.
After words such as *pubba*, the substitution *anha* occurs in place of the final syllable *aha* of the following member: *pubbanha*; *aparanha*; *ajajanha*; *sāyanha*; *majjhanha*.
Thus ends the third section, on compounds, in the *Vutti* commentary on the *Moggallāna-vyākaraṇa*.

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after a noun ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*), optionally, when the sense of "born" (*hotapacce*) is to be expressed. The letter *ṇ* serves the purpose of indicating vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). This applies elsewhere as well: for example, "the descendant of Vasiṭṭha" is *Vāsiṭṭha*, or *Vāsiṭṭhī*;

likewise, *Opagava*, or *Opagavī*. The word *vā* (or) is used in the rule to signify an option regarding the compound formation. Its governing scope extends up to the end of the section on words used in their own sense (*sakattha*).

The suffixes *ṇa*, *ana*, and *āyana* [are applied] after words such as *vaccha* that do not already end in the suffix *pappa*, and after words such as *hotṛ*. Thus, there are the suffixes *ṇa*, *ana*, and *āyana*, or the suffix *bho* (possessive).
For example: from *vaccha*—*vacchāna*, *vacchāyana*; from *kacca*—*kaccāna*, *kaccāyana*; with the augment (*yāgama*)—*kātyāyana*; *moggallāna*, *moggallāyana*.
*Sākaṭāna*, *sākaṭāyana*; *kaṇbhāna*, *kaṇbhāyana*; and so forth.

From words such as *kattika* and those beginning with *vidhava*, the suffixes *ṇeya*, *aṇ*, and *era* occur respectively as optional substitutes. Examples include: *kattikeyya*; *venateyya*; *bhāgineyya*, and so forth—[from *vidhava*: ] *vedhavera*; [from *vandhaka*: ] *vandhakera*; [from *nāḷika*: ] *nāḷikera*; [from *samaṇa*: ] *sāmaṇera*, and so forth. The suffix *ṇya* occurs after words such as *ditti*.
After [bases ending in] *diti* and so forth, the suffix *ṇya* optionally occurs in the sense of "to be obtained. Examples include: *decca*, *ādicca*, *koṇḍañña*, *gaggya*, *bhātabba*, and so on.
After a base ending in long *ā*, the suffix *ṇi* optionally occurs in the sense of "to be obtained. Examples include: *dakkhi*, *doṇi*, *vāsavi*, *vāruṇi*, and so on.
*Rājato ñño jātiyaṃ*:

After the word *rāja*, another [suffix] occurs when a descendant (*vā hota-pacce*) of noble birth (*jāti*) is to be understood. *Rājāñño*—why "of noble birth"? [Answer: *Rājāpaccaṃ* (a mere descendant of a king). *Khattā yiyā-*:

After the word *khatta*, the suffixes *yi* and *yā* occur when a descendant of noble birth is to be understood. *Khatto*; *khattiyo*. Why "of noble birth"? [Answer: *Khatti* (one who merely belongs to the *khatta* class).

From the word *manu*, the suffix *ssasaṇ* occurs in the sense of genus (*jāti*). Thus: *manusso* (masculine) or *mānuso*; in the feminine: *manussā* or *mānusī*. In the sense of genus alone, [the form] is *māṇavo*.
From the names of countries, the suffix *ṇo* occurs in the sense of a Kshatriya or a king.

The suffix *ṇo* is applied after the name of a country to form the name of a Kṣatriya who is a descendant (*apacca*) of that very king. Examples: Pañcāla; Kosala; Māgadha; Okkāka. Why [is it] "by the name of a country"?
[Consider: Dāsarathi; why [is it] "a Kṣatriya"? [Answer: "The descendant of the Brahmin Pañcāla" is Pañcāla. The suffix *ṇya* is applied after the names of the Kurus and Sivis.
The suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *kuru* when it means "king" or "ruler": *korabyo* (a Kuru king), *seyyo* (a ruler).
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after a third-case ending that expresses passion (*rāga*) in the sense of "colored by that": *kasāvena rattaṃ* (dyed with yellowish-brown) becomes *kāsāvaṃ*; *kosumbhaṃ*.
"Hāliddaṃ" [is used] for "redness," as in: "the cloth dyed by Devadatta. Why is it not so used here [in the case of *nīla* and *pīta*]?
Because they are quality-denoting words (*guṇavacana*), they express the state of being [dyed] even without the suffix *ṇa*.
[The rule applies] to time joined with the moon and a lunar mansion.
The suffix *ṇo* occurs when the time is characterized by a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*) from the third case on, provided that the lunar mansion is conjoined with the moon (*indu*).

Examples: *Phussī* (the night), *phusso* (the day)—[these are] "by the lunar mansion. [Question: What is the purpose of saying "by the lunar mansion"? Answer: [To exclude cases like] "the night characterized by the teacher" (*gurunā lakkhitā ratti*). [Question: What is the purpose of saying "conjoined with the moon"? Answer:

[To exclude cases like] "the moment characterized by the month of Kattikā" (*kattikāya lakkhito muhutto*). [Question: What is the purpose of saying "at the time" (*kāle*)? Answer: [To exclude cases like] "success of purpose not characterized by the month of Phussa"—such as "today is Kattikā" (*ajja kattikā*).
When the moon is conjoined with Kattikā, the word "Kattikā" is employed.

That is its deity; because it dwells (*seti*) on the full moon, the suffix *ṇo* occurs in the sense of the genitive (sixth case) for that which is in the nominative. That nominative [term] is indeed the deity, the full moon.
‘Sugata’ means ‘the deity is Sugata’; [thus] Sogata; Māhinda; Yāma; Vāruṇa; ‘Phussa’ means ‘the full-moon day belongs to Phussa’;
[thus] Phussa; Māgha; Māgha; Phagguṇa; Citta; Vesākha; Jeṭṭhamūla; Āsāḷha; Sāvaṇa; Poṭṭhapāda; Assayuja; Kattika;
Māgasira—the full-moon day. What is it? It is the fifth of Phussa, just as the full-moon day belongs to the month that has passed.

‘May it not be non-full’—from this etymological derivation, *ṇo* is a particle (*nipāta*), and there is the augment *s*. The rule applies specifically to the month (*māsa*) and the fortnight (*pakkha*) consisting of fifteen nights, and so forth.
One who studies that, or one who knows that, is a *kaṇika*.
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after the word *dutiya* in the sense of “he studies that” or “he knows that,” just like the suffix *ṇika*. For example:
one who studies or knows grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is a *veyyākaraṇa*; a *chāndasa*; a *kammaka*; a *padaka*; a *venayika*; a *suttantika*.

The inclusion of the word *dutiya* is for the purpose of establishing a separate rule, for the purpose of showing that knowing is the object of study, and for the purpose of including the *pasibba* (the shoulder-bag).

In the sense of "domain" (*visaya*), the suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case when it denotes a region (*desa*). For example: *vasātīnaṃ visayo deso* becomes *vāsāto*—meaning "the domain of the Vasātis. Why say "in the sense of a region"? [Consider: *cakkhussa visayo rūpaṃ* (the visible form is the domain of the eye), and *devadattassa visayo anuvāko* (the lesson is the domain of Devadatta). [The suffix *ṇo* also occurs] in the sense of "dwelling place" (*nivāsa*) when that is the name [of the place].

The suffix *ṇo* does not occur after a word ending in the sixth case when it signifies the name of the country where [the people] dwell; for example, "the dwelling place of the *Sivis*" is *Sevī*. [This applies] from the word *vāsa* (dwelling).

When signifying a location not far from something, the suffix *ṇo* does not occur after a word ending in the sixth case when it signifies the name of that location; for example, "not far from the *Vedi*" is *Vedisaṃ*.
*Tena nibbatte*:

The suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word in the third case (*tatiyanta*) when expressing that which is produced by something. For example: *kusambena nibbattā kosambī nagarī* (the city of Kosambī was produced by *kusamba*); *kākandī*, *mākandī*; *sahassena nibbattā sāhassī parikhā* (a moat produced by a thousand [pieces of gold]). In these cases, the third case ending is used according to the requirements for the cause (*hetu*), the agent (*kattari*), and the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is the meaning here.

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after words ending in the nominative case in the sense of the locative (*idha*), provided that the name of the place is present; for example, "there are *udumbara* trees in this place" becomes *odumbaro*, *bādaro*, or *babbajo*. The suffix *ṇa* occurs after words ending in the locative case in the sense of "being there" (*tatra bhave*);
for example: *udake bhavo* = *odako* (aquatic), *oraso* (born from the breast), *jānapado* (of the country), *māgadho* (of Magadha), *kāpilavatthavo* (of Kapilavatthu), *kosambo* (of Kosambī).
From *ajja* and so forth, *tano* is added in the sense of "being" (*bhav-attha*). From *ajja*, there is *ajjatano*; from *sva*, *svātano*; from *hiyyo*, *hiyyattano*.
From *purā*, *ṇo* is also [added].
*Purā* becomes *purāṇa* and *purātana* in the sense of "formerly" (*bhavatthe*).
After the word *amā*, the suffix *-acca* occurs in the sense of "formerly"; thus, *amacca*. From the group beginning with *majjha*, the suffix *-ima* occurs.

The suffix *ima* occurs in the sense of "being located in" (*bhavattha*) after words ending in the locative case, such as *majjha* and others: *majjhima*, *antima*—namely, *majjha*, *anta*, *heṭṭhā*, *upari*, *ora*, *pāra*, *pacchā*, *abbhantara*, *paccanta*.

The suffixes *-kaṇa*, *-eyaṇa*, *-eyyaka*, and *-iya* are affixes occurring in the sense of "being located in" after words ending in the locative case: *kusinārāyaṃ bhavo* (that which exists in Kusinārā) is *kosināraka*; likewise, *māgadhaka*.
In the forest-dwelling [tradition], there is the Vihāreyya, Gaṅgeyya, Pabbateyya, Vāneyeyyā-ṇeyyaka-koleyyaka, Bārāṇaseyyaka, Campeyyaka;
the Mithileyyaka-eyyaka-eyyagamma, the divine (dibba); the iyagāmiya, Udariya, Diviya, Pañcāliya, Bodhapakkhīya, and Lokiya.

The suffix *ṇika*: after a word ending in the locative case, the suffix *ṇika* occurs in the sense of "belonging to that. Examples: *sāradiko divaso* (an autumn day); *sāradikā ratti* (an autumn night).
[The suffix *ṇika* also occurs] when the word denotes his craft (*sippa*), character (*sīla*), merchandise (*paṇya*), weapon (*paharaṇa*), or purpose (*payojana*).
The suffix *ṇika* occurs in the sense of the sixth case (*chaṭṭhatthe*) after words denoting the first [member of a compound], such as crafts (*sippa*) and so forth:
"Vīṇāvādanaṃ sippam assa" means *veṇiko*, *modaṅgiko*, *vaṃsiko*; "Paṃsukūladhāraṇaṃ sīlam assa" means *paṃsukūliko*, *tecīvariko*;
"Gandho paṇyam assa" means *gandhiko*, *teliko*, *goḷiko*; "Cāpo paharaṇam assa" means *cāpiko*, *tomariko*, *muggariko*; "Upadhi... [and so on].
“*Yojanaṃ assa opadhikaṃ, sātikaṃ, sāhassikaṃ.
Taṃ hantārahatigacchatuñchaticarati.*” From the second [vowel] onwards, the suffix *ṇika* occurs in these senses:
“*pakkhīhi ‘pakkhino hantī’ti pakkhiko*, sākuṇiko, māyuriko—[from] fish: *macchiko*, meniko—[from] deer: *migehi*.”
A deer-hunter (*māgavika*), a hunter of antelopes (*hāriṇika*), a hunter of pigs (*sūkarika*); "it is worth a hundred" (*satam arahati*) thus it is *sātaka*; "visible here and now" (*sandṛṣṭika*);

"come and see the method, it is worth it" (*ehi passa vidhim arahati*) thus it is *ehipassika*; "worth a thousand" (*sāhasrika*)—here *-iya* becomes *-iya*; "he goes to another's wife" (*paradāram gacchati*) thus he is an adulterer (*pāradārika*);

a path-follower (*maggika*), one who travels fifty leagues (*paññāsayojanika*); "he gathers wild dates" (*badare uñchati*) thus he is a gatherer of dates (*bādarika*), a gatherer of millet (*sāmākika*); "the Dhamma..."
‘He practices,’ thus it is *dhammika* (righteous), *adhammika* (unrighteous). From that [root], the suffix *-ika* occurs in the sense of “done by,” etc.:
‘done by the body’ is *kāyika*, *vācasika* (verbal), *mānasika* (mental); ‘done by the wind’ is *vātika*.
‘Afflicted by wind’—*vātiko*; ‘bought for a hundred’—*sātikaṃ*, *sāhassikaṃ*;

[the suffix] does not occur after a word denoting the price itself, as in ‘bought by Devadatta,’ because there is no comprehension of that specific meaning—‘bound with leather’—*vārattiko*, *āyasiko*, *pāsiko*;
‘prepared with or mixed with ghee’—*ghātikaṃ*, *goḷikaṃ*, *dādhikaṃ*, *māricikaṃ*; ‘killed with a net’—*jālikaṃ*.
One who kills is a *jālika* (trapper); one who catches fish with a net is a *bāḷisika*.
One who wins or plays with dice is an *akkhika*; one who wins or plays with dice is an *akkhika*. One who digs with a spade is a *khāṇittika*; one who digs with a hoe is a *kuddālika*.

[The forms] *devadattena jitam*, *aṅgulyā khaṇati*, and so on, do not occur because their meanings are not understood. One who crosses by means of a raft is an *oḷumpika*; the suffix *-ika* is used here [to form *oḷumpika*].
*Gopucchika*; *nāvika*—one who travels by cart is a *sākaṭika*. *Rathika*—*parappika*: the suffix *-ika* [is added];
one who carries on the shoulder is a *khandhika*, an *aṃsika*; one who lives by wages (*vetana*) is a *vetanika*, a *bhatika*, a *kayika*, a *vikkayika*;
one who buys and sells is a *kayavikkayika*. The suffix *-ika* [is applied in these ways].

It conduces to that—when the sense is "it conduces to this," the suffix -ika is applied after a word ending in the fourth case (dative). For example: "it conduces to renewed existence" is *ponobhavika*;
in the feminine, *ponobhavikā*. "It conduces to the world" is *lokika*. "A very excellent summit" is *sagga*; [thus] "it conduces to heaven" is *saggika*.
‘It conduces to heaven’ (*sovaggika*); ‘it conduces to grain’ (*sassāvaka*)—this is the reading: ‘it conduces to wealth’ (*dhanāya saṃvattati*), thus it is ‘wealthy’ (*dhaniya*).

From these meanings, namely ‘arisen from’ (*sambhuta*) and ‘come from’ (*āgata*), the suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the fifth case (the ablative). For example: ‘arisen or come from a mother’ (*mātito sambhutamāgataṃ vā*).
From the mother—[variants such as] *pettika*, *mātṛka*, and *paitṛka* are also seen—the word *sorabhya* means "produced from the mother";
*thañña* means "produced from the breast"; *pettiyo*, *mātiyo*, and *mattiyo* mean "produced from the mother," or else "a mortal.
In that regard, he dwells, known, devoted, and appointed.

The suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the seventh case (*sattamyanta*) in the sense of "dwelling" (*vasati*) and similar meanings: *rukkhamūle vasati* ("he dwells at the foot of a tree") becomes *rukkhamūlika*;
*āraññika*, *sosānika*; *loke vidito* ("known in the world") becomes *lokika*; *cātumahārājesu bhattā* ("devoted to the Four Great Kings") becomes *cātummahārājika*;

*dvāre niyutto* ("appointed at the gate") becomes *dovārika*. From the readings *dassoka*, *tadamina*, etc., we have *bhaṇḍāgārika*; with the suffix *-ika*: *navakammika*; with the suffix *-iya*: *jātikiya*, *andhakiya*.
Regarding this:
after a word ending in the sixth case, the suffix *ṇika* occurs in the sense of "belonging to this. For example: *saṅghassa idaṃ* (this belongs to the Saṅgha) becomes *saṅghikaṃ*;
