*puggalikaṃ*, *sakyaputtiko*, *nāthaputtiko*, *jenadattiko*. After a word ending in *kiya*: *sakiyo*, *parakiyo*. After a word ending in *niya*: *attaniyaṃ*. After a word ending in *ka*: *sako*, *rājakaṃ*, *bhaddhaṃ*.

Ṇo—The suffix *ṇo* occurs after words ending in the sixth case (genitive) in the sense of "this belongs to. For example: *kaccāyanassa idaṃ* becomes *kaccāyanaṃ*, meaning "the grammar [of Kaccāyana]"; *sogataṃ*, meaning "the teaching [of the Sugata]"; *māhisaṃ*, meaning "beef" and so forth. After words such as *go* (cow), the suffix *ya* is used.

The suffix *ya* occurs after words ending in the sixth case, such as *go*, etc., in the sense of "belonging to this"; for example, "this belongs to a cow" is *gavyaṃ* (cow's product), such as meat and so forth; *kavyaṃ* (belonging to a goat) and *dabbaṃ* (belonging to a deer).
The suffix *reyyaṇa* occurs after the word *pitu* in the sense of "brother of that"; for example, "brother of the father" is *petteyyo*.
*Cho* [is applied] to a sister on the mother’s side.

*Cho* is applied to their sister on both the mother’s and father’s sides: “mother’s sister” is *mātucchā*; “father’s sister” is *pitucchā*. How is it [applied] to a maternal uncle? By means of the grammatical rule of irregular formation (*nipātanā*) stating “from *mātula* and so forth. [It is applied] to the maternal grandfather and paternal grandfather.

“By their parents” means: the mother’s father is the maternal grandfather (*mātusvāmaha*); the mother’s mother is the maternal grandmother (*mātumāta*); the mother’s father is the maternal grandfather (*mātupitā*); the father’s mother is the paternal grandmother (*pitumāta*); the father’s father is the paternal grandfather (*pitupitā*).

These are not to be connected respectively [in pairs], but rather individually. “Beneficial to mother and father” means: one who is beneficial to mother and father is *mātāpituhi hito reyyaṇo*; [such a person is] filial toward the mother (*matteyyo*) and filial toward the father (*petteyyo*).
In the senses of censure, unknown, resemblance, and compassion, [the suffix] *ko* [is applied].
After a noun, *ko* occurs in the meanings of censure and so forth: in the sense of censure—*muṇḍako*, *samaṇako*; in the sense of "unknown"—"Whose horse is this?"—*assako*.

Through the power of usage, the specific relationship which was not previously understood is thereby comprehended. In the sense of "little"—*telakaṃ*, *ghatakaṃ*; in the sense of "resemblance"—*hatthiko*.

In the sense of resemblance: *hatthiko* (an elephant-like one), *assako* (a horse-like one), *balivaddako* (an ox-like one) [and] *mānusako* (a human-like one); in the sense of a tree: *rukkhako* (a small tree), *pilakkhako* (a wood-apple tree);
in the sense of compassion: *dayāyaṃ puttako* (a dear child), *vacchako* (a calf); in the sense of a concept (*saññā*): *moroviya morako* (a peacock-like thing). Its suffixes are *-ka* and *-ika*.
The suffixes *ṇika* and *ka* occur after a word ending in the nominative case (*paṭhamantā*) in the sense of "belonging to this," provided that the nominative-ending word is a measure (*parimāṇa*).
A measure is that by which something is measured. For example: "A *doṇa* is its measure" → *doṇiko* rice; *khārasatiko*, *khārasahassiko*, *āsītiko* (referring to) age;
*upaḍḍhakāyikaṃ*, *bimbohanaṃ* (a bolster); *pañcakaṃ*, *chakkaṃ*.

“By means of the first-case endings *yādīhi*, the sixth-case sense [of measure] becomes *ttako*, *etto*, and *tako*; that indeed is the first-case measure. ‘This is its limit (*yantaka*), so much (*tattaka*), so much (*ettaka*); as much as (*āvatake*), as much as (*yāvatako*), so much as (*tāvatako*).
And all [forms] ending in *-vantu* [are included].”

After all [words] ending in the nominative case (*paṭhamanta*), the suffix *āvantu* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhatthe*); that which ends in the nominative becomes the measure (*parimāṇa*). For example: "that whose measure is all" is *sabbāvantaṃ*; likewise *yāvantaṃ*, *tāvantaṃ*, and *etāvantaṃ*.
After what [word] do the suffixes *rati*, *ivarī*, *vata*, *karitta*, and *kā* occur?

After a word ending in the nominative, these suffixes—*rati*, *ivarī*, *vata*, *karitta*, and *kā*—occur in the sense of the genitive, provided that the word ending in the nominative is such [a measure].

It is a measure (*parimāṇa*). What is the enumeration (*saṃkhyāna*) that measures these? "How many? (*kati*); "how much? (*kiva*, *kīvatakaṃ*, *kittakaṃ*). "How many are there?"—by their very nature, they are innumerable (*asaṃkheyya*).

[The suffix] *-ita* is applied after words beginning with *tāraka* when they are in the nominative case, in the sense of the genitive (the sixth case), meaning "that which has arisen from them. Thus: "that from which stars have arisen" is *tārakitaṃ*, the sky; *pupphīto*, a tree; *pallavitā*, a creeper.
Regarding *māne matto*:
after a word ending in the first case, when the sense is "measuring" (*māna*) or "belonging to it," the suffix *matto* occurs. For example: ‘*palam ummānam assa’* becomes *palamattaṃ*;

‘*hattho pamāṇam assa’* becomes *hatthamattaṃ*; ‘*sataṃ mānam assa’* becomes *satamattaṃ*; ‘*doṇo parimāṇam assa’* becomes *doṇamattaṃ*. Furthermore, by way of non-differentiation (*abhedopacāra*), the word *doṇa* itself is also used [in this sense].
*Taggha* [is used] after *vuddha*.

Because it expresses the sense of "reaching up to" (*uddhamānavuttito*), *taggha* occurs in the sense of the sixth case (*chaṭṭhatthe*); for example, *jaṇṇutaggha*, meaning "as high as the knee" (*jaṇṇumattaṃ*).
And [the suffix] *ṇo* [occurs] after *purisa*.

After words ending in the nominative case, such as *purisa* (man), when they denote a measure or the like, the suffix *aya* does not occur; thus we have *porisaṃ*, *purisamattaṃ*, and *purisatagghaṃ*.
Regarding the rule "after *ubho* and *ubhayo*":

after the words *ubho* and *ubhayo*, which denote parts and end in the nominative case, the suffix *aya* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*asseti*); for example, "having both shoulders" is *ubhayaṃ*, *dvayaṃ*, and *tayaṃ*.

After enumerating [a number] ending in *sat* (hundred), *anta* (end), *īsa* (lord), *āsa* (face), or *dasa* (ten), the suffix *ḍo* occurs in the sense of the locative case marker *asmin* (in this), provided that the number enumerated is an addition (*adhika*) and that "in this" refers to a hundred or a thousand; for example:
"twenty is added to this hundred" becomes *vīsaṃsataṃ*, *ekavīsaṃsataṃ*, or *sahassaṃ*.
One hundred thousand or thirty-one hundred; up to ninety-nine hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand;

forty-one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand; fifty-one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand; sixty-one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand; seventy-one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand;
eighty-one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand; ninety-one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand; and one hundred twenty-one hundred, one thousand, or one hundred thousand.
What is "kiṃ"? It means "more" in this context of a hundred (*sate*); what does "more" mean? It means "fifteen less" in this context of a hundred;

what does "in this" (*asmiṃ*) mean? It refers to "twenty more than this hundred"; what does "of a hundred thousand" (*satasahasse*) mean? It refers to "eleven more than twenty. From that, by filling [the number] starting from eleven, etc.—
The suffix *ḍo* optionally occurs after numerals ending in *-cha*, *-ṭṭhī*, *-iyantā*, and those beginning with *ekādasa*, in the sense of completion (*pūraṇattha*).

That by which a number is completed is "completion" (*pūraṇa*); for example, "completing eleven" is *ekādaso* or *ekādasamo*; *vīso* or *vīsatimo*; *tiṃso* or *tīṃsatimo*; *cattālīso* or *paññāso*. [The suffix *ma* occurs] after numerals beginning with *pañca*.
The suffix *mo* occurs after numerals ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*), beginning with five, in the sense of completion (*pūraṇatthe*). Thus: *pañcamo*, *sattamo*, *aṭṭhamo*; *katimo*, *katimī*.

And for numerals beginning with one hundred (*satādi*): the suffix *mo* occurs after numerals beginning with one hundred that end in the sixth case in the sense of completion; furthermore, there is a substitution of the final vowel (*anta*) with *i*. Thus: *satimo*, *sahassimo*.

*Chā ddhaddhamā*: From the word *cha*, the forms *dha*, *ddha*, and *mā* arise in the sense of completing that [number]. Thus: *chaṭṭho*, *chaṭṭhamo*; in the feminine: *chaṭṭhi*, *chaṭṭhami*. How is it that [the forms] *dutiyaṃ*, *tatiyaṃ*, and *catutthaṃ* are used? [They are so] because of the specific grammatical rule (*nipātanā*) stating "for the second, third, and fourth.
*Ekā kākyasahāye*: [The form] *ekā* is used when there is no companion.
In the sense of being alone (*asahāya*), from the word *eka*, there are the forms *kaāki*, *vā*; or *ekako*, *ekāki*, *eko*.

From words such as *vaccha* (calf) and others, when their smallness (*tanutta*) is implied, the suffix *-tara-* is applied. When the smallness of the nature of words like *vaccha* is understood, *-tara-* occurs; for example, when the smallness of a well-taught [calf] is meant, there is *vacchataro*.
A female calf (*vacchatarī*) due to the diminution of the female state; a mule (*okkhataro*) due to the diminution of youth; a mule (*assataro*) due to the diminution of the nature of a horse;
a young bull (*usabhataro*) due to the diminution of strength. From what [is this derived]?
From the comparative suffix *-tara* used in the sense of selection (*nidhāraṇe*).

The word *kiṃ* is used for specification (*niddhāraṇa*). [Examples: *ratarataraṃ honti*; "Which among you is Devadatta? Which among you is Kaṭha? [Or: *katamo bhavataṃ devadatto*; "Which one among you is Devadatta? Which one among you is Kaṭha? [Or: *bhāradvājānaṃ katamo’si brahme*. *Tena datte liyā-*:

After a word ending in the third case, when *datto* is the object to be expressed, the suffixes *lai* and *yā* are applied. [Examples: *devena datto* → *devadatto*; *devalaḥ*; *deviyaḥ*; *brahmaṇā datto* → *brahmadatto*; *brahmayo*; *śivena datto* → *śivalo*; *śiviyaḥ*. [In these cases] there is lengthening of the vowel *i*.

In the case of the abstract (bhāva) and the object (kamma), the suffixes *tta*, *tā*, *taṇa*, *ṇya*, *ṇeya*, *ṇiya*, and *ṇiyaya*—beginning with *tta*—are frequently used after words ending in the sixth case (genitive). However, they do not occur after every [word] from every [suffix], except for those ending in *tta*.
"That from which cognitions arise" is the abstract (*bhāva*); it is the basis for the occurrence of a word, as in "of a blue cloth."

The state (*bhāva*) is "blueness" (*nīlattam*); the quality (*guṇa*) is "blueness" (*nīlatā*). The state of the quality "blue" is blueness; the genus (*jāti*) of the quality "blue" is blueness. "Cowness" (*gottaṃ*) is "cowness" (*gotā*), the genus of cows.

"Cookness," "staffness," "hornedness," and "king's-manhood" refer to the state of being connected with actions and so forth. "Devadattahood," "moonhood," and "sunhood" refer to the commonality of specific particular states.
"Space-ness" (*ākāsattaṃ*) and "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvaccaṃ*) refer to the commonality of metaphorical distinctions. [Likewise,] "the state of an ordinary person" (*puthujjanattaṃ*).

The state of being a feeling; the state of being a husband, the state of being a lover;—*ṇya*, *ālasya*, *brahmañña*, *cāpalya*, *nepuñña*, *pesuñña*, *rajja*, *ādhipacca*, *dāyajja*, *vesamma*; some say *vesama*;
friendship, trade;—*ṇeyya*, *soceyya*, *ādhipateyya*,—*ṇa*, *gārava*, *pāṭava*, *ajjava*, *maddava*,—*iya*, *adhipatiya*, *paṇḍitiya*, *bahussutiya*, *naggiya*.
*Sūriyaṃ*—*ṇiya-ālasiyaṃ*, *kālusiyaṃ*, *mandiyaṃ*, *dakkhiyaṃ*, *porohitiyaṃ*, *veyyattiyaṃ*. How so? In the sense of "beloved" (*rāmaṇīyaka*), it is established by means of the suffix *-ka*;
[here] *kammaṃ* means action (*kriyā*). In that context: "the action of one who is lazy" is *alasattaṃ*, *alasatā*, or *alasattanaṃ*;
or *ālasyaṃ* and *ālasiyaṃ*—this is in the sense of the word itself (*sakatthe*). Even in the sense of the word itself, as in *yathābhuccaṃ* and *kāruññaṃ*.
It is appropriate [to state]: *ākāsānañcāyatana* (the base of infinite space) and *kāyapaguññatā* (proficiency of body). Regarding the suffixes *-bya*, *-vaddha*, and *-dāsa*:

the suffixes *-vaddha* and *-dāsa* occur after sixth-case endings (*chaṭṭhyanta*) in the senses of state (*bhāva*) and object (*kamma*), or with the suffix *-byo*. Examples are *vaddhabbaṃ* (to be increased), *vaddhatā* (increase); *dāsabyaṃ* (slavery), *dāsatā* (servitude)—how so? Because the augment *ṇ* is inserted before these suffixes.

The suffix *naṇ* is used after words ending in *yu* when expressing the sense of age (*vassa*) or state (*bhāva*), as well as the object (*kamma*). Thus: *yobbanaṃ*; and also *yuvattaṃ* and *yuvatā*. The suffix *ima* is used after words beginning with *aṇu*, etc.

The suffix *ima* occurs after words ending in the sixth case (genitive), either expressing a state (*bhāva*) or something produced by that [cause]. For example: *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, *kasimā*; and when there is the substitution of *vā* for *tva*, as in *aṇuttaṃ* or *aṇutā*.
Regarding "produced by that" (*tena nibbatte*):

this suffix occurs when a word denoting a state (*bhāvavācaka*) is the expressed object (*abhidheya*) of something produced by that [state]. For example: ‘produced by cooking’ (*pākena nibbattaṃ*) is *pākimaṃ*; *sekimaṃ*.
Regarding the suffixes *taratama* and *isi*:
these suffixes occur when expressing excellence (*atisaya*). For example: from *pāpa* (evil), we have *pāpatara* (more evil), *pāpatama* (most evil), *pāpissika*, *pāpiya*, and *pāpiṭṭha*;
in the feminine, *pāpatarā*. Also, from the superlative form itself, there is the suffix of excellence: from *pāpiṭṭha*, we have *pāpiṭṭhatara* (more extremely evil).
*Tannissite llo-*:

The suffix *llo* occurs after a word ending in the second case (*dutiya*) in the sense of "dependent on that. For example: ‘dependent on *veda*’ is *vedalla*; ‘dependent on *duṭṭhu*’ is *duṭṭhulla*. [Also: *ille*, *saṅkhārilla*. *Tassa vikārāvayavesu ṇṇikaṇeyyamayā-*: The suffixes *ṇṇika*, *ṇeya*, *maya*, and *ya* occur after a word in the sixth case (*tassa*) in the senses of modification (*vikāra*) and part (*avayava*).

A modification (*vikāra*) is a subsequent state different from the original nature (*pakati*). After a noun ending in the sixth case, the suffixes *ṇa* and others occur abundantly (*bahulam*) to denote a modification or a part (*avayava*).
Examples: *Ṇa*: *āyasaṃ* (made of iron), meaning "a bond"; *odumbaraṃ*, meaning "a leaf"; *odumbaraṃ*, meaning "ashes"; *kāpātaṃ*, meaning "flesh";
*kāpotaṃ*, meaning "bone. *Ṇika*: *kappāsikaṃ*, meaning "cloth. *Ṇeyya*: *eṇeyyaṃ*, meaning "flesh"; *eṇeyyaṃ*, meaning "bone"; *koseyyaṃ*, [meaning "silk cloth"].
*Vatthaṃ*—made of grass, made of wood, made of reeds, made of clay—‘in another [material]’. Also ‘made of cow dung’ (*gomayaṃ*).

From *jata*, the suffix *saṇva* occurs after a name ending in the sixth case (genitive) when expressing a modification or a part. ‘A modification of *jata*’: *jātussaṃ*, *jātumayaṃ*—[here] by the rule “there is elision” (*lopo*).

There is also frequent elision of the conditional suffix (*paccaya-lopa*) in the case of derivatives denoting fruits, flowers, and roots, as well as parts [of a whole]. For example: "the fruits of the *piyāla*" become "*piyālāni*";

"the flowers of the *mallikā*" become "*mallikā-pallikā*"; "the root of the *usīra*" becomes "*usīraṃ*. By this term, that which is designated by it is expressed. In the sense of a collection (*samūha*), there is the suffix *-kaṇṇaṇikā*.

The suffixes *kaṇ* and *ṇikā* occur after words ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) when expressing a collection (*samūha*). After words ending in a patronymic suffix (*gotta-paccaya*), the suffix *ka* occurs—e.g., *rājaññaka*.

After words denoting humans (*mānussa*), the suffix *ka* occurs following *ukkha*, etc.—e.g., *okkhaka*; *oṭṭhaka*; *orabbhaka*; *rājaka*; *rājaputtaka*; *hatthika*; *dhenuka*. After words ending in *ṇa*, the suffix *ka* occurs—e.g., *kāka*.
After words ending in *ṇika*, the suffix *ka* occurs provided they do not denote a mental state (*acitta*)—e.g., *āpūpika*; *saṃkulika*.

With words beginning with *jana* ending in the sixth case, the suffix *tā* occurs to denote a collection: *janatā* (a multitude of people), *gajatā* (a herd of elephants), *bandhutā* (a circle of kinsmen), *gāmatā* (a group of villages), *sahāyatā* (companionship), *nāgaratā* (citizenship).
Those ending in *tā* are feminine by nature. [The suffix] *-anīya-* is established in the sense of the object (*karaṇe*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇe*), as in *madanīya*.
Regarding *dhūmāyitattaṃ*: this is established as a feminine noun derived from a denominative root (*nāmadhātu*) by means of the suffix *-tā*.

In the sense of "beneficial" (*hita*), the suffix *-iya* occurs after a word ending in the genitive case: *upādāniyaṃ*. Furthermore, the suffix *-iya* occurs even outside of these [specific rules], such as in *asamānādare* (from *asamāna-adara*) and *sayito* (from *saya*), as in *sodariyo* ("uterine brother").
*Cakkhavādito sso-*:

after words beginning with *cakkhu*, the suffix *sso* is applied when [the word] is beneficial (*hita*) by means of the sixth case, such as *cakkhussaṃ* (beneficial for the eye) or *āyussaṃ* (beneficial for life). *Ṇyo tattha sādhū*:
the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of "skilled therein" (*tattha sādhū*).

The suffix *ṇya* occurs after a word ending in the seventh case (locative) in the sense of "good for that" (*tattha sādhūti*). Examples: *sabbañño*, *pārisajjo*. [In this sense,] it is used even outside [the locative], as in *rathaṃ vahantīti racchā* ("a street because it carries chariots").

The suffixes *niya* and *ñña* occur after a word ending in the seventh case in the sense of "good for that action" (*kammasadadā tattha sādhūti*). Example: "good for the work" (*kamme sādhu*) = *kammaññam*, *kammaññam*.

*Kathādīhi-iko:* After *kathā* and other words ending in the locative case, the suffix *ika* occurs in the sense of "skilled therein"; e.g., *kathika*, *dhammakathika*, *saṅgāmika*, *pavāsika*, *upavāsika*. *Pathādīhi-ṇeyya:* [The suffix *ṇeyya* occurs] after *patha* and other words.

The suffix *ṇeya* occurs in the sense of "good for that" (*tattha sādhū*) after words ending in the locative case, such as *patha*; thus: *pātheyya* (provisions for a journey) and *sāpateyya* (property).
After the word *dakkhiṇā*, the suffix *ṇeya* occurs in the sense of "worthy of" (*arahatthe*); thus: "one who is worthy of an offering" (*dakkhiṇaṃ arahati*) is a *dakkhiṇeyya*.
*Rāyo tumantā-*:

After a word ending in *-tum*, *rā* is substituted for the suffix *-tu* when expressing the sense of the agent (*arahattha*). For example: “This one is capable of killing, or capable of causing to kill, or capable of causing to cause to kill; this one is capable of making recite, or capable of causing to make recite, or capable of causing to cause to make recite; this one is capable of causing to go forth, or capable of causing to cause to go forth, or capable of causing to cause to cause to go forth.
In this context, *mantu* means “there is a capacity for this.”
The suffix *mantu* occurs in these senses: "there is" (*atthi*) and "belongs to" (*assa*). For example: "A village exists in this place," or "It belongs to this person," [forming] *gomā*.

Because the present tense is specified, one does not say *gomā* based on cows that have already existed or will exist in the future. How then can one say, "He was a cow-owner" (*gomā āsi*) or "He will be a cow-owner" (*gomā bhavissati*)?
Even then, he is a cow-owner (*gomā*) precisely because of cows existing at that time; [the words] "was" (*āsi*) and "will be" (*bhavissati*) merely indicate the past and future tenses.
*Padantara* means another word; *kālantara* means another time. Due to the use of the particle *iti*, there is a restriction of the object.
Furthermore, these suffixes—*mantu*, etc.—occur in the senses of abundance, praise, censure, excess, constant connection, and association.

In the case of *goassa* (of the cow), because nouns denoting a genus (*jāti-sadda*) have the capacity to denote the substance (*dabba*), the suffixes *mantu*, etc., do not occur; the same applies to adjectives (*guṇa-sadda*).

"A white cloth" (*seto paṭo*); those [words] which lack the capacity to denote the substance of words expressing qualities (such as *sattu*) do indeed occur—e.g., *buddhimā*, *rūpavā*, *rasavā*, *gandhavā*, *essavā*, *saddavā*;
*rasī*, *rasiko*; *rūpī*, *rūpiko*; *gandhī*, *gandhiko*. [These] are those whose colors have been vomited out.

The suffix *vantu* occurs after words ending in *avaṇṇa* (a, ā) in the sense of possession (*mantvattha*). Examples: *sīlavā* (possessing virtue), *paññavā* (possessing wisdom). Why "ending in *avaṇṇa*"? Consider: *satimā* (possessing mindfulness), *bandhumā* (possessing relatives).
The suffix *ika* or *ī* optionally follows words such as *daṇḍa* in the sense of possession. Because the rule is formulated broadly (*bahulaṃ*), sometimes two suffixes occur, and sometimes only one.
*Daṇḍaka*, *daṇḍi*, *daṇḍavā*; *gandhika*, *gandhī*, *gandhavā*; *rūpika*, *rūpī*, *rūpavā*—the suffix *-ika* is used for those who possess wealth as their highest [possession], such as *dhanika*;

others [possessing wealth] are *dhanī* or *dhanavā*. For the sense of "not being present" (*asannittha*), there is *atthika*; otherwise, for "possessing," there is *atthavā*. And those ending in *-tad* [take *-ika*]:
*puññatthika*, *puññatthi*. Those ending in *-vaṇṇa* take only *-ī*: *brahmavaṇṇī*, *devavaṇṇī*—[as in the case of] hands and teeth.
*Jātiyaṃ*: “elephant” (*hatthī*); “tusked one” (*dantī*); except for *hatthavā*, it is *dantavā*. Regarding color: in the case of a celibate practitioner (*brahmacārimhi*), [the suffix -in] is used:

“one of good complexion” (*vaṇṇī*, *brahmacārī*). Regarding possession: *vaṇṇavā* means “possessing another [quality]”. From the word *pokkhara* onwards, in a particular location: *pokkharaṇī* (lotus pond), *uppalinī*, *kumudinī*, *bhisinī*, *muḷālinī*, *sālukinī*;

even when there is a substitution (*kvāvādese’pi*), there is *padumanī*, *paduminī*. Regarding the leaf: *paṇṇaṃ*. Except for *pokkharavā*, [it applies to] “elephant” (*hatthi*) and “boatman” (*nāvāyika*).
The mariner;—one who experiences pleasure and pain, one who is happy or miserable; one with a crest or one who teaches the crest; one with a garland or one who wears no garland;
one with virtue or virtuous; one with strength or strong; one with strong arms and thighs, one with arm-strength, and one with thigh-strength;
[these are] from austerity and so forth.

After *tapas* and so forth, when expressing the sense of possession (*mantvatthe*), the suffix *ssi* becomes *ssī*; thus: *tapassī*, *yasassī*, *tejassī*, *manassī*, *payassī*. Alternatively, it may simply be *yasavā*. After *mukha* and so forth, the suffix *ro* occurs.

After *mukha* and other such words, when expressing the sense of possession, the suffix *ro* occurs; thus: *mukharo*, *susiro*, *ūsaro*, *madhuro*, *kharo*, *kujaro*, *nagaro*. Furthermore, after the word *danta*, when referring to having protruding teeth, the form is *danturo*.

After *tuṇḍi* and so forth, the suffix *bha* optionally occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *mat*. Thus: *tuṇḍibha*, *sāḷibha*, *valibha*; but when the suffix *vā* [is applied], it becomes *tuṇḍimā*. This is because they belong to the *saddhā* group.
The suffix *a* optionally occurs after *saddhā* and others in the sense of the possessive suffix *-mant*; thus: *saddho*, *pañño*. In the feminine:
*saddhā*; and likewise: *paññavā*. After *tapas*, the suffix *ṇo* occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *-mant*; thus: *tāpaso*; in the feminine: *tāpasī*.

*Ālvāhijjhādīhi-*: The suffix *ālu* occurs after words such as *abhijjhā* (covetousness) in the sense of possessive suffixes (*mantvatthe*); e.g., *abhijjhālu*, *sītālu*, *dhajālu*, *dayālu*. However, it is also [formed] as *dayāvā*. *Picchāditvilo-*:

The suffix *ilo* occurs after words such as *piccha* (feather) in the sense of possessive suffixes; e.g., *picchilo* (feathery), *picchavā*; *pheṇilo* (foamy), *pheṇavā*; *jaṭilo* (wearing matted hair), *jaṭāvā*. How is *vālālo* formed? It is by the elision of the initial vowel of *ila* after the negative particle *na* (in the sense of censure), according to the rule “*paro kvacī*” (sometimes the subsequent [element applies]).
*Silādihi vo-*:

The suffix *va* occurs after words beginning with *sīla*, etc., in the sense of the possessive (*mantvattha*). Examples: *sīlavo*, *sīlavā*; *kesavo*, *kesavā*. The suffix *aṇ* is always [added] after the following: *anna* (food) becomes *annava*; *gāṇḍi* and *rājī* take *aṇ* in the sense of a name: *gāṇḍivaṃ* (a bow); *rājivaṃ* (a lotus). After *māyā* and *medhā*, the suffix *vī* [is added].
With these two [suffixes], *vin* occurs in the sense of possession (*mantvattha*): *māyāvin*, *medhāvin*.
With the suffix *issara*, there is *āmyuvāmī*:

when the word *issara* (lord) is to be expressed as the object of possession (*abhidheya*) in the sense of possession, the suffixes *āmu*, *yu*, and *āmī* occur: *samassatthiti* becomes *sāmī*; *suvāmī*.

*Lakkhyā ṇo a-*. After the word *lakkhī*, the suffix *ṇo* occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *-mant*; the letter *a* is substituted for the final *i*; the letter *ṇ* is included for the sake of the entire suffix; thus, *lakkhaṇo*.
[The rule] *aṅgā no kalyāṇe* [is also applied].
In the sense of expressing possession (*mantvatthe*), the suffix *aṅga* is applied after the word *kalyāṇa*. Thus: *kalyāṇa-aṅga* becomes *kalyāṇaṅga*;
in the feminine, *kalyāṇaṅgī*. The suffix *so* is applied after the word *loma* in the sense of expressing possession. Thus: *loma-so* becomes *lomaso*; in the feminine, *lomasā*.
*Imiyā-*:

In the sense of the suffix *mant*, the forms *imiyā* occur frequently; for example: *puttimo*, *kittimo*, *puttiyo*, *kappiyo*, *jaṭiyo*, *hānabhāgiyo*, *seniyo*. [The suffix] *to* occurs in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

After the five endings (*pañcavyanta*), the suffix *to* generally occurs optionally. Examples: from the village he comes—*gāmato āgacchati*, *gāmasmā āgacchati*; he fears the thief—*corato bhāyati*, *corehi bhāyati*; fallen away from the caravan—*satthatoparihīno*, *satthā parihīno*. Regarding *ito*, *etto*, and *kuto*:

the suffix *to* is substituted for this [demonstrative pronoun] *ima* by means of the *ṭi*-rule; for *eta*, the suffix *ta* is substituted; and for the word *kiṃ*, the suffix *tu* is substituted. Examples: *ito* (from this), *imasmā*; *ato* (from that), *etto*, *etasmā*; *kuto* (from where), *kasmā*.
With *abhi* and others:
it becomes *-to* after *abhi* and others; namely, *abhito*, *parito*, *pacchato*, *heṭṭhato*. With *ādi* and others:
[the same applies].

The suffix *tra* optionally occurs after words beginning with *ādi*. [Examples: *ādo*, *ādito*; *majjhato*, *antato*, *piṭṭhito*, *passato*, *mukhato*. The meaning is: "wherever there is water, there it is seen; that very water which exists is what is seen.

The suffix *tra* occurs after the group of words beginning with *sabba* when they end in the locative case (*sattamī*). [Examples: *sabbatra*, *sabbattha*, *sabbasmiṃ*; *yatra*, *yattha*, *yasmiṃ*. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), it does not occur after the words *tumha* and *amha*.
*Kattha*, *kutra*, *atrā*, and *kvehidha*—these words are derived [from the locative case].
In *kasmin* we have *kattha*, *kutra*, and *kva*; in *etasmin* we have *ettha* and *atra*; in *asmin* we have *iha* and *idha*. Or rather, all [of these] are [derived from the locative].
After any word ending in the locative case (*sattamyanta*), the suffix *dhi* or *vā* is used; thus: *sabbadhi*, *sabbattha*.
After a word ending in the ablative case (*yato*), the suffix *hiṃ* or *vā* is used; thus: *yahiṃ*, *yattha*.

From the seventh case-ending (the locative), *haṃ* may optionally be substituted for *vā*, *hiṃ*, and *ca*; thus: *tāhaṃ*, *tahiṃ*, and *tatra*. From the interrogative pronoun *ku-*, *hiṃ* and *kaṃ* are added; thus:
*kuhiṃ* and *kahaṃ*.

The word *kiṃ* ending in the locative case takes the suffixes *-hiṃ*, *-haṃ*, and the particle *nipaccaṃ*; [it also becomes] *kissa* and *ku*. Thus: *kihiṃ*, *kahaṃ*, *kathaṃ*, *kuhidvaṃ*. *Canaṃ* is another particle; in *kihidvī*, the particle *vi* is likewise [used].

Regarding time, after words ending in the locative case such as *sabba*, *eka*, *añña*, and *ya*, the suffix *-dā* is added. When these locative endings are present, *-dā* occurs for time: *sabbadā* (at all times), *ekadā* (once), *aññadā* (at another time), *yadā* (when), *tadā* (then). Why "for time"? [To exclude: *sabbattha dese* (everywhere in the place).
*Kadā*, *kudā*, *sadā*, and *adhunā*—these words are derived as follows: at that time, *kadā*; at all times, *sadā*; at this time, *adhunā* or *idāni*.
[The suffixes] *-ajja*, *-sajja*, *-apara*, *-ajje*, *-itarahi*, and *-kara* [are added to the stem].

These words are derived through grammatical derivation (*nipacca*); that the suffix *-tī* is a substitute (*ādesa*), and that it signifies a specific time—all this is obtained through *nipātana* (conventional rule).

The word *ajja* ("today") is derived from the base *asmin* ("in this") with the suffix *-tī* and the replacement of the vowel *a* by *j*. In the same way, from the base *asabhāva* ("not being"), one obtains *sajju* ("immediately");
from *apara* ("other"), one obtains *aparajju* ("the day after"). From the base *ima* ("this") at this very time, one obtains *rahi* ("now") or *imasmiṃ* ("in this").
In the present time—what is the meaning of the word *kiṃ*? It means "what" (*ko*) and also "nowadays" (*ajjatanē*). In that [past] time, it is *karaha*.

The suffix *thā* occurs after the words *sabba-* and others when expressing a manner (*pakāra*). A particularity (*visesa*) that distinguishes a general category (*sāmañña*) is "manner" (*pakāra*). When the words *sabba-* and others are used in that sense, the suffix *thā* is applied: *sabbenapakārena* becomes *sabbathā*; likewise, *yathā*, *tathā*.
How is *itthaṃ* formed?

These words are derived in the sense of manner (*pakāra*). What is the suffix here? It is *thaṃ*. And what is their respective [substitution]? *Kathaṃ* and *itthaṃ*. [The suffix *thaṃ* is applied] after the word *dhā* and after numerals.
The suffix *dhā* follows numerals expressing modes (*pakāra*). For example: ‘He does it in two ways (*dvehi pakārehi*) or as two ways (*dve vā pakāre*)’ is expressed as *vidhākaroti*;
‘he does it in many ways’ is *bahudhā karoti*; ‘he makes one heap into five modes’ is *pañcadhā karoti*; ‘he makes that which has five modes into one mode’ is *ekadhākaroti*.
*Vekājjhaṃ*:
After a single vowel, *jjhaṃ* may optionally occur; for example, *ekajjhaṃ karoti* or *ekadhā karoti*. *Dvitīhedhā*: [The suffix] *-dhā* occurs after the second vowel.
In two ways it possesses a mode (*pakāravat*): as *vedhā*, *tedhā*; as *dvidhā*, *tidhā*.

"Classes possessing that"—this refers to classes of words (*saddajātī*) which denote a general property (*taṃsāmaññavācaka*) while possessing that [mode]; for example, *paṭujātīyo* (sharp classes) and *mudujātīyo* (soft classes).
"By number of times (vārasaṃkhyāya) means:

it occurs by way of a number connected with a turn (vāra); 'he eats twice' means he eats two times during the day. Why is 'turn' (vāra) mentioned? [To exclude: 'He eats five times. Why is 'by number' (saṃkhyāya) mentioned? [To exclude: 'He eats many turns. From what [is this derived]? From *katimhā*.

The suffix *kkhattum* occurs after a numeral related to a number of times (*vāra*), as in: “How many times does he eat?”—“He eats three times. After a plural numeral related to a number of times, the suffixes *dhā* and *kkhattum* occur when there is proximity (*paccāsatti*) between the times;

for example: “He eats many times a day” (*bahudhā divasassa bhuñjati*, *bahukkhattum*). Why is it said “when there is proximity”? Consider: “He eats many times a month” (*bahukkhattum māsassa bhuñjati*). In this case, because the times are not proximate, the suffix *kkhattum* alone is used.
*Sakiṃ* or *vā*:

The particle *sakiṃ* is used in the sense of "once" (*ekavāraṃ*) or "perhaps" (*icchamhi atthe*). For example, in *sakiṃ vā bhuñjati*, what does it mean? It means *ekakkhattuṃ bhuñjati* ("he eats once"). It is also used in the sense of repetition (*vicchā*) and smallness (*appakāra*).

The suffix *cī* occurs frequently in the sense of division (*vīcchāya*) and in the sense of manner (*pakāra*). In the sense of division: *khaṇḍaso*, *bilaso*; in the sense of manner: *puthuso*, *sabbaso*. In the sense of becoming something else (*abhūtatabbhāva*), when there is a connection with the agent (*karaka*) or the instrument (*sādhana*), the suffix *cī* follows words expressing a modification (*vikāra*).

When there is a connection with the agent or the instrument, the suffix *cī* is added to a word denoting a modification to express the state of that which did not previously exist in one state but comes to exist in another state.
"becomes"; "he makes what is not white white," i.e., he whitens it;

"what was not white may become white," "may be white," "becomes white"—this refers to the transformation of one state into another. What [is the object]? He makes a jar, there is curd, the jar comes into being.
Why specify "in connection with the agent"? [Example: "What was not white becomes white. Why specify "transformation"? [Example: By nature...
Let it not be so; gold makes earrings.
Other conditions are also seen—other conditions are seen besides those stated, regarding both stated and unstated meanings: ‘various mothers,’ ‘stepmothers,’ ‘of them.’
"Those who go on a path" are *pathāvino* (from *patha* + *avī*). "One in whom envy exists" is *issukī* (from *issa* + *ukī*).
"Those who bear the yoke" are *dhorayhā* (from *dhura* + *yhaṇa*).
[The suffix] *-añña-*...

Suffixes already mentioned are also seen used in other senses. For example: ‘lord of the Magadhas’ is *māgadho*, with the suffix *-ṇo*; ‘a thousand [pieces] of Kāsi’—it is worth that, thus it is *kāsiyo*, with the suffix *-iyo*. Regarding their own meaning:
suffixes are also seen used in their own sense, as in *hīnako*, *potako*, and *kicacayayaṃ*.
Lopa: Elision of suffixes is also observed; for example, in *buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ* and *cakkhuṃ suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā*, there is elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvappaccaya*).
[The rule] *sarānamādissāyuvaṇṇassāño ṇānubandhe* [applies here].

The suffix *āñ* occurs, respectively, after those vowels that have become initial [in a compound] which are not *a*-vowels or *va*-vowels, provided they are not followed by the consonant *ṇ*. Examples: *rāghavo*, *vainateyyo*, *meniko*, *oḷumpiko*, *dohaggaṃ*. Why say "not followed by *ṇ*"? Witness: *purātano*.

In some instances, when there is a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), the suffix *āñ* occurs after those *a*-vowels that have become initial, even if they are followed by *ṇ*, provided it is in a conjunct context. Examples: *decco*, *koṇḍañño*. Why say "in some instances"? Witness: *kattikeyyo*.
In the middle—sometimes, even when *yu*-vowels (*i* and *u*) occur in the middle, they become *ā* [before a following consonant]; for example: *aḍḍhateyyā*, *vāseṭṭho*.
[Also in the following cases: *kosajja*, *ājjava*, *pārisajja*, *subhajja*, *maddava*, *ārissa*, *asabhājañña*, *theyya*, *bāhusacca*.
These words are derived with the suffix *ṇa*, which does not leave a trace [as a visible phoneme]: “the state of one who is indolent” is *kosajja*; “the state of one who is upright” is *ujupa*;

“one who is good among assemblies” is *pārisajja*; “one who has a good heart” is *suhajja*, and “the state of that” is *sohajja*; “the state of one who is gentle” is *maddava*; “this belongs to a seer (*isi*), or his state” is *ārissaṃ*;
“this belongs to a bull (*usabha*), or his state” is *āsabhaṃ*; “the state of one who is well-bred (*ājānīya*)” is *so*.

Or else, *ājañña* is [the state or action] of one who is to be urged on (*ājāniya*); *theyya* is the state or action of stealing (*theyya*); *bāhusacca* is the state of being much-learned (*bahussuta*).

Among these, that which possesses the characteristic of a twin is established by means of a grammatical convention (*nipātana*). [This applies to] *manā* and so forth, according to their respective [rules].

The suffix *ṇa* is applied to words such as *māna*, provided no other consonant follows [the suffix]. For example: "existing in the mind" (*manasi bhavam*) becomes *mānasaṃ*; "the state of being dejected in mind" (*dummanaso bhāvo*) becomes *domanassaṃ*;

likewise, *somanassaṃ*. The vowel *u* is substituted for the suffix *vaṇ*; for example: *rāghavo* and *jāmbavaṃ*. Furthermore, [the vowel *o* is substituted] for the word *go* when followed by the suffix *yaṃ*.
Before an affix beginning with the letter *y*, the substitution of *avaṅ* occurs for the vowel *o* and the vowel *u*; thus: *gabyaṃ*, *gātabyo*.

There is elision (*lopa*) of the vowels *a* and *i* before an affix beginning with the letter *y*; thus: *dāyyaṃ*, *kāruññaṃ*, *ādhipaccaṃ*, *deppaṃ*. In some instances, the rule regarding the addition of the suffix *ba* to form the word *bahu* does not apply; thus: *kiccayaṃ*.
When followed by *r* or *n* as an affix, there is elision of that member which has a vowel at its beginning. For example: *kittakaṃ*, *petteyyaṃ*.
[The suffixes] *kismahā* and *mahā* are derived from *kisama-* and *mahata-*.
Why do these [suffixes] become *kasma* and *maham* respectively? From *kasim* and *mahim*.
In the case of the word *āyu*, there is a substitution of *āyas* for *āyu* before the suffix *mantu*; thus, *āyasmā*.
Regarding "jo vuddhassiyiḍhesu":
for the word *vuddha* (grown), when followed by *iya* or *iṭṭha*, [the suffix] *ja* is substituted; thus, *jeyya* and *jeṭṭha*.
For the words *bāḷha*, *antika*, and *pasattha*, the suffix *ida* is the means of formation.

In the case of words ending in -iya and -iṭṭha, when they denote praise, the suffixes -sādhika and -sādhita, as well as -nedika and -nediṭṭha, and -seyya and -seṭṭha, occur respectively: *sādhiyo*, *sādhiṭṭho*;
*nediyo*, *nediṭṭho*; *seyyo*, *seṭṭho*.

In the case of words ending in -iya and -iṭṭha, when they denote "younger," the suffixes -kaṇika and -kaṇiṭṭha, as well as -kaniya and -kaniṭṭha, occur respectively: *kaṇiyo*, *kaṇiṭṭho*; *kaniyo*, *kaniṭṭho*.

There is elision of the suffixes *vīm*, *tu*, and *vantu* before the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha*. For example: ‘one who is exceedingly wise’ becomes *medhiya*, *medhiṭṭha*; ‘one who is exceedingly mindful’ becomes *satiya*, *satiṭṭha*; ‘one who is exceedingly virtuous’ becomes *guṇiya*, *guṇiṭṭha*.
[The same applies] for *stia* and *issa* before *tissa*.
There is the elision of the *ti* of *santassa*; thus, *vīsaṃ sataṃ* (twenty hundred) and *tiṃsaṃ sataṃ* (thirty hundred).
When *ttake* follows, *eṭa* is substituted for this [word]; thus, *ettakaṃ* (so much).
*Ṇikassiyo vā*:

after *Ṇikassa*, *iyo* occurs; [e.g.,] *sakyaputtiyo*, *sakyaputtiko*. *Adhātussa ke’syādito ghe’ssī*: for a word that does not end in a *dhātu*, *ke* is substituted for *asya* when it begins with *gha*, and *i* is substituted for *ssī*.

When the letter *ka* follows a non-stem (*adhātu*) vowel, the letter *i* frequently replaces the preceding vowel *a*, provided that the word begins with *gho-na* (nasal) or *syādi* (the suffixes beginning with *si*).

Examples: *bālikā*, *kārikā*. Why "of a non-stem"? Consider *sakā* (where the stem is *saka*). Why "beginning with *ke*"? Consider *nandanā* (where the stem ends in *na*). Why "beginning with *syādi*"?

Consider *bahuparibbājakā*, *madhurā*—in these cases, the rule is established because they are separated from the suffix *si* by the letter *ka*. Why "after *gho*"? Consider [examples where the preceding sound is not *gho*].
"Bālaka"; what is the example? "Bahukattukā sālā" (a hall with many builders).
Thus ends the fourth section, beginning with "ṇa," in the Vutti of the Moggallāna Vyākaraṇa. [Now follows:
"Tijamānehi khasā khamāvīmaṃsāsu. (The suffix *khas* is used after roots ending in *t* or *j*, when the sense is 'to endure' or 'to investigate').

In the case of *khanti* (patience), *tijā* (sharpness/energy) and *vīmaṃsā* (investigation) are the respective conditions for *māna* (pride). [The roots] *titikkhā* and *vīmaṃsā*: one endures (*titikkhati*), one investigates (*vīmaṃsati*). What is the meaning of *khamā-vīmaṃsā-suti*? [It means] piercing (*tejanaṃ*), fire (*tejo*), it burns (*tejayati*);

honoring (*mānanaṃ*), pride (*māno*), it honors (*māneti*). Regarding *kitā* (inquiry) in the senses of medical treatment (*tikicchā*) and doubt (*saṃsaya*): when *kitā* occurs in the sense of medical treatment or doubt, it becomes *jo*. Thus: medical treatment (*tikicchā*), doubt (*vicikicchā*)—one treats (*tikicchati*), one doubts (*vicikicchati*). Except for *niketa*, *saṅketa*, *ketanaṃ*, *keto*, and *ketayati*.

In the sense of loathing, there is the elision of the suffixes *jo*, *bassa*, and *bho* after the present participles *gup* and *badh*. When the roots *gup* and *badh* occur in the sense of loathing (*nindā*), the suffixes *jo*, *bassa*, and *bho* are applied: *jigucchā* (loathing), *bībhacchā* (revulsion); *jigucchati* (he loathes), *bībhacchati* (he reviles). Furthermore, in the sense of protecting (*gopana*), there are the forms *gope*, *popeti*, and *badhako*.
The suffix *tum* is elided when followed by the suffix *smā* in the sense of repetition (*vicchā*).

In the sense of desire (*icchā*), the suffix *tuṃ* becomes *khasa* when followed by a root with a heavy syllable (*bahukula*); furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *tuṃ* suffix because it has been taught [as such]—as in *bubhukkhā*, *jigimsā*, and *jighacchā*;
and as in *bubhukkhati*, *jigimsati*, and *jighacchati*. Why is it not so in the case of "he desires to eat" (*bhottum icchati*)? Because it is expressed by means of another word (*padantara*).
What is the example for "when *tuṃ* follows"? "He desires food" (*bhojanaṃ icchati*). What is the example for "in the sense of desire"? "He goes to eat" (*bhuñjituṃ gacchati*).
"How does one wish for a family to fall? Just as the sentence "one wishes for a family to fall" exists, so too will there be such a verbal form (*vutti*).
But how indeed does a sentence come to be? Through the world's desire for such expression. This is the function of the suffix *ī*.

The suffix *īya* occurs after a verb root in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) when [the object] is the direct object (*kamma*). For example: *puttam icchati* becomes *puttīyati*. Why is it not so in the case of *āsam icchati*?
And why does it not occur here in *rañño puttam icchati*? Because of the presence of a relation (*sāpekkhattā*);
for one that is related to another cannot enter into a state of identity with something else. If this were the case, then it would also not occur in *attanoputtam icchati*.
One should not think thus: "For it does not exist as 'one's own' (attanoputtiyati). How, then, is the meaning of "belonging to oneself" understood from what has been said?
Because [the word] is not heard used for anything else, and because desire has that [self] as its object. This is established through analogy and usage.

The suffix *īya* occurs after a word denoting an object of comparison (*upamāna*) in the sense of behaving like that object. For example: *puttam-iva ācarati* = *puttīyati māṇavakaṃ* (“he behaves toward the young brahmin as toward a son”). Why say “after a word denoting an object of comparison”? [Observe: *puttam-ācarati* (“he behaves toward his son [as toward himself]”).

[The suffix *īya* occurs] after a word denoting a locus (*ādhāra*) in the sense of behaving like that locus. For example: *kuṭiyam-iva ācarati* = *kuṭiyati pāsāde* (“he behaves in the palace as if in a hut”), and *pāsādīyati kuṭiyam* (“he behaves in the hut as if in a palace”).
*Kattutāyo-*:

The suffix *āya* occurs in the sense of an agent (*katta*) when used as a comparison (*upamāna*) for an action (*ācāra*); for example, ‘he moves like a mountain’ is *pabbatāyati*. It also occurs in the sense of departing (*cyattha*).

The suffix *āya* is frequently used after a word denoting the agent (*kattū*) in the sense of "becoming that which it was not before" (*abhūtatabbhāve*); for example: *bhusāyati*, *paṭapaṭāyati*, *lohitāyati*—meaning, simply, "it acts intensely" (*bhusaṃ karoti*). Why does it not occur here in the sense of "it becomes intense" (*bhusi bhavati*)?

Because the meaning has already been expressed [by the base itself]. Regarding *saddādīhi*: after words such as *sadda* ending in the accusative case, the suffix *āya* occurs in the sense of "he performs" (*karoti*); for example: *saddāyati*, *verāyati*, *kalahāyati*, *dhūpāyati*.
*Namotvasso-*:
In the sense of "he makes *namo* thus," there is the suffix *-asso*; he pays homage (*namassati*) to the Tathāgata.
In the sense of a verbal root, there is the suffix *-nāma*.
The suffix *smā* frequently occurs after the meaning of a verbal root: ‘he passes by with an elephant’ becomes *hatthayati*; ‘he sings along with a lute’ becomes *upavīṇayati*;
‘he makes firm’ becomes *vinayaṃ daḷhayati*; ‘the night becomes pure’ becomes *ratti visuddhayati*;
‘he asks about what is wholesome’ becomes *kusalayati*.
Also after *sacca* and others:

the suffix *āpi* occurs after the verbal roots *sacca*, etc., in the sense of their root-meanings. Examples: *saccāpeti*, *atthāpeti*, *vedāpeti*, *sukkha-āpeti*, *sukha-āpeti*, *dukkha-āpeti*. Also after roots meaning action (*kriyattha*).

This is the governing rule up to the completion of the section on verbal roots (*dhātu*). "That whose purpose is action is *kriyārtha*"; this refers to a verbal root (*dhātu*). From the class beginning with *cur*, the suffix *ṇi* is added in the sense of the action itself (*sakatthe*) for the most part.

The letter *ṇ* serves the purpose of causing vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*)—as it does elsewhere as well—such as in *corayati* and *lāḷayati*. How is it that [the suffix is applied] in the case of *rajjaṃ kāreti* ("he causes the kingdom to be ruled")? It is by means of a division of the grammatical rules (*yogavibhāgato*).
And [the suffix] *ṇi* occurs also in the sense of the instigator’s activity (*payojakabyāpāra*).

When one causes an agent to act, the suffixes *ṇi* and *ṇāp* frequently occur after verbal roots in that sense: *kāreti*, *kārāpeti*. But surely the agent is also an instigator of the instrument and other factors;
would not the suffixes *ṇi* and *ṇāp* therefore apply to their activity as well? No, because of the force of the specific mention of the "instigator" (*payojaka*).

They will not [occur], because of their capacity for separate verbal expression from *cura* and the others, and because there is no suffix *ṇa* beyond *ā*; nor is there *ṇi*, because it follows a vowel (*vuvaṇṇa*).

From two [roots] and others, [the suffix *kyo* occurs]. The suffix *kyo* occurs after roots meaning "to buy" (*krayattha*) when they are used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the passive (*kamma*), in the non-evident tenses (*aparokkha*) such as the optative (*māna*) and the infinitive (*tatiya*), etc., provided these are prescribed for the abstract state or the passive and exclude the past tense (*parokkhā*). The mention of *nta* is for the sake of what follows.

The letter *ka* has the sense of non-perception (*abuddhi*). The same applies in subsequent cases: *ṭhiyamānaṃ*, *ṭhiyate*; *sūyamānaṃ*, *sūyate*. [Question: Why [is the condition] "in the absence of the immediate" (*aparokkhesu*) stated?

[Answer: *Babhuva devadattena* (Devadatta became); *bibhida kusūlo* (the granary split). In *bhijjate kusūlo sayameva* (the granary splits by itself), the state of being an object (*kamma-tā*) is understood from the hearing [of the suffix];

in *atibhijjate* (it splits excessively), the state of being an agent (*kattu-tā*) is understood from the hearing [of the suffix]. However, when there is a desire to express the state of being an agent, one says *bhindati kusūlo*.

"Self" (attānaṃ) occurs; in this manner, other [terms] should also be understood according to the scriptures. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *mānantatthādi* and so forth when they are not proximate," this is the governing rule (*adhikāra*).

Because [suffixes] such as *tya* and so forth are prescribed after roots beginning with *āta* and so forth—specifically after those that follow [the root] and are formed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*kamma*), or the state (*bhāva*)—they are understood to apply only to those [roots].

Thus, in the case of intransitive roots (*akammaka-dhātu*), [the suffixes] are used in the sense of the agent, while in the case of transitive roots (*sakammaka*), they are used in the sense of both the agent and the object when there is a desire for the verbal expression (*kammāvacanicchā*).
It should be understood that [roots] are "intransitive" (bhāveva) when they occur as such:

it should be known that a root whose action requires an object (*kamma*) is "transitive" (*sakammaka*), whereas a root whose action requires only an agent (*kattumatta*) is "intransitive" (*akammaka*). [The suffix -lo occurs] in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).
*Kattari lo-*:

After verbal roots meaning "action" (*kriyāttha*), when the agent (*katta*) is proximate (*aparokkha*), the suffix *lo* occurs for the first person singular and subsequent persons. The letter *l* [in *lo*] is for the purpose of [triggering] the rule "for *ñi*, *la*, and *se*" (*ñilasse*). This is for the sake of distinction—e.g., *pacamāno*, *pacanto*; *pavati*.
And [the suffix *lo* applies] after roots such as *mañc* and *rudh*.

After roots beginning with *rudh* (the *rudhādigaṇa*), the substitution *lo* occurs in place of *māna* and other suffixes prescribed for the agent (*kattū*). The letter *m* is a phonetic marker (*anubandha*); the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. Thus: *rundhamāno*, *rundhanto*, *rundhati*. [The rule] “optionally by means of *ṇa*, *ṇāpi*, and *āpī*”:

after [roots] with the affixes *ṇi*, *ṇāpi*, and *āpi*, the substitution *lo* optionally occurs in place of *māna* and other suffixes prescribed for the agent. Thus: *corayanto*, *corento*; *kārayantā*.
*kārento*; *kārāpiyanto*, *kārāpento*; *saccāpayanto*, *saccāpento*; *corayati*, *coreti*; *kārayati*, *kāreti*;
*kārāpayati*, *kārāpeti*; *saccāpayati*, *saccāpeti*—this word has the sense of expressing the meaning of the verbal root (*vaca*) as it stands;
therefore, it is always used with the suffix *-māna*: *corayamāno*, *kārayamāno*, *kārāpayamāno*, *saccāpayamāno*.
The suffix *yaka* is applied after roots beginning with *dip-* and those beginning with *div-*. Thus: *dibbanto*; *dibbati*. The suffix *ko* is applied after roots beginning with *tud-*.
With roots beginning with *tud*, the suffix *ko* occurs in the domain of the *la*-affixes: *tudamāno*, *tudanto*; [in the present tense] *kudati*.

With roots beginning with *ji*, the suffix *knā* occurs in the domain of the *la*-affixes: *jinanto*, *jināti*. How is it that [the forms] *jayanto* and *jayatī* occur? Because they belong to the *bhū*-class (the first class).
*ky-ādihi kṇā-*:

after roots beginning with *ki*, the suffix *kṇā* occurs in the sense of buying; as in *kiṇanto* (buying) and *kiṇāti* (he buys). *sv-ādihi kṇo-*: after roots beginning with *su*, the suffix *kṇo* [occurs].

The suffix *kṇa* occurs after roots beginning with *su* in the sense of the *la*-affixes: *suṇamāno*, *suṇanto*, *suṇoti*. How does one hear? Because of their inclusion in the list beginning with *kyā*.
From roots beginning with *tan*: the suffix *o* occurs after roots beginning with *tan* in the sense of the *la*-affixes; [thus] *tanoti*.
Regarding the suffixes *tabba* and *anīya*:

when followed by verbal roots (*kriyattha*), the suffixes *tabba* and *anīya* frequently occur in the sense of the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*). Examples: *kattabbaṃ*, *karaṇīyaṃ* (that which is to be done); *kattabbo kaṭo*, *karaṇīyo* (the mat that is to be made).

Because of the frequent use of the term "frequently" (*bahulaṃ*), they also occur in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth: *sinānīyaṃ cuṇṇaṃ* (powder for bathing); *dānīyo brāhmaṇo* (the Brahmin worthy of gifts); *samāvattanīyo guru* (the teacher to be attended upon); *pavacanīyo upajjhāyo* (the preceptor to be spoken to); *upaṭṭhānīyo sisso* (the student to be served).
Ghyaṇa.

The suffix *ghyaṇ* frequently occurs after verbal roots in the sense of an action (*bhāva*) or an object (*kamma*). Examples: *vākyaṃ*, *kāriyaṃ*, *veyyaṃ*, *jeyyaṃ*. And after the root *ās* (to sit), [the suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs].

The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after the root *ā* in the senses of state (*bhāva*) and object (*kamma*), and the vowel *ā* is replaced by *e*; thus, *deyyaṃ*. After roots such as *vada*, the suffix *ya* occurs frequently in the senses of state and object;

These suffixes beginning with *tabba*—namely *tabba*, *anīya*, *ya*, and *tavya*—are prescribed generally for all roots, even when the meanings of necessity (*pesa*), excellence (*atisagga*), attainment (*patta*), or time (*kāla*) are implied.

For instance: *kaṭo kattabbo* (the mat must be made), *karaṇīyo*, *kāriyo*, or *kicco*; likewise, *evam tvayā kaṭo kattabbo* (thus must the mat be made by you); or *hotā kaṭo kattabbo* (it is necessary that the mat be made). Similarly, *hoto*.

For the time for doing the mat has indeed arrived—even so, when [the action] is occurring within a period of more than a moment (*uddhamuhuttika*), it is established as being [already] accomplished in the case of the agent (*pesa*, etc.).

Likewise, when the agent is understood as distinguished by capability and distinguished by the necessity of the duty (*āvassakādhammiṇatā*), it is established from the state of being (*bhāvādo*). From a period of more than a moment:

Vāco and bhāvo. Regarding verbal derivatives (*kāraka*), first, in the sense of a noun (*saññā*): that by which one goes is a *pāda*; that which breaks is a *roga*;

Even in the sense of non-verbal nouns (*asaññā*): a gift is a *dāya*, given is *datto*; gain is *lābho*, obtained is *laddho*; *gha*—*vakko*, *nipako*; *ka*—*piyo*, *khipo*, *bhujo*, *āyudhaṃ*.

Dādhātvi-: The root *dā* (to give) frequently becomes *dādhā* when expressing the sense of the action or the agent; e.g., *ādi*, *nidhi*. *Vāladhi*: [from *vala* with suffix *-dhi*]. *Vamādīhathu-*: [from roots beginning with *vam* with suffix *-thu*].
The suffix *thu* occurs after roots beginning with *vam* in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the agent (*kāraka*); examples: *vamathu*, *vepathu*. *Kvi*:

The suffix *kvi* occurs frequently in the sense of the action or the agent—the letter *k* serves the purpose of causing the addition of the *kā* augment—examples: *abhibhū*, *sayambhū*, *bhattaggaṃ*, *salākaggaṃ*, *sabhā*, *pabhā*.

The [suffix] *ano-* occurs after verbal roots (*kriyāttha*) expressing a state (*bhāva*) or an agent (*kāraka*); for example: *gamanaṃ*, *dānaṃ*, *sampadānaṃ*, *apādānaṃ*, *adhikaraṇaṃ*, *calano*, *jalano*, *kodhano*, *kopano*, *maṇḍano*, *bhusano*.
[The suffixes] *itthi*, *ya*, *maṇ*, *ktika*, *ya*, and *kā* also [occur].

In the feminine gender, when used as a noun (bhāva) or an agent (kāraka), roots ending in vowels such as *ā* take the suffixes *a*, *ti*, *kkhā*, *vīmaṃsā*, *jigucchā*, *pipāsā*, *puttīyā*, *īhā*, *bhikkhā*, *āpadā*, *medhā*, *godhā*—those ending in *ṇa*: *hārā*, *tārā*, *dhārā*, *ārā*—*kti*:

Success (ijjā), lying down (seyyā), assemblies (samajjā), going forth (pabbajjā), service (paricariyā), wakefulness (jāgariyā)—these are the reasons [for the suffix -ana]; [the suffixes] -hāra, -ṇā, -vedanā, -vandanā, and -upāsanā.
[The suffix] -jā occurs after the roots *jah* and *ah*; thus, from these [roots], there are the feminine forms *jāni* and *hāni*.

From the root *kar*, the suffix *riri* occurs in the feminine (*itthiyaṃ*). *Akaraṇaṃ* is *kiriyā*; how is it that it becomes *kriyā*? It is due to the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātanā*) from the word *kriyā*. *Ikitī sarūpe-*: [The suffixes] *i* and *ki* occur when the following suffix is identical in form (*sarūpe*).

When a verbal root meaning an action (*kriyāttha*) is expressed in its own form (*sarūpa*), and another word meaning an action follows it, the suffixes *i* and *ti* occur; for example, *vaci* and *yudhi*. In *pacati*, the word *kāra* is used in compounds such as "the letter *a*" (*akāra*) or "the letter *k*" (*kakāra*), as in the expression *evakāra*.

The suffix *ṇi* occurs when the meanings of habit (*sīla*), fitness (*abhikkhañña*), or necessity (*avassaka*) are understood; for example: *uṇhabhoji* (one who habitually eats hot food), *khīrapāyī* (one who drinks milk), *avassakārī* (one who acts out of necessity), and *satatadāyī* (one who gives constantly).

When the agent is expressed in the past tense, the suffixes *-ktavantu*, *-kta*, and *-āvī* are applied.

When occurring in the sense of what has already come to pass (*bhūtātthe*), verbal roots meaning "action" (*kriyāttha*) take the suffixes *ktavantu* and *ktavī* in the agentive case (*kattari*); for example, *vijitavā*, *vijitāvī*. The governing rule "when what has already come to pass" (*bhūte*) applies up until the section on the meanings of "eating" (*āhārattha*).

The suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of state (*bhāve*) and object (*kamme*). When in the sense of state or object, the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of what has already come to pass; for example, *āsitaṃ bhavatā* ("you have sat") and *kato kaṭo bhavatā* ("a mat was made by you").

The suffix *kta* occurs after a verbal root when expressing the agent (*kattar*) at the commencement of an action (*kriyārambha*), and according to the specific requirements of each case; for example: *pakato bhavaṃ kaṭaṃ* (you have made the mat), *pakato kaṭo bhavatā* (the mat has been made by you); *pasutto bhavaṃ* (you have slept), *pasuttaṃ bhavatā* (it has been slept by you).
[This applies] except after the roots *ṭhā*, *vas*, *silisa*, *ghiruha*, *jara*, and *jan*.

The suffix *kta* occurs after the roots *ṭhā* and others in the sense of the agent (*kattari*), according to the specific requirements of each case: *upaṭṭhito* you were waited upon by the teacher, [or] the teacher was waited upon by you;
*upāsito* you were attended upon by the teacher, [or] the teacher was attended upon by you; *anuvusito* you were served by the teacher, [or] the teacher was served by you;
*āsiliṭṭho* you were embraced by the teacher, [or] the teacher was embraced by you.
"You have slept upon the bed, brother; the bed has been slept upon by you.

The suffix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "going" (*gamanattha*) and after intransitive roots (*akammaka*), when used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*) and the locus (*ādhāre*), according to the rules as they have been received. For example:

*idamesaṃ yātaṃ* ("this has been traveled by them"), *iha te yātaṃ* ("here it has been traveled by you [plural]"), *ihatehi yātaṃ* ("here it has been traveled by those [plural]"), *ayaṃ tehi yāto patho* ("this is the path traveled by them"). "They have eaten by them, they have drunk here by them; rice has been eaten by them, water has been drunk by them"—this is a grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*) where the sense of the agent is absent.

How is it that "the cows have drunk"? Is it "drunk" because "drinking exists in them"? Or rather, by virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulika*), as in the case of *passina*—here, the suffix *-kta* denotes the past tense.
Likewise: "honored by the king," "desired by the king," "awakened by the king," "worshipped by the king"—and similarly, "practiced."
