It goes. [Question: Why "prior" (*pubba*)? [Example: "He eats and he cooks"—here, because the root *bhū* (to eat) occurs in all instances, its having a single agent and its being prior in time is understood: "The mountain is before the river," "The river is beyond the mountain.

By the very expression "having eaten and eaten, he goes," the sense of repetition (*ābhikkhañña*) is understood through the word itself—how could it be grasped by a living being? (*jīvagāhaṃ*) [End of passage].
[The question] "Did you go shaking your body? and so forth is established by means of a verbal noun (*ghana*) functioning as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāvisesana*);
for example, [the expression] "he lies down cooking rice" (*odanapākaṃ sayati*). This is because the suffix *-nta* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is in the present tense.
Because it occurs in the sense of the present tense, the suffix *ta* is added to a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) to express the agent (*kartari*); e.g., *tiṭṭhanto*.
The suffix *māna*—because it occurs in the sense of the present tense—is added to a verbal root to express the agent; e.g., *tiṭṭhamāno*.

Regarding the suffix *māna* in the sense of becoming (*bhāva*) and action (*kamma*): after a verbal root expressing an action, when used in the present tense, *māna* occurs in the sense of becoming and action; for example, *ṭhīyamānaṃ* (being stood) and *paccamāno odano* (the rice being cooked). [The suffix *māna* also occurs] after those [roots] preceded by *te*, as well as in the future tense.

In the sense of the future, verbal roots meaning "action" take the suffixes *nta*, *māna*, and *ssa* preceded by the augment *p*. Examples: *ṭhassanto*, *ṭhassamāno*, *ṭhissamānaṃ*, *paccassamāno odanaṃ* (rice being cooked).
The *ṇv*-class suffixes:
Suffixes beginning with *ṇv* follow verbal roots meaning "action" to form nouns belonging to various classes (*bahukula*). Examples: *cāru*, *dāru*.
A single vowel at the beginning of a verbal root ending in the suffixes *kha*, *cha*, or *sa* becomes double; for example: *titikkhā*, *jigucchā*, *vīmaṃsā*.
And also in the case of the *parokkhā* (aorist) tense.

In the parokkhā (aorist) tense, a monosyllabic verbal root first becomes double. [The rule applies] even elsewhere according to the tradition, as indicated by the particle *ca*, which has the sense of an unexpressed inclusion (*avuttasamuccaya*).

Thus: *jahāti* (he abandons), *jahitabbaṃ* (should be abandoned), *jahituṃ* (to abandon); *daddallati* (shines); *vaṅkamati* (wanders). [Examples of roots beginning with vowels: *lolupo* (greedy), *momuho* (deluded)—these are included by the rule "tadaminādi" (Pāṇini 6.1.75). From a vowel at the beginning [of a reduplicated syllable].
When a vowel (*sara*) is preceded by another vowel, it becomes a single long vowel (*ekassara*). What are the examples starting with *asisissati*?
*Jajāgāra*. Why "vowel" (*sara*)? *Papāca*. Not again—when a consonant (*gaṃ*) has become double, it does not undergo doubling again: *titikkhasati*, *jigucchisati*.
*Yathiṭṭhaṃ syādino-*:

For a word ending in *syādi*, the first syllable—whether it consists of one vowel or more—is reduplicated as it stands, according to the traditional grammatical authority (*yathāgama*). Examples: *puputtiyisati*, *putittīyisatī*, *puttīyiyisati*. *Rasso pubbassa-*:
[The first syllable] becomes short.
In the case of *citte pubbasalāro*, it becomes short; [the rule] is:
"There is elision of the initial consonant.
In the case of doubling (*dvitte*), there is elision of any consonant other than the first of the preceding [vowel]; [as in] *asisisati*.

*Khachasesvassi*: In the presence of *kha*, *cha*, and the remaining [consonants], the substitute *i* occurs for the preceding *assa* (the genitive singular ending); e.g., *pipāsati*. Why say "in the presence of *kha*, *cha*, and the remaining"? [Observe: *jahāti*. Why say "*assa*"? [Observe: *bubhukkhati*. *Gupissussa*: [The suffix] *issa* follows *gup*.
In a double consonant cluster (*dvitte*), the *u* of the preceding *guṇa* vowel becomes *i* before *kh* and *ch*-ending suffixes: *jigucchati*.
In a double consonant cluster, the fourth and second vowels of the preceding syllable become the third and first vowels respectively: *bubhukkhati*, *ciccheda*.
When there is a doubling of letters, gutturals (*kavagga*) are replaced by palatals (*cavagga*) according to their respective order; as in *cukopa* and *jahāti*.
[The suffix] *-māna* is applied after a vowel and after the word *para*.
In the case of *dvitta* (doubling), for the preceding [vowel] that is being dropped (*cattamāna*), there is *vī*; and for the following [vowel], *maṃ*.

Or, in the sense of "he investigates" (*vīmaṃsati*)—that is, "he is doubtful" (*kitassāsaṃsayeti*)—in place of the preceding [vowel] that is being dropped due to doubt (*saṃsayato’ññasmiṃ cattamānassa*), there is *kitassava*. Examples: *tikicchati*, *cikicchati*. Why "without doubt" (*asaṃsayeti*)? [Because] *vicikicchati* [is not used here].
*Yuvaṇṇānam ño paccaye*:
For verbal roots ending in *i*-vowels or *u*-vowels, the suffix *ñ* is substituted for them respectively when a suffix follows; e.g., *cetabbaṃ*, *netabbaṃ*, *sotabbaṃ*, *bhavitabbaṃ*.
[The suffix] *lahu* is added to the present participle (*upantassa*).

The letters *ya*, *va*, *ṇa*, and *ña* respectively replace the vowel *a* of a light (*lahu*) penultimate syllable; [this] is to be sought, [this] is to be pierced—[in these cases] "light" (*lahussa*) is used.
Why "penultimate" (*upantassa*)?
[As in: *rundhati*. When a suffix (*paccaya*) having *ṇ* as its marker follows, the vowel *a* of a penultimate syllable becomes *ā*; [as in: *kārako*.
They have no connection with or arrival at anything whatsoever;
they are neither known, heard, seen, nor touched—there is no arrival by means of wood and so forth. That which is to be piled up is for the purpose of piling up;
that which is to be heard is for the purpose of hearing; that which is to be reached is for the purpose of reaching; that which is to be shaken off...

To shake off, shaking off, that which is to be shaken off, that which is to be caused to be shaken off, having shaken off, having caused to be shaken off, the act of shaking off, the act of causing to be shaken off, he shakes off, he causes to be shaken off; that which is to be made fat, to make fat, the act of making fat, to become fat, he makes fat;
he hears, he binds, he distresses, he impels; that which is to be sent, to send, the act of sending.
Or, in some cases, these [substitutes] do not occur before suffixes with the *kān* augment or before the *āgama* suffixes; as in *mudito*, *modito*; *ruditaṃ*, *roditaṃ*.
Also elsewhere.
Due to the arrival of the *kā* suffix, those [suffixes] do not occur elsewhere in some instances: *khipako*, *panudanaṃ*, *vadhako*.
In *pye sissā*:
the substitution of *pya* for *sissa*; thus, *nissāya*.
Ñonamayava before a vowel (sara).
When followed by a vowel, ño, na, ma, ya, and va become [nasalized]. What is meant by "before a vowel"? As in *jeti* and *anubhoti*.
[The rule] *āyāvā ṇānubandhe* [applies].

The suffix *yuka* occurs after a verbal root ending in a long vowel (*ā*) when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṇa* or *ā*, provided that *ṇa* is not an *anubandha*. It causes the [root] to be caused to go (*nayati*) or to be cultivated (*bhāvayati*). Regarding "having made sit" (*sayāpetvā*), etc., this refers to the state of being a sentient being (*sattattha*).

In the case of roots ending in long *ā*, the suffix *yuka* is added when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṇa* or *ā*, other than one where *ṇa* is an *anubandha*; for example, *dāyaka*. Why specify "other than one where *ṇa* is an *anubandha"*? Because in the case of *dānaṃ*, *ṇa* is indeed an *anubandha*. What is the purpose of saying "when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṇa* or *ā*" (*aṇāpimhi*)? Consider *dāpayati*. (In this case, the suffix begins with *pa*, not *ṇa* or *ā*, so *yuka* does not apply.)

The *yuk* suffix occurs in certain instances after roots beginning with *pad*. Examples: *nipajjitabbaṃ*, *nipajjituṃ*, *nipajjanaṃ*; *pamajjitabbaṃ*, *pamajjituṃ*, *pamajjanaṃ*. Why "in certain instances"? [Answer: *pādo*.
Also, the *maṃ* suffix occurs after roots beginning with *rudh*.
In some instances, *ma* optionally replaces [the suffix] after roots beginning with *rudh*. For example: *rundhitum* or *rujjhitum*—only in certain cases? [The result is] *nirodho*.
In the case of the suffix *kva*, there is elision of the final consonant.
There is elision of the final consonant before the suffix *kva*; for example: "They eat or take their meal here" (*ettha*) becomes *bhattaggaṃ*.
Regarding the rule *pararūpamayakāre byañjane*:

the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs for the final consonant of a verbal root when followed by a consonant other than the letter *y*. [This] must be understood. Why is it said "when followed by a consonant"? [Consider: *bhinditabbaṃ* (it is to be split). Why is it said "after the letter *a*"? [Consider: *bhijjati* (it is broken).
Regarding the rule *manānaṃ niggahītaṃ*: [the nasal substitute occurs] for the letters *m* and *n*.

The *niggahīta* (anusvāra) is substituted for the final consonants *m* and *k* when followed by the consonant *y*, provided they function as the object of an action (*kriyattha*); e.g., *gantabbaṃ* (to be gone), *jaṅghā* (shank). [Is it only when followed by a consonant? *Gamanaṃ* (going). [Is it only when *y* follows? *Gamyate* (it is gone). [The rule] "not for *brū*" applies:
the *o* of *brū* does not become *u* when followed by a consonant; e.g., *brūmi* (I say). [Is it only when followed by a consonant? *Abravi* (he spoke).
*Kagā* [are substituted] for *ca* and *ja* when followed by a nasal (*ṇa*).
When followed by a nasal, *ka* and *ga* are substituted respectively for *ca* and *ja* that denote an action; as in *vākyaṃ* and *bhāgyaṃ*.
For the root *han*, *gha* is substituted when followed by a suffix with the marker *ṇ*.
In the case of *hanassa*, there is the substitution of *gha* for *ha* when followed by *anubandhe*; thus, *āghāto*.
In the case of *kvimhi*, there is the substitution of *gha* for *ha* after *pari*, *paca*, and *samoha-*.

After *paṭi* and others, there is the substitution of *gha* for *ha* of *parassaha*; thus, *paligho*, *paṭigho*, and *aghaṃ* (where the shortening occurs by way of a grammatical rule); *saṅgho*, *ogho*.
*Ghaṃ* replaces *han* of another [word] before *se*; *jighaṃsā*.
*Giṃ* replaces *hi* and *harānaṃ*.
In a reduplicated form, the *j* of the root *ji* becomes *g* when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant other than a double consonant;
thus, *vijigīsā* and *jigīsā*.
In a reduplicated form, the *dh* of the root *dhā* becomes *h*; thus, *dahati*.
In the case of the suffix *ṇi*, there is lengthening of the vowel of *dus*. The vowel of *dus* becomes long before the suffix *ṇi*; as in *dūsita*. Why "before *ṇi*"? [Answer: As in *duṭṭha*.
[The rule] applies to the vowels of *guh*.
The vowel following *gu* becomes long when followed by a vowel; what is the example for “when followed by a vowel”?

*Guyhaṃ*. And for words ending in *mu* or *ba*, there is lengthening of the vowel before a suffix beginning with *t* that does not have *k* or *n* as its indicatory letter (*it*); examples: *mūḷho*, *bāḷehā*.

Regarding the rule *guḷho*: what is the purpose of the phrase *neti*? [To show: *muyahati*. What is the purpose of the phrase *kānubandhe*? [To show: *mu-hitabbaṃ*. What is the purpose of the phrase *atve*?

[To show: *muyhitvāna*, *muyhitvā*. The governing rule (*adhikāra*) "after a consonant" (*kānubandhe*) extends as far as the word "*sāsassasisve*". Regarding the rule *vahassussa-*: [the following applies].
The vowel *u* becomes long before the suffix *kā*, provided that *tvā* and *ana* are excluded;
[the suffix] is *cūḷha*. For the root *dhā*, [there is *hi*]: *dhā* becomes *hi* before the suffix *kā*, provided that *tvā* and *ana* are excluded; [examples are] *nihito* and *nihitavā*.
There is elision of the final [consonant] of *ham* and so forth.
There is elision of the final [consonant] of those words beginning with *ham* that end in *r*, when followed by an *ā*-suffixed suffix, provided it is not *tvā* or *an*. Examples:
*gato*, *khato*, *hato*, *mato*, *tato*, *saññato*, *rato*, *kato*. Is it only before *te*? No: *gamyate*. Is it only before an *ā*-suffixed suffix? No: *gantabbaṃ*.
Only when *atva* and *etva* [apply]? After [the roots] *gam* etc., it becomes so.

For [the roots] *vac* etc., *vassa* or *uṭa* occurs before a suffix having *kā* as its consonantal ligature (*kānubandha*) when *atva* and *etva* apply: *uttā*, *vuttaṃ*; *utthaṃ*, *vutthaṃ*. Only when *atva* and *etva* [apply]? After [the roots] *vad* etc., [it becomes so]: *vatvāna*, *vatvā*.
In the case of *assu* and so forth, when followed by a consonant suffix, *u* occurs [in place of *a*]; thus we have *vuttaṃ* and *vutthaṃ*.
Or, in the case of *vaddha*, it is optional.

In the case of *vaddha*, when followed by the suffix *kā* with the phonetic marker *u*, there is the substitution of *ū*. Thus, *vuddho* and *vaddho*—is it only in the cases of *atva* and *etva*? [No,] as in *vaddhitvāna* and *vaddhitvā*. How is this stated? It is stated: "The substitution occurs in the sense of 'becoming' (*vutti*). This is due to a grammatical convention (*nipātana*); thus, it indeed becomes *vatti* according to the formal rule.

In the case of *yaj*, when followed by the suffix *kā* with the phonetic markers *ṭi* and *ī*, there is the substitution of *i*. Thus, *iṭṭhaṃ* and *siṭṭhaṃ*—is it only in the cases of *atva* and *etva*? [No,] as in *yajitvāna* and *yajitvā*.
*Ṭhāssi-*:
[The suffix] *i* occurs after the root *ṭhā* when followed by a *kānubandha* (a suffix marked with *k*) or the particle *atva*; thus, *ṭhito*. Only when followed by *atva*? *Ṭhatvāna*, *ṭhatvā*.

*Gāpānam i* occurs after *gā* and *pā* when followed by a *kānubandha* or *atva*; thus, *gītaṃ*, *pītaṃ*. Only when followed by *atva*? *Gāyitvā*. [In these cases,] the augment *y* is always applied; however, for *pā*, it becomes *pī* due to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikārā*).
*Janissa-*:

*Janissa* becomes *ā* when followed by *ā*, *tu*, or *tve*; [e.g.,] *jāto*. Is it only when followed by *ā*, *tu*, or *tve*? [No, for example: *janitvā*. *Sāsassasisvā-*: [The suffixes] *-sā*, *-ssā*, *-ssi*, and *-svā* [are added].

In the case of *sāsassa*, [the suffix] *si* is added when followed by *tu*; thus, *satthaṃ* (taught) and *sisso* (a pupil), [and] *sāsiyo* (one who instructs). Is it only when followed by *tu*? No; as in *anusāsitvāna* (having instructed).
In the case of *karassa*, *ā* occurs before *tave*; thus, *kātave* (to do).
In the case of *tum*, *tun*, *tata*, *bbe*, and *su*:
after these, the suffix *ssā* occurs [for the infinitive]. [Examples: *kātuṃ*, *kattuṃ*, *kātuna*, *kattuna*; *kātabbaṃ*, *kattabbaṃ*.
When *ñ* follows, *ne* replaces *jā*.
The augment *jā* occurs after the root *ñā* before the suffix *nakāra*: *jānituṃ*, *jānatto*. Why "after *ñā*"? [Example: *ñāto*.

The augments *kuk* and *ūṇe* occur after the roots *sak* and *āp* before the suffix *ṇa*. [Examples: *sakkūṇanto*, *pāpuṇanto*; *sakkūṇoti*, *pāpuṇoti*. Why "before *ṇa*"? [Counter-examples: *sakkoti*, *pāpeti*.
And his joy is led away.
From this, for another, there is sorrow; this is certain.
This is the gift of old age. Or—
The suffix *īma* optionally follows the root *jaras* (to grow old). [Examples: *jīraṇā*, *jīrati*, *jīrāpeti*; *nisīditabbaṃ*, *nisīdanaṃ*, *nisīdituṃ*, *nisīdati*.

Why [is it optional]? [Counter-examples: *jarā*, *nisajjā*. Does it also apply to other roots because of the rule "optionally" (*veti*) being separated from the preceding rule? [Yes. For example, in *abhiratha*, there is the elision of the initial consonant of the suffix *attha*.
*Disa*, *passa*, *dassana*, *dakkha*.
There is an analysis of the forms *disa*, *passa*, and so forth: *vipassanā*, *vipassituṃ*, *vipassati*;
*sudassī*, *piyadassī*, *dhammadassī*, *sudassaṃ*, *dassanaṃ*, *dasseti*; *daṭṭhabbaṃ*, *daṭṭhā*, *daṭṭhuṃ*, *duddaso*, *addasa*.
*addā*, *addaṃ*; *addakkhi*, *dakkhissati*—is it not so? "Fools are seen" (*dissanti bālā*).
Regarding the rule *samānā ro rīrikkhakesu*:
after the word *samāna*, the letter *ra* optionally becomes *rī* before words beginning with *ri* or *rikkha*. Thus: *sarī*, *sadī*; *sarikkho*, *sadikkho*; *sariso*, *sadiso*.
In place of the *da* of the root *dah*, a *ḍa* optionally occurs; thus, *ḍāha* and *ḍāho*, *dāho*; [the forms] *ḍahati* and *dahati*.
After the words *an*, *agha*, *na*, *sva*, and *apari*, an *ḷa* [optionally occurs].
*Āparīhi parassa da-hassa da-ssa ḷo hoti na-ghaṇ-su*: after *āpa*, *rī*, and *hi*, the *da* of another [word] becomes *ḷ* before the suffixes *na*, *gha*, and *ṇu*;
for example, *pariḷāho*. *Atyādi-ne-sv-atthissa bhu-*:
when the suffixes beginning with *ati* and excluding *ne* follow, *bhu* replaces *assa* of the word *atthi*; for example, *bhavitabbaṃ*.

The rule for substitution (*ādesavidhāna*) in this context is for the purpose of excluding the usage of *as* (the root *as*); by this, it is indicated that in certain instances, even the non-usage of a particular verbal root [is intended]. [Question: What is the purpose of the phrase "in the case of *ati*, *ādi*, and *anta*"?

[Answer: [It is to show: *atthi*, *santo*. [Question: Why is the phrase "of *atthi*" used? [Answer: So that it does not apply to *assati*. Regarding the rule "*aāssaādisu*": when preceded by *a*, *ā*, or *ss*, the form *bhu* replaces the root *atthi*; thus: *babhuva*, *abhavā*, *abhavissā*, *bhavissati*.

*Ntamānāntiyiyuṃsvādilopo*: In the case of *nta*, *ādi*, *sva*, *atthi*, and so forth, there is elision of the initial [consonant]. This occurs in the forms *santo*, *samāno*, *santi*, *santu*, *siyā*, and *siyuṃ*. Why is this stated? [To exclude] *atthi*.
*Pādito ṭhāssa vā ṭhago kvaci*: In some instances, the substitution of *ṭha* for *tha* occurs after a word beginning with *pāda*.
Before words beginning with *pā-* that indicate a specific action, the letter *ṭha* may optionally become *tha*;

as in *saṇṭhahanto*, *santiṭṭhanto*, *saṇṭhahati*, and *santiṭṭhati*. [The prefixes are: *parā*, *apa*, *sam*, *anu*, *ava*, *o*, *ni*, *du*, *vi*, *adhi*, *api*, *ati*, *su*, *u*, *abhi*, *pati*, *pari*, *upa*, *ā*, *pādi*.
Why "optionally" (*kvaci*)? [Because] in *saṇṭhiti*, it does not change.
Regarding *dāssiyaṅi*:

in some instances, after the root *dā*, the suffix *iyaṅ* is applied in the sense of "giving" (*henāti*). [This occurs] without [the root] being specified [as having a specific vowel]; for example, *samādiyati*. Why is it only in some cases? As in *ādāya*.

After the root *kṛ*, in some instances, *kha* is substituted; thus, *saṅkhāro*, *saṅkharī yati*. By stating "after *kṛ*" instead of saying "after *karoti*," it is made known that the suffix *ti* arises as a verbal affix (*vikaraṇa*).
*Purasmā-*:

After the particle *pura*, the following [suffix] *ka* becomes *kha*; as in *purakkhatvā* (having placed before) and *purekkhāro* (precedence). These are included in the list beginning with *ettam*. *Tito kamassa-*: [The suffix] *ka* becomes *kha* after *ti*.
After *ni*, the substitute *kh* occurs in place of *ka* in another word in certain instances: *purakkhatvā* (having placed before), *purekkhāro* (precedence);
these are examples from the beginning of the recitation. After *ni*, the substitute *kh* occurs in place of *ka* in another word in certain instances: *nikkhamati*; in what instances only? *Nikkamo*.
*Yuvaṇṇānam iyaṅuvaṅi sare*:

For verbal roots ending in *ivaṇṇa* or *uvaṇṇa*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occur before a vowel in the *kvaci* (present tense) [and other tenses]; e.g., *vediyati*, *bruvanti*. Why "before a vowel"? [Counter-example: *nivedeti*, *brūti*. Is it only in some cases? [Yes: *jayati*, *bhavati*. *Aññādissāssī kye*: [The substitution occurs] for a root different from those [ending in *ivaṇṇa* or *uvaṇṇa*] before the suffix *sī* in the *kye* (imperative).
The vowel *ī* is substituted for another *ā*-ending verbal root when followed by the suffix *kye*; e.g., *diyati*. Why say "another"? [Because it does not apply to] *ñāyati* or *tāyati*.
For a root ending in *-tan*, the vowel *ā* is optionally substituted before *kye*; e.g., *tāyate* or *taññate*.
A long vowel occurs for a verbal root ending in *s* before the vocative particle *kye*: *cīyate*, *sūyate*.
The letter *ṭha* replaces the immediately following *t* after a verbal root ending in *s*: *kuṭṭho*, *tuṭṭhavā*, *tuṭṭhabbaṃ*, *tuṭṭhī*. Why "immediately following"? (Consider: *tussitvā*.
*Kasassa ima ca vā*:

for the word *kasa*, the substitute *ṭha* occurs after a following [word] that begins with a vowel, or else the suffix *ima*; as in *kiṭṭhaṃ* and *kaṭṭhaṃ*. Why is it said "only after a following [vowel]"? Because it must be cultivated (*kasitabbaṃ*). [The rules concerning] *dha*, *sto*, and *trasta* follow.
These words are derived [as follows].
From "puccha" and so forth:

after the roots beginning with *puccha* when used in the sense of an action (*kriyāttha*), the letter *t* of the following suffix is replaced by *ṭh*; thus, *puṭṭho*, *bhaṭṭho*, *yiṭṭho*. Is it only after the immediately preceding [root] that this occurs? Yes; for example, *pucchitvā*.
*Sāsavasasaṃsasasā tho-*:

After these [sounds], *tha* occurs in place of the immediately following *ta*. Examples: *satthaṃ*, *vutthaṃ*, *pasatthaṃ*, *satthaṃ*. How is *anusiṭṭho* formed? [It is by the rule] “*Kathanarānaṃ ṭaṭhaṇalā*,” thus *ṭha* is substituted. [Is this substitution] only for the immediately following [sound]? Yes: *sāsatuṃ*. *Dho dahabhehi-*: [The substitute *dha* occurs] after *da*, *ha*, and *bha*.
The letter *t* following a root ending in *dh*, *h*, or *bh* becomes *dh*. Examples: *vuddho*, *duddhaṃ*, *laddhaṃ*.
*Dahā ḍho*:
After *da*, the following *t* becomes *ḍh*. Example: *daṅḍho*.
And in *bahassuma*:
after the letter *b*, there is *h* for the immediately following *s*; and in *bahassuma*, by virtue of its own connection, [the *s* becomes *h*]. [The suffix] *buḍḍha*.
After *ruh* and the others, *ho* [occurs], and *ḷa* as well.

After *ruh* and other [roots], the following *t* becomes *h*, and *ḷ* replaces the final *t*; for example: *āruḷho*, *guḷho*, *vuḷho*, *bāḷho*. Is it only after an immediate [preceding vowel]? Yes, as in *ārogatuṃ*. Or, after *muh*:
*muhā*—after an immediate [preceding vowel], the following *t* optionally becomes *h*, and *ḷ* replaces the final *t* when joined with the root *has*; for example: *muḷho*, *muddho*.
*After roots beginning with *bhid*, the suffix *tasan* is substituted for the suffixes *kta*, *ktavantu*, and *tuṇ*.
After roots beginning with *bhid*, the suffix *tasan* occurs in place of the suffixes *kta*, *ktavantu*, and *tuṇ*: *bhinno*, *bhinnavā*; *chinno*, *chinnavā*;
*channo*, *channavā*; *khinno*, *khinnavā*; *uppanno*, *uppannavā*; *sinno*, *sinnavā*, *sannenā*, *sannavā*; *pīno*, *pīnavā*; *sūno*, *sūnavā*; *dīno*, *dīnavā*; *ḍīno*.
*ḍīna*, *līna*, *līnavā*, *lūna*, *lūnavā*—[these are examples of] the suffixes *kta*, *ktavantu*, and *na*. What [is the purpose]? *Bhitti*; *chitti*, *bhottuṃ*, *chettuṃ*.
**Dātthīnno**:
After the root *dā*, the suffixes *kta*, *ktavantu*, and *na* become *inna*; thus, *dinna*, *dinnavā*.

After *kiṛ* and other [roots], the suffix *ṇa* does not occur for the *kta* and *ktavantu* suffixes of others immediately following it; e.g., *kiṇṇo*, *kiṇṇavā*, *puṇṇo*, *puṇṇavā*, *khīṇo*, *khīṇavā*.
After *tṛ* and other [roots], *riṇṇo* [occurs].
After *tarā* and other such roots, the suffixes *-ta*, *-tavant*, and *-na* take the augment *tassa-ra*; for example: *tiṇṇo*, *tiṇṇavā*, *jiṇṇo*, *jiṇṇavā*, *ciṇṇo*, *ciṇṇavā*.

After *bhañj* and other such roots—the suffixes *-ta*, *-tavant*, and *-na* take the augment *tassā-nantara-sa*; for example: *bhaggo*, *bhaggavā*, *laggo*, *laggavā*, *nimuggo*, *nimuggavā*, *saṃviggo*, *saṃviggavā*.
*Susā* [is substituted] for *paresaṃ*, *ktā*, and *ktavantu*. For example: *tassa kho hoti*; *sukkheṃ*, *sukkha-vā*.
*Pacā* [is substituted] for *ko*.
After the root *pac*, the suffix *k* (of the past participle and gerund) becomes *ka*; thus: *pakko*, *pakkavā*. After the root *muc*, *k* optionally becomes *ka*;

thus: *mukko*, *mutto*; *mukkavā*, *muttavā*—this is established by the rule for *ṇv* and other suffixes. When the suffixes *kta* and *ktavantu* follow, the root *satt* remains as *satta* even when expressing the state of being (*bhāva*).
The elision of *vaḍḍha* in *ktissa*:
the *t* of *vaḍḍha*, which is a *parasmaipada* suffix ending in *k*, is elided; [thus] *vaḍḍhi*.
[Also] in *kvissa*.

When the sense is that of an action performed for another, there is the elision of *kvip*; thus, *abhibhū*. Regarding the rule "of *ṇi*, *ṇā*, and *pī*, there is elision before those [suffixes] beginning with *ṇi*, *ṇā*, and *pī*":

there is elision of *ṇi*, *ṇā*, and *pī* before those suffixes beginning with *ṇi*, *ṇā*, and *pī*; thus, from "he causes one who is making to act," we have *kārāpayati*, which becomes *kāreti* (he causes to do) or *kārāpeti* (he causes to cause to do).
In some instances, there is the elision of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*); for example: *udapādi*, *hanti*. In the case of the suffix *māna*, there is the substitution of *ma*.
In certain instances, there is the elision of the letter *m* following a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) that ends in *māna*. For example: *karāṇo*. Why "in certain instances"?

[Consider: *kurumāno*. [The rule] *eilasse-*: In certain instances, the suffix *elāna* occurs after a word ending in *e*. For example: *gahetvā*, *adenti*. Why "only in certain instances"? [Consider: *vapitvā*.
*Pyo vā tvāssa samāse*: In a compound, *tvā* becomes *pyo*;

[the letter] *p* also [occurs] before *s* and *sa*. These are for the purpose of distinction: *abhibhūya*, *abhibhavitvā*. Why "in a compound"? [Counter-example: *patvā*. Why "even in a non-compound"? Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *bahukula*: *lataṃ dantehi chindiya*. *Tuṃyānā-*...

The suffix *tvā* becomes *tuṃ* optionally in a compound (*samāsa*), in certain instances: *abhihaṭhuṃ*, *abhiharitvā*; *anumodiyāna*, *anumoditvā*. Even when not in a compound, it occurs by virtue of the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*). Examples: *daṭhuṃ*, *disvā*. This division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of making known that these [forms] do not fall within the scope of the following rule.
*Hanā racco*: After the root *han*, the suffix *tvā* optionally becomes *racca* in a compound. Examples: *ahacca*, *ahanitvā*.
The suffixes *sā*, *sādhi*, *kāra*, and *caccariccha*—

or rather, *sā*, *sādhi*, *kāra*, *parā*, *kāra*, *tvā*, and *assa*— follow [the preceding word] respectively, as in *sakkacca*, *sakkaritvā*, *asakkacca*, *asakkaritvā*, *adhikicca*, and *adhikaritvā*. From here on, the suffix *cca* [is treated].
From this [rule], for the word *tvā*, there is either *cco* or *ccu*; that is, after *adhicca*, *adhiyitvā*, *samecca*, or *sametvā*.
Or else, *disā* and *vānavā* [are substituted].
For *disa*, there are *tvā*, *ssa*, *vā*, or *nuvā*; and the letter *ta* of *disassa* is replaced by *sa* through connection with *santi*; the rule for *sa* is as follows.

For the purpose of subverting the form of another [suffix]: having seen (*disvāna*, *disvā*, *passitvā*)—how is it that they do not incur a fault later on? Because this is an indicator (*ñāpaka*), there is elision of the vowel;
thus in cases such as *laddhāna-dhanaṃ* and so forth.
[The suffix] *ei* replaces a consonant.

After a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) ending in *r*, the suffix *ñi* optionally occurs before another suffix beginning with *byañjana* (a consonant); e.g., *bhuñjituṃ*, *hottu*. Why "of a consonant" (*byañjanassa*)?
[Consider] *pācako*. *Rā nassa ṇo-*:
After a verbal root ending in *r*, the suffix *ṇa* is substituted for the suffix *na* that follows; e.g., *araṇaṃ*, *saraṇaṃ*.
Regarding *ntam*, *āna*, *ty* and so forth:
after a root ending in *r*, the *n* of subsequent suffixes such as *ntam*, *āna*, and *ty* does not become *ṇ*. For example: *karonto*, *kurumāno*; *karonti*.
Or, for roots such as *gam*, *yam*, *is*, and *as*, [the *n* becomes *ṇ*] before the suffix *chaṅ*.
Or, for these [roots], the suffix *chaṅ* occurs in the forms *nta*, *māna*, etc.; as in: *gacchanto*, *gacchamāno*, *gacchati*; *yacchanto*, *yacchamāno*, *yacchati*;
*icchanto*, *icchamāno*, *icchati*; *acchanto*, *acchamāno*, *acchati*; *dicchanto*, *dicchamāno*, *dicchati*.
Why is *vā* (optionally) mentioned? [To show: *gamissati*; and because the state of dwelling (*vihāsatta*) is fixed, it does not occur in others.
And where [is it applied]? It should be desired: *icchitabbaṃ*, *icchā*, *icchituṃ*; it should be satiated: *acchitabbaṃ*, *acchatuṃ*; and from other divisions of grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*):
*pavecchati*. Regarding the rule *jaramarānamīyaṅi*:

for these roots, the suffix *īyaṅ* optionally occurs before suffixes such as *nta*, *māna*, and so forth; thus: *jīyanto*, *jīranto*; *jīyamāno*, *jīramāno*; *jīyati*, *jīrati*; *mīyanto*, *maranto*; *mīyamāno*, *maramāno*; *mīyati*, *marati*.
*Ṭhāpānaṃ tiṭṭhapivā*:

for the roots *ṭhā* and *pā*, there are the substitutions *tiṭṭha* and *piva* respectively in the cases of the suffixes *-nta*, *-māna*, *-tya*, and so forth; thus, *tiṭṭhanto*, *tiṭṭhamāno*, *tiṭṭhati*; *pivanto*, *pivati*. Is it only in these cases? No; [it also occurs as] *ṭhāti*, *pāti*.
For the roots *gam*, *vad*, and *dā*, there are the substitutions *ghamma*, *vajja*, and *dajja* respectively.

For roots beginning with *gam*, *gham* and so forth occur before suffixes such as *nta*, *māna*, and *tya*; for example: *gacchanto* (going), *vajjanto* (speaking), *vadanto* (speaking), *dajjanto* (giving), *dadanto* (giving).
For the root *kar*, after the letter *s*, *kubba*, *kuru*, and *kayira* occur before suffixes such as *nta*, *māna*, and *tya*; for example: *kubbanto*, *kayiranto*, *karonto*.
*kubbamāno*, *kurumāno*, *kayiramāno*, *karāṇo*; *kubbati*, *kayirati*, *karoti*;

*kubbate*, *kurute*, *kayirate*—because the governing rule (*vādhikāra*) is stated as an option (*vibhāsattā*), the suffixes *māna*, *para*, and *cchakka* (the sixth case endings) follow *ku*, while *pubbacchakka* (the first case endings) occur only in certain instances?
"May your honor deign to value it for us" (*agghaṃ kurutu no bhavaṃ*); because it is said "he will hear" (*sossāti*), these [suffixes] occur only in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).
The substitution of *gha* for *ga*.

In the case of the root *gaṇhāti*, [the letter *g*] is replaced by *gh* in forms such as the present participle (*nta*), the middle voice (*māna*), and so forth: *gheppanto*, *gheppamāno*, *gheppati*. Is it only in these cases? No; it also occurs in *gaṇhāti*.
[Furthermore,] the rule "for the *ṇo* of a nasal" applies.
In the case of *gaha* (to take) and *niggaha* (to restrain), there is no [nasal stop]; [the forms are] *gaṇhitabbaṃ*, *gaṇhituṃ*, and *gaṇhanto*.
Thus ends the fifth section, on *khādi* and others, in the *Vutti* commentary on the *Moggallāna-vyākaraṇa*.
[Now follows: In the present tense (*vattamāna*), the suffixes are *ti*, *anti*, *sitha*, *mima*, *tña*, *se*, *vhñe*, *mhe*.
When the sense of an action already commenced is intended, the forms beginning with *ti* (the verb endings) occur from the present tense:
*gacchati*, *gacchanti*, *gacchasi*, *gacchatha*, *gacchāmi*, *gacchāma*; *gacchate*, *gacchante*, *gacchase*, *gacchavhe*, *gacche*, *gacchamhe*.
How so? As in: "How could unrighteousness shine forth? and "Before I die. These belong to the present tense alone.

Because [the word *vattamāna*] is intended to be expressed, it is grasped by means of grasping the presence [of the action] in proximity to it; or rather, by the words *pure* and *purā*, the future state is understood, since at that time it is present;

or else, this is a transposition of time (*kālavyatti*), for according to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffixes *tya* and so forth occur even in another time when [the sense of] "being" (*bhavanta*) is present.
"While these [pleasures] exist, I conceal them and give nothing from them; after the breaking up of the body, in the life hereafter..."
“He goes to the companionship of Vāsava; I shall wander through the saṃsāra of many births; they will pay homage excessively.
*Bhavissati*, *ssati*, *santī*, *ssasī*, *ssatha*, *ssāmi*, *ssāma*, *ssate*, *ssante*, *ssase*, *ssavhe*, *ssaṃ*, *ssāmhē*:

these suffixes beginning with *ssati* occur after verbal roots (*kriyattha*) when expressing a future meaning (*bhavissati*) regarding a matter not yet commenced (*anāraddhe atthe*). For example: *gamissati*, *gamissanti*.
You will go, you (plural) will go; I will go, we (plural) will go; he will go, they (plural) will go; you (singular) will go, you (plural) will go;
I (singular) will go, we (plural) will go—[these forms occur] when the root *gam* is followed by names, censure, or fear.
When the particle *nāma* occurs, it signifies censure or incredulity, and in these senses, *atthi* and other verbs are used:
"Indeed, they will claim to possess such virtuous qualities"; "For surely, monks, that foolish man will have no compassion for living beings";
"How indeed, monks, can that foolish man build a hut made entirely of clay?"
"In that case, O foolish man, you will surely cause [others] to dwell in passion when the Dhamma has been taught for the sake of dispassion!
Dear Sudinna, will you really eat this overnight sour gruel? There is indeed a removal of blame even here. Do you not trust me?
It is wonderful, truly marvelous, how those who have gone forth do not tire of a dwelling that is so peaceful!"
For it is truly remarkable that one who is conscious and awake should neither see nor hear five hundred carts passing by right next to him;
it is a marvel indeed that a blind man should climb a mountain and a deaf man should hear a sound!

In the past tense (*bhūte*), *ī*, *ottha*, *em*, *bhā*, *ū*, *se*, *vhaṃ*, *a*, *mbhe* [are the suffixes]. When the meaning of the past tense has been completed, the suffixes beginning with *ī* occur after verbal roots (*kriyātthā*) that are currently being used; for example:
*agamī*, *agamuṃ*, *agamo*, *agamittha*, *agamim*, *agamimhā*; *agamā*, *agamū*, *agamise*, *agamivhaṃ*, *agama*, *agamimhe*. — Past.
Is there also [the use of] the common verbal suffixes when the sense is not of today (*anajjatana*)?

*Suvo ahosi Ānando*. In the sense of "not of today" (*anajjatane*), the suffixes *ā*, *u*, *attha*, *amhā*, *atthuṃ*, *se*, *vhaṃ*, *iṃ*, *m*, *bha*, and *se* occur after verbal roots (*kriyatthā*) when they express an action that has occurred in the past (*bhute’atthe*) but is not of the present day.
The time for rising is appropriate, and the time for reclining is appropriate;
this is one's own time, whether it be the day or both halves of the night.

[Examples of the verb *gam* (to go): agamā, agamu, agamo, agamattha, agama, agamamhā; agamittha, agamatthuṃ, agamase, agamavhaṃ, gamiṃ, agamamhase. [Question: What is the meaning of another word (*aññapadattha*)? [Answer: He went either today or yesterday.

In the absence of the agent (*parokkhe*), when the action has occurred in the past but is not witnessed by the speaker (*apaccakkhe*), and refers to the present day (*bhūtājjatane*), the roots *as* and others (*cattamānato*) take the suffixes *ittha*, *amha*, *re*, *ttha*, *uho*, and *imhe*. Thus:
*jagāma*, *jagamu*, *jagame*, *jagamittha*, *jagama*, *jagamimha*; *jagamittha*, *jagamire*, *jagamittho*, *jagamivho*, *jagamimhe*.

*jagami*, *jagamimhe*. — Even when an action performed by one whose mind is deluded, distracted, or deranged is not perceived at the time of its production, it is inferred through this [verb] and is thus considered "remote" (*parokkhā*) with respect to its objective basis (*vatthu*); therefore, the occurrence of the verbal suffixes is possible even in the past tense.
Or rather, for the sake of avoiding errors, here [are the forms]: *eyya*, etc.; *ssā*, *ssaṃ*, *ssu*, *ssatha*, *ssam*, *ssahā*, *ssatha*, *ssiṃ*, *ssu*, *ssassu*, *ssavha*, *ssiṃ*, *ssāma*, *ase*.
In the case of the past conditional (*eyyādo*), the suffixes *ssā* and so forth occur optionally (*vibhāsā*) when there is a non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*).
Non-occurrence of the action is the failure of the action to take place due to the onset of adverse conditions or a deficiency in its causes.
Furthermore, these suffixes *ssā* and so forth apply only to the past and future, not to the present, because the non-occurrence of the action is impossible in the present.

The cart will not be able to turn around. Why does he say "if"? If it goes by the right [side], the cart will not be able to turn around.
Regarding *eyya*, *eyyuṃ*, *eyyāsi*, *eyyātha*, *eyyāmi*, *eyyāma*, *etha*, *eraṃ*, *etho*, *eyyavho*, *eyyaṃ*, and *eyyāmhe*:
these verbal forms beginning with *eyyā* optionally occur when expressing an action that is either a cause (*hetu*) or a result (*phala*), provided that the action is occurring in the present tense.
If formations were permanent, they would not cease; if they were to go to the right, the cart would not turn over—if they were to go to the right, [one might say:
"you would go," "you two would go," "I would go," "we would go"; "you (plural) would go," "I (plural) would go," "you two would go," "you (plural) would go," "I would go," "we would go."
The cart will not be able to pass through; the going to the house is the cause, and the inability to pass through is the result—why is this not the case here?
[Is it that] "it strikes" means it flees, "it rains" means it runs, and "it will strike" means it will flee?
No, because the relationship between cause and effect is already manifested by the word "iti" itself. Or rather: "If he goes by the right-hand path, the cart will not be able to pass through."
The method for the section on questions (*pañhapaṭṭhānavidhi*):
A question (*pañha*) is an inquiry, a holding together, an investigation, and a determination of what is to be done. An aspiration (*paṭṭhanā*) is a reaching out, a longing, and a desire.
A rule (*vidhāna*) is a method (*vidhi*), an injunction, and the directing toward activities. And that [method] is of two kinds: by way of respect and lack of respect.
Even though they are distinguished by their difference in objective domain, they do not transcend those two [categories].

Among these, such as questions and so forth, the optative suffixes (*eyya*) and others function as the meaning of the action (*kriyārtha*). In a question: "Would the Venerable One master the Vinaya, or rather the Dhamma? In an expression of possibility:
"Should I go to the Uposatha, or should I not go? In an expression of aspiration: "May I obtain a robe from you, sir."
"May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive full ordination; may I see him for a hundred years free from illness.
"In this case? "May you cook the rice-porridge; may you perform a meritorious deed; may you eat here; may you sit here;
may you teach the young brahmin"—in these cases too, [the wish] is fulfilled at the time it is granted; and there too...

From the perspective of the formal procedure (*vidhi*): [Is it] permitted? "You should do it thus. At the appropriate time? "You should perform the task; the time for you to perform the task has arrived.
"If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha;

this is the time for the Blessed One, this is the time for the Sugata, that the Blessed One should lay down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) for his disciples"—[they say] even regarding such an instruction. Do they desire it? Yes.
"O messenger, you should go to the village for the sake of your own welfare and for our benefit.
In interrogative sentences such as these, [the suffixes] occur after verbal roots (*kriyārtha*): *yacchatu*, *gacchantu*, *gacchāhi*, *gacchatha*.
*gacchāmi*, *gacchāma*, *gacchataṃ*, *gacchantaṃ*, *gacchassu*, *gacchavho*, *gacche*, *gacchāmase*—in questions? *Kinnu balu ho vyākaraṇamadhiyassu?* ("Will you study grammar?

In expressions of aspiration? *Dadāhi me, jivatu bhavaṃ.* ("Give to me; may your honor live! In commands? *Kaṭaṃ karotu bhavaṃ, puññaṃ karotu bhavaṃ, iha bhavaṃ bhuñjatu, iha bhavaṃ nisīdatu, uddisatu.* ("May your honor make a mat;
may your honor perform merit; may your honor eat here; may your honor sit here; may your honor recite.")
"Venerable Sir, the Blessed One [is authorized] by way of the Pātimokkha. By way of sending? 'Go, my man, to the village. By way of consent? 'Do it thus. By way of the proper time?
'This is the time for you, O Great Hero, to arise from the mother's womb.
[And so on with] weapons, arrows, and the like."

The suffixes *eyya* and others occur after verbal roots (*kriyattha*) when expressing capability (*satti*) and worthiness (*arahatta*); for example: "May your majesty indeed rule the kingdom" (*bhavaṃ khalu rajjaṃ kareyya*), and "Your majesty is capable" (*bhavaṃ satto*).

Or, when expressing probability (*sambhāvana*), provided that the root is explicitly stated, the suffixes *eyya* and others occur optionally (*vibhāsā*); for example: "He might even [climb] the mountain with his head."
One might destroy it. Regarding the past conditional (*kriyātipatti*) with *ussa*: even if struck by a thunderbolt, I do not believe, I do not trust, I do not accept that you would eat;

you will eat, sir; you have eaten, sir. Regarding the past conditional with *nāussa*: I believe that you would not eat, sir. In the case of the particle *mā*, [the suffixes] *ī*, *ā*, etc., [are used].

When *mā* is joined [with a verb], *ī*-class and *ā*-class [verbal roots] optionally take the suffixes; for example: *māssupunapi evarūpamakāsi* (do not do such a thing again), *mā bhavaṃ agamā vanaṃ* (may you not go to the forest). What is the meaning of *vā* (optionally)? It is:

*mā te kāmaguṇe bhamassu cittaṃ* (let not your mind wander among the strands of sensual pleasure), *mā tvaṃ karissasi* (you shall not do), *mā tvaṃ kareyyāsi* (you might not do)—this undertaking has the sense of a non-past time (*asakkakāla*).
By connection with another word, such as *buddho abhavissati* (the Buddha will be), future tense is understood; likewise: *kato kaṭo* (the mat was made).
"‘Sve bhavissati,’ ‘bhāvi kaccam āsi’—‘lunāhi, lunāhi’ indeed does this one cut; ‘lunassu, lunassu’ indeed does this one cut.
This is the frequent expression (*ābhikkhañña*) of the second person singular of the imperative (*tvādīnaṃ majjhimapurisa-ekavacanānaṃ*); this is what is meant:
‘In this way, being hurried, he performs the action as if enjoining others. Likewise, ‘lunātha, lunātha’ indeed does this one [cut].”
He reaps; he reaps, indeed, reaps, reaps—thus he reaps. Likewise, even in other times: "reap," "reap," "indeed he reaps"; "he has reaped," "he has reaped," "he reaped," "he will reap.

In this same way, it should be applied to the optative suffix (*sum*): likewise in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), "he wanders from monastery to monastery," "he wanders from monastery to monastery, indeed, he wanders";
"he shall wander from monastery to monastery," "he shall wander from monastery to monastery, indeed, he wanders"—but in the case of a difference in activity (*byāpāra-bheda*)...
Is there non-application [of the suffix] because the general term itself is all-encompassing? "Eat the rice, drink the gruel, or having chewed the parched grains, he swallows this.

Regarding the six preceding and following [cases], whether they be singular or plural, when the forms *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* remain, two [suffixes] each—namely the middle, the highest, and the first—are applied.

Among those agents denoted by the words *eka*, *aneka*, *tumha*, and *amha*, as well as those denoted by other words, there are two forms each for the first person and the second person from among the preceding and following sets of six, respectively, when they function as the object of the action (*kriyattha*).
This word *uttama* (first person) is conventionally established (*ruḷha*) by its own nature within the third-person pair: *tvaṃ gacchasi*, *tumhe gacchatha*, *tvaṃ gacchase*, *tumhe*...
*gacchavhe*; *tvaṃ gacchasi*, *tumhe gacchatha*, *tvaṃ gacchase*, *tumhe gacchavhe*; *ahaṃ gacchāmi*, *mayaṃ gacchāma*, *ahaṃ gacche*, *mayaṃ gacchāmhe*;

*so gacchati*, *te gacchanti*, *so gacchate*, *te gacchante*. By virtue of their capacity, the endings for the second person plural (*tumhāmhasesesu*) occur even when they are not being directly addressed—*gacchasi*, *gacchatha*.
*gacchase*, *gacchavhe*; *gacchāmi*, *gacchāma*, *gacche*, *gacchāmhe*; *gacchati*, *gacchanti*, *gacchate*, *gacchante*. *Āīssādisvaña vā-*:

After a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) beginning with *ā*, *ī*, or *ssā*, the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs; the letter *ñ* is an *anubandha*. Examples: *agamā*, *gamā*; *agamī*, *gamī*; *agamissā*, *gamissā*.
*Ādisvāho brūssa-*: After *brū*, *āho* is substituted for it when followed by vowels (*aādi*) and so forth; thus, *āha* (he said) and *āhu* (they said). *Bhussa cuka-*:

After *bhū*, *cuka* is substituted for it when followed by vowels and so forth; the letter *k* is a phonetic marker (*anubandha*), and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation; thus, *babhūva* (he became).
In the case of reduplication of *a* and other vowels, the preceding vowel becomes *bu* or *ssu*; thus, *babhūva*. [The suffixes] *ussa*, *ṃ*, *svāhā*, and *vā* [are also used].
*Āhā* becomes *parassa* (the third person) and *ussaaṃ* (the first person);
[thus] *āhaṃsu* and *āhu*. *Tyantīnaṃ ṭaṭū*:

after *āhā*, the third-person endings (*ti-antīnaṃ*) become *ṭa* and *ṭū*; the letter *ṭ* serves the purpose of indicating all substitutions; thus, *āha* and *āhu*. And from this very indicative mark, *brū* becomes *sāha* in the third-person endings (*ti-antisu*).

*Īādovacassoma-*: After [a word ending in] *ī*, *ā*, etc., there is *oma* for *avaca*; the letter *m* is an *anubandha*. Example: *avoca*. Why "after *ī*, *ā*, etc."? [Counter-example: *avaca*. *Dāssa daṃ vā mamesvadvitte-*:
For the *d* of *da*, there is optionally *daṃ* when followed by *ma*, *me*, *sva*, *itthi*, or *tte*.

For the root *dā* when occurring with a prefix (*añcitte*), the substitution of *da* for *da* occurs optionally before the suffixes *mi*, *me*, *mha*, and *ma*: *dammi*, *demi*; *damma*, *dema*. Why "with a prefix"?
[Because in the absence of a prefix:
*dadāmi*, *dadāma*. For the root *kṛ*, the substitution of *kuṃ* for the vowel *o* occurs optionally before the suffixes *mi*, *me*, *mha*, and *ma*: *kummi*, *kumma*; *karomi*, *karoma*.

In the case of *kā* and so forth: for the root *kar*, the letter *a* optionally becomes *ī* when followed by vowels beginning with *ī*. [Examples: *akāsi*, *akari*; *akaṃsu*, *akariṃsu*; *akā*, *akarā*. [This applies] when followed by *hāssa*, *cāhaṃ*, or *ssi*.
The suffix *chaṅ* optionally occurs after the roots *kar*, *ass*, *sos*, *hās*, and *āhaṅ*, together with the suffix *ssa*. [Examples: *kāhati*, *karissati*;
*akāhā*, *akarissā*; *hāhati*, *hāyissati*; *āhāhā*, *ahāyissā*.
The suffix *chaṅ* optionally occurs after the roots *labh*, *vas*, *chid*, *bhid*, and *rud*, together with the suffix *ssa*. [Examples: *alacchā*, *alabhissā*, *lacchati*, *labhissati*; *avacchā*.
*avasissā*; *vacchati*, *vasissati*; *cchecchā*, *acchindissā*; *checchati*. *Chindissati*; *heccā*, *bhindissā*; *bhecchati*, *bhindissati*;
*arucchā*, *arodissā*; *rucchati*, *rodissati*. Also in other cases, for the root *chid*, [the suffix] *chaṅ* occurs due to the analysis of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*):
*acchecchuṃ*, *acchindiṃsu*. Or from others: *gacchaṃ*, *gacchissaṃ*.
For the roots *bhuj* (to eat), *muc* (to release), *vac* (to speak), and *kkhaṇ* (to cut), the suffix *ssena* optionally becomes *kkhaṅi*; [examples are: *abhokkhā*, *abhuñjissā*;
*bhokkhati*, *bhuñjissati*; *amokkhā*, *amuñcissā*; *mokkhati*, *muñcissati*; *acakkhā*, *avacissā*; *cakkhati*, *vacissati*.

*pāvekkhā*, *pāvisissā*; *pavekkhati*, *pavisissati*. [The suffix] *kkha* may also occur after *vi* in other instances due to the analysis of grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*): *pāvekkhi*, *pāvisi*. Regarding the substitution of *ha* for *sa* after *ā* and so forth:
"After *ā* and *ī*, there is optionally the substitution of *ha* for *sa*"; thus: *ahā*, *aharā*; *abhāsi*, *abhari*.
The substitution of *gamissa-* [for *gaccha*] occurs optionally before vowels beginning with *ā*. Thus: *agā*, *agamā*; *agā*, *agami*.

And for *saṃsa-* as well as *gamissa-*, the substitution occurs optionally before the suffix *chaṅ* when vowels beginning with *ā* follow. Thus: *aḍañchā*, *aḍaṃsā*; *aḍañchi*, *aḍaṃsi*; *agañchā*, *agacchā*; *agañchi*, *agacchi*.
*Hūssahehehihohī* [are used] after *ssacca*.
The forms *hū*, *ssa*, *ha*, *ñā*, and so forth, occur after *ssacca*; thus: *hessati*, *hehissati*, *hohissati*. In the case of various suffixes (*ṇānāsu*), there is shortening.
In the *kaṇa* (present) tense, a long vowel becomes short: *kiṇāti*, *dhunāti*.
For the endings *-āī-ūmhāssāssamhānaṃ*, there is optionally a short vowel: *gama*, *gamā*; *gami*, *gamī*; *gamu*; *gamimha*, *gamimhā*; *gamissa*, *gamissā*; *gamissamha*, *gamissamhā*.
*Kusaruhehiṃsa chi-*:
*Kusā* (grass), *ruhā* (grown), and *parassa* (of another) become *īssa*; *chi* becomes *vā*. [Examples: *akkocchi*, *akkosi*; *abhirucchi*, *abhiruhi*.
[In the case of] *aīssa* and so forth, the consonant *s* becomes *ñ*.
In the case of other roots beginning with *kṛ*, such as *ī* and others, the suffix *ssa* optionally replaces the consonant of the root. Examples:

*babhuvittha*, *abhavittha*, *abhavissā*, *anubhavissā*, *anubhavissati*, *anubhossati*, (*harissati*), *hassati*. [Question: Why "of these" (*etesam*)? [Answer: Because it applies to these specific roots. [Question: Why "of the consonant" (*byañjanassa*)? [Answer:
Because otherwise it would apply to the vowel as well, as in *babhuva*.
*Brūto tissiṇa-*:
After the root *brū*, the suffixes *tissa* and *īna* may occur; [thus] *bravīti* or *brūti*. *Kyassa-*: [The suffix *ssa* occurs after the root *kī*].
In the case of another person (parassapada), the suffix *ī* occurs after a verb root ending in a consonant (*kriyattha*).
Examples: *pacīyati*, *paccati*. Regarding the substitutes for *eyyātha*, *a*, *ñā*, *ītha*, and *a*:
*o*, *a*, *aṃ*, *attha*, *attho*, and *vho*—the suffixes beginning with *o* optionally replace *eyyātha* and the others respectively. Examples: *tumhe bhaveyyātho*, *bhaveyyātha*; *tvaṃ abhavissa*.

*abhavisse*; *ahaṃ abhavaṃ*, *abhava*; *so abhavittha*, *abhavā*; *so abhavittho*, *abhavī*; *tumhe bhavathavho*, *bhavatha*—the letter *a* is understood here as it was in the preceding examples (*āsahavari*).

However, because it is specified at the end [of the rule], it relates only to the suffixes beginning with *tvā*, or else because that very [suffix] is unrestricted (*nissīta*); for the authors of the Suttas have also intended [this rule] to apply to the formation of nouns (*nissaya*).
*Uṃssiṃsvaṃsu*:
after *umiccassa*, *iṃsu* or *aṃsu* occur; [for example], *agamiṃsu*, *agamaṃsu*, *agamuṃ*.
After *emanta*, *suṃ* occurs.

After *ñā* and *o*, the suffix *umicca* optionally becomes *suṃ*; [examples are] *nesuṃ*, *nayiṃsu*; *assosuṃ*, *assuṃ*. The inclusion of *tta* is for the purpose of indicating that it is a substitute (*ādesatta*).
After *hū*, the suffix *umicca* optionally becomes *resuṃ*; [examples are] *ahesuṃ*, *ahavuṃ*.
*Ossa*: the meaning is "you were.
After *si*, the forms *aādayo* optionally occur: *tvaṃ abhava*, *abhavi*, *abhavittha*, *abhavittho*, *abhavo*.
*Si*.
*Ossa* optionally occurs for *asi*; [for example: *ahosi*, *tvaṃ ahuvo*.
For *ī* following a long vowel, *ssa* optionally occurs; [for example: *akāsi*, *akā*; *adāsi*, *adā*.
The suffix *muṇ* is substituted for the [suffixes] *mha* and *tha*. Thus, there are *agamumhā*, *agamimhā*; *agamuttha*, *agamittha*.
And for the [suffix] *iṃ*, *siṇ* is substituted.
For the suffix *eyya*, there is optionally the substitution of *si* or *mhātthāna*. For *akāsiṃ*, *akariṃ*; *akāsimhā*, *akarimhā*; *akāsittha*, *akarittha*.
For *eyyuṃ*, there is optionally the substitution of *uṃ*. Examples: *gacchuṃ*, *gaccheyyuṃ*.
*Hissato lopo*:

After *ata*, the elision (*lopa*) of the following *hissa* optionally occurs; e.g., *gaccha*, *gacchāhi*. Why say "after *ata*"? [Example: *karohi*. *Kyassa sse*: [The substitution of] *sse* for *kyassa* [occurs].
There is the elision of *ky* before *sse*: *andhabhavissā*, *anvabhuyissā*, *anubhavissati*, *anubhuyissati*.

When *atthi* [is present], for the suffixes beginning with *eyya* and ending with *chana*, *ssu*, *sas*, *tha*, *saṃ*, and *sāma* are substituted respectively after the roots *asa* and *bhū*: *assa*, *assu*, *assa*, *assatha*, *assaṃ*, *assāma*.
*Ādidvīnnamiyāiyuṃ*:
For the two initial [forms] beginning with *atthi*, *iyāsuṃ* and *honti* occur respectively as *siyā* and *siyuṃ*. *Tassatho*: [The suffix] *tha* occurs for that [verb].
After *atthi*, the letter *t* of the following word becomes *th*; thus: *attha*, *atthu*.
[In the rule] *sihisvaṭa-*, *aṭa* is substituted for *atthi* before *si* and *hi*; *ṭ* serves the purpose of indicating a complete replacement (*sabbādesattha*); thus: *asi*, *ahi*.
*Mimānaṃ* or *mhimhā*:

after *atthi*, *paresaṃ*, *mimānaṃ*, or *mhimhā*, there are [the endings] *-taṃ*, *-santi*, *-yena*, *atthi*, *assa*, *aṭa*, *ca*; *amhi*, *asmi*; *amha*, *asma*. In these cases, *sa-* [is substituted].
In these [forms], the letter *s* of *atthi* becomes *sakāra*; [the forms are] *asmi*, *asma*. This is for the purpose of overriding the rule of *pararūpa*.
"A long vowel after *ī* and *ā*":
after *atthi*, a long vowel occurs when followed by *ī* and so on; [the forms are] *āsi*, *āsuṃ*, *āsi*, *āsittha*, *āsiṃ*, *āsimhā*.
*Himimesu assa-*: Before *him* and *me*, the vowel *a* becomes long; [as in] *pavāhi*, *pavāmi*, *pavāma*;
*muyhāmi*. *Sakā ṇāssa kha īādo-*:
After *sak*, the *ṇā* suffix becomes *kha* before vowels beginning with *ī*; [as in] *asakkhi*, *asakkhiṃsu*.
*Sse* or *vā-*:
from *sakam*, it becomes *ssekho vā*; [from *sakkoti*] *sakkhissā*, *sakkuṇissā*; *sakkhissati*, *sakkuṇissati*.
Among those, *suto* [is used] for *keṇa* and *akaṇa* with the suffix *-roṭa-*.
In these [words] ending in -ī, -ā, and -issa, there is the substitution of *ro* for *e*, *o*, and *a* before the suffix *ti*. Thus: *assosi*, *asuṇi*; *assossā*, *asuṇissā*; *sossati*, *suṇissati*.
Regarding the suffixes *-ñā*, *-sanā*, and *-nā*:
the substitution of *nā* occurs optionally for *-ñā* and *-sanā* before the suffix *ti*; hence *nāyati*. [The present form is] *jānāti*.
Regarding *ñamhi jaṃ*:
after the substitution of *ñā* for *sanā*, *jaṃ* optionally occurs for *ñā*; thus, *jaññā* or *jāneyya*.
Regarding *eyyassiyāñā vā*: [the same applies].
The suffix *kan* is optionally elided after *ñāta* when followed by *eyya*, *iyāna*, *jāniyā*, *jaññā*, or *jāneyya*. Regarding the forms beginning with *īsa* and those beginning with *ssa*:
the suffix *kan* is optionally elided after *ñāta* when followed by forms beginning with *ī* or *ssa*; thus, *aññasi* or *ajāni*; *ñassati* or *jānissati*.
For his [own] action—
whether it be known by himself or known by another— he will be recognized, he will become manifest; from this [it follows].
And for this reason, the future endings *ssasi* or *ehi*, and *essati* occur after another [verb].
After the root *han*, the endings *che* or *khā* optionally occur for *ssassa*: *hañchema* or *hanissāma*; *paṭihaṃkhāmi* or *paṭihanissāmi*.
After *hā*, the *s* of the third person singular (*ssa*) becomes *ha* optionally: *hāhati* or *chahissati*.
[In the case of] *dakkha-kha-he-hi-ho-hī-hi*, there is elision (*lopa*).

The elision of the *assa* suffix of the third person plural (*parassa*) optionally occurs after the substitutes *dakkha*, etc.; thus: *dakkhati*, *dakkhissati*; *sakkhati*, *sakkhissati*; *hehiti*, *hehissati*; *hohiti*, *hohissati*.
Regarding *kayireyya*, *asseyyum*, and so forth:
the elision of the *eyya* suffix of *asseyyum*, etc., occurs after *kayira*; thus: *kayiruṃ*, *kayirāsi*, *kayirātha*, *kayirāmi*, *kayirāma*.
One who would do what is beneficial for another becomes one who brings happiness; one who would cause sorrow becomes one who brings grief.
Thus it is said.
*Kayirā* [is used] for *parassa etassa ā hoti*; [it becomes] *kayirātha*.
After *labha*, *iṃ*, *ī*, *ic*, and *esa*, *thaṃ* and *tha* optionally occur: *alatthaṃ*, *alabhiṃ*; *alattha*, *alabhi*.
*Gurupubbā rassā re ntentīnaṃ*:
After a short vowel preceded by a heavy syllable, *re* optionally replaces the endings *-nti* and *-nte*. Examples: *gacchare*, *gacchanti*;

*gacchare*, *gacchante*; *gamissare*, *gamissanti*; *gamissare*, *gamissante*. Why say "preceded by a heavy syllable" (*gurupubbā*)? [Counter-example: *pacanti*. Why say "short vowel" (*rassā*)? [Counter-example: *honti*.
*Eyyeyyāseyyantaṃ te-*: For *eyya*, *eyyā*, and *seyya* endings, *te* optionally occurs;
as in: *so kare*, *so kareyya*; *tvaṃ kare*, *tvaṃ kareyyāsi*; *ahaṃ kare*, *ahaṃ kareyyaṃ*.
In the second half [of this section], for the *o*-vocalization (*ovikaraṇa*), *u* [occurs].
The vowel *u* occurs for the suffix *o* when it falls within the scope of the subsequent group of six [consonants]; as in *tanute*.
Or, in some cases, it occurs within the preceding group of six; as in *vanuti* or *vanoti*.
*Eyyāmassemu ca*:
*eyyāmasse* becomes either *eyyāmasse* or *uca*; [thus] *bhavemu*, *bhaveyyāmu*, *bhaveyyāma*.
Thus ends the sixth section, beginning with the suffixes *ti* and so forth, in the *Vutti* of the *Moggallāna-vyākaraṇa*.
And this *Moggallānavutti* is completed in six recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*).
By the power of that king, the world— though crowded with beings whose minds are developed,
yet entirely undisturbed by wicked monks who have acquired various attainments— remains untroubled.
The teaching of the Sage-King in Laṅkā is well-established,
and through union with Puṇṇavanda, it increases like the ocean;
while that Parakkamabhuja flourishes, endowed with the virtues of faith and wisdom.
While the descendant of Manu, bearing the white parasol, ruled over the island of Laṅkā, this work—
composed by the wise Elder Māggallāna, whose speech is pure,
easy to understand, free from doubt, and unconfused— was written.
The commentary on that *Saddasattha*, which pervades all objects [of knowledge],
relies upon the proclamations of the Jina, is easily mastered without effort,
increases the intellect, and succinctly elucidates its vast meaning—
Furthermore, it was composed by that very same person who illuminates the Teaching.
